entries.title: Avoid quadratic name lookups when loading safetensors with CPU fallback
entries.head: d31250bad01c8fb0d3b0357a976721daa5dd63dd
entries.published_body:
## What does this PR do?

The mixed-device safetensors loader rebuilds the flattened list of assigned weight names for every checkpoint key, then performs a linear membership search. This makes the CPU-fallback name-selection phase quadratic in the number of weights, even for a device map with only two entries.

Build the assigned-name set once, append fallback names in their original order, and release the set before materializing tensors. Existing module-prefix assignment, overlapping entries, disk-to-CPU fallback and single-device fast paths retain their behavior.

## Measured loading improvement

[Successful native before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/accelerate/actions/runs/43415172502), exact source `d31250bad01c8fb0d3b0357a976721daa5dd63dd`, upstream base `3bd795f7cfb763b994b4ba8ba59e5a305a7c528a`.

Full `load_state_dict` calls on real safetensors files, with half the keys assigned to CPU and half to disk. Medians of three warm-cache loads on the same GitHub-hosted CPU runner; normal progress rendering is retained and its stderr is redirected to the null device in both measurements.

| Weights | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 | 5.876 ms | 5.787 ms | 1.02x |
| 4,096 | 242.194 ms | 177.454 ms | 1.36x |
| 32,768 | 5.850 s | 1.485 s | 3.94x |

All output-name/value SHA-256 digests match. The 32,768-weight file is 2,811,696 bytes. This isolates name-heavy checkpoint overhead; it is not a throughput claim for large tensor payloads or GPU loading. The temporary set uses linear additional storage; measured Python peak allocation for that case is 13,015,107 versus 13,043,563 bytes. These tracemalloc numbers are not process RSS or native tensor memory.

## Correctness validation

Python 3.12.16, PyTorch 2.9.0+cpu, safetensors 0.8.0.

- All 26 new tests pass on both unchanged upstream and the fixed source. This is a performance improvement; no numerical failure is claimed for the baseline.
- New tests plus the entire existing `tests/test_modeling_utils.py`: **64 passed, 10 skipped, 4 subtests passed** on both revisions.
- Cases cover mixed CPU/disk maps, missing and overlapping module prefixes, reversed map order, root and absent mappings, single-device controls, FP32/FP64 weights, boolean buffers and empty tensors.
- Real SGD-with-momentum and AdamW checkpoints resume after two updates. Losses, parameter gradients, weights and optimizer state match uninterrupted training exactly for three further updates.
- Project-pinned Ruff 0.13.1 lint/format and `git diff --check` pass.

GPU execution, end-to-end disk-offloaded model inference and the full repository suite were not run.

## Prior work checked

All-state issue/PR searches, the complete 175-commit history of the affected file, and all seven existing non-validation fork branch heads were checked. #1121 introduced the fallback expression; #1321 deduplicated the device list, #1557 corrected the single-device shortcut, #1853 changed checkpoint file discovery and #3674 optimized tensor transfers. None changes this repeated fallback membership work.

## Before submitting

- [x] Read the contributor guideline and searched existing work.
- [ ] Prior issue discussion: this isolated performance change was not proposed in an issue.
- [x] Added necessary correctness and resumed-training tests.
- [x] No API or documented loading behavior changes; benchmark method and limits are described above.

entries.title: Honor direct tensor offload entries on split modules
entries.head: dc6600f6dc7fbc2b9536072ff802663df6ce74e3
entries.published_body:
# What does this PR do?

Honor direct parameter and buffer entries in split-module device maps during CPU/disk dispatch.

A map such as `{"parent.child": "cpu", "first": "disk", "parent.weight": "disk"}` is accepted for coverage, but hook installation only visits module names. The direct `parent.weight` entry therefore receives no offload hook and stays resident. This is the runtime limitation reproduced in the [follow-up on #4531](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/pull/4531#issuecomment-6834185084).

Add a tensor-name filter to `AlignDevicesHook`, and attach filtered hooks to a split parent's direct tensors when it has individual tensor entries instead of a module-level entry. Group direct tensors by execution device and offload policy while leaving separately placed children to their own hooks. Accept registered parameter/buffer names in device-map validation.

Ordinary module-level maps keep the existing path. The verified case is CPU/disk offload with a common execution device; this does not claim support for running one operation with its weight and bias on different accelerators.

## Validation

[Native before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/accelerate/actions/runs/43415810211), Python 3.12 and official PyTorch 2.9.0 CPU:

- Original source: 19 failures and 3 passing controls.
- Patched source: all 22 new cases pass.
- Existing hooks, offload, and map-validation tests: 19 pass, 4 skips.
- Ruff checks and formatting pass.

For the 908-byte model in the linked report, live CPU parameter storage during repeated forwards changes from 908 bytes to **108 bytes in the first layer and 808 bytes in the parent**, within the 850-byte budget, with matching outputs. These are live tensor-storage measurements, not RSS or GPU memory measurements.

The tests also train small models with real SGD before checkpointing, load them into meta-initialized models, and compare repeated inference against the trained reference. Coverage includes root/nested direct tensors, float32/float64, resident bias alongside offloaded weights, optional buffer offload, tied weights, unchanged whole-module maps, hook removal, and recovery by removing hooks after a forward exception.

## Before submitting

- [x] Read the contributor guideline.
- [x] Documented the hook's optional tensor filter.
- [x] Added native disk/checkpoint and live-storage regressions.
- [x] Verified relevant existing tests.

entries.title: Preserve all model parameters when preparing multiple models on XLA
entries.head: 04023a70f672c058cf0f3a9128550e38b80780a9
entries.published_body:
## Summary

Preparing multiple models on XLA can silently leave an optimizer attached to the original CPU parameters. `_get_named_parameters` combines all model parameters in a dictionary keyed only by names such as `weight` and `bias`. A later model overwrites the earlier entries. When XLA device placement replaces the parameters, the replacement map therefore contains only the last model's parameters.

A native PyTorch/XLA CPU reproduction with two Linear models shows the first model on `xla:0` while its optimizer still owns CPU parameters. Its forward and backward produce a loss and nonzero gradients, but `optimizer.step()` does not update that model.

Prefix parameter-map keys with the argument position when multiple models are present. Both the object and `drop_refs=True` paths use the same keys, and a single model retains its existing names. The ordered arguments and prepared results therefore identify every model independently.

## Validation

[Native before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/accelerate/actions/runs/43408741278), exact source `04023a70f672c058cf0f3a9128550e38b80780a9`, upstream base `3bd795f7cfb763b994b4ba8ba59e5a305a7c528a`.

- PyTorch 2.9.0+cpu, Python 3.12.16; the XLA job also installs the real PyTorch/XLA 2.9.0 runtime and uses `PJRT_DEVICE=CPU`.
- The same 28 new tests on XLA CPU: upstream **20 failed / 8 passed**; fixed **28 passed**, with no skipped tests or collection errors.
- Twelve native XLA training cases cover one, two and three models; separate and joint optimizers; interleaved model/optimizer arguments; SGD with momentum and AdamW. Every loss, parameter gradient, updated parameter and optimizer state matches an independent native XLA reference exactly for three updates.
- Parameter-map cases cover both reference and address modes, repeated names, empty modules and unchanged single-model names.
- The ordinary CPU job passes all **16 applicable new tests** and skips the 12 XLA cases. Its unchanged-base result is **10 failed / 6 passed / 12 skipped**.
- The existing `tests/test_optimizer.py` module passes its applicable test in both jobs, with one backend-specific skip in each.
- Project-pinned Ruff 0.13.1 lint/format and `git diff --check` pass.

```bash
PJRT_DEVICE=CPU python -m pytest -q tests/test_multiple_model_parameters.py
python -m pytest -q tests/test_optimizer.py
```

This validates the actual XLA CPU backend. TPU hardware, tensor-parallel execution, FSDP and the full repository suite were not run.

## Prior work checked

I checked all-state issue/PR searches, the affected file's 434-commit history and the existing fork branches. The original TPU optimizer-transfer implementation, #3394's address-based FSDP2 mapping, #3845's tensor-parallel name/accessor changes and #3052's separate modeling utility do not namespace multiple model arguments. Existing proposals about optimizer-state transfer, shared tensor storage and checkpoint aliases address different paths.

entries.title: Avoid retaining full batches in the dispatcher padding cache
entries.head: a95ee5bdda6c74e93e59878a5e5e5db69d554950
entries.published_body:
## What does this PR do?

`DataLoaderDispatcher` keeps a prefix of the first dispatched batch to pad the last batch. The default tensor slicing returns views, so this small prefix retains the storage of the entire first global batch for the rest of the iterator's lifetime.

Clone the tensor leaves of that cached prefix after calling the configured slice function. This releases the full first batch once its consumer and the iterator have moved on. The usual yielded batches, custom slicing behavior, and `drop_last=True` path retain their existing behavior.

## Measured storage reduction

[Native before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/accelerate/actions/runs/43421394225), exact source `a95ee5bdda6c74e93e59878a5e5e5db69d554950` on current upstream `f5cc53877677eb7fa0ef7091fe41536a777fee6a`:

A real dispatcher with 256 samples per batch and 2,048 FP32 features per sample caches one sample on a single CPU process. After advancing to the second batch, the padding cache's actual tensor storage changes from **2,097,152 bytes to 8,192 bytes**, while its logical contents stay 8,192 bytes.

This measures the live cache's tensor storage, not process RSS or GPU peak memory. The change adds one prefix-sized clone per iterator when padding is enabled.

## Correctness validation

Python 3.12, official PyTorch 2.9.0+cpu:

- Unchanged source: 12 storage-lifetime regressions fail; 20 controls/training cases pass.
- Fixed source: all 32 new cases pass.
- The entire existing `tests/test_data_loader.py`: 39 pass, 1 conditional skip.
- Weak-reference tests check that the original first batch is released for tensor, nested mapping, and namedtuple batches, both split modes, and FP32/FP64. The no-padding controls pass before and after.
- Eight real two-process Gloo DDP runs cover split/unsplit dispatch, SGD with momentum and AdamW, and FP32/FP64. All gradients, updated parameters, and optimizer state match an independent global-batch reference for three updates, including a padded tail and in-place input normalization. Gathered metric samples are exactly the nine original examples, and final parameters agree between ranks.
- Ruff check, Ruff format, and diff whitespace checks pass.

## Prior work checked

All-state issue/PR searches, all 126 commits touching `data_loader.py`, and the existing author PRs were checked. #1846 introduces custom dispatch slicing; #4374 handles empty/undersized dispatch; #4507 and #4509 address sampler-owned index-list mutation. Their actual patches do not release the dispatcher's cached tensor-view storage.

entries.title: Include direct parameters in maximum layer memory reservations
entries.head: afff12fe664b31fea12a049a4580ed7d9aecd583
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`get_max_layer_size` descends into child modules but skips parameters directly owned by a parent that has children. In addition, the three reservation recalculations in `infer_auto_device_map` discard pending `Parameter`/`Tensor` entries. The reserved space can therefore be smaller than the next weight that needs to return from offload.

For a 908-byte model containing a 100-byte linear layer, a parent's 800-byte direct parameter and an 8-byte child, `calculate_maximum_sizes` reports a largest layer of only 100 bytes. With a CPU budget of 850 bytes, the original planner assigns the 100-byte layer to CPU and the 800-byte parameter to disk. Those planned placements require 100 + 800 = 900 bytes for the resident layer and pending parameter together, exceeding the requested planning budget.

## Changes

- Include direct parameters when descending into a splittable module, matching the units used by the existing device-map splitting logic.
- Retain tensor entries when recomputing the largest pending layer after allocation or splitting.
- Add native CPU/meta coverage for nested parameters, float32/float64 sizing, no-split classes, equal maxima, leaf modules, fallback allocation and root parameters/buffers.
- Correct the existing tied-partner split test's memory budget to 8704 bytes: 512 resident bytes plus the 8192-byte offloaded parameter. The complete model still needs 8832 bytes, so this preserves the split and tied-placement assertions. The original 4096-byte fixture could only satisfy its placement assertion because the 8192-byte parameter was omitted from the reservation.

## Validation

Base: `f47439c1fb24721ea71ab98f9b512726b5a97828`.

- Identical 30 new cases on unchanged main: **17 failed, 13 passed**. With the fix: **30 passed**.
- New cases plus all 11 existing size/device-map tests selected below: **41 passed**.
- The final test files, including the corrected tied-partner budget, were also run against unchanged main: **17 failed, 24 passed**. All 11 existing selected cases still pass on the original implementation.
- Tests calculate planned resident tensor bytes from the returned `device_map` and require room for the known 800-byte pending parameter, alongside exact hand-calculated maximum sizes and controls where the complete model fits. These assertions check planner arithmetic, not live storage after dispatch.
- Ruff lint/format checks and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_max_layer_direct_parameters.py tests/test_modeling_utils.py \
  -k '(test_maximum_size or test_no_split_parent or test_equal_parent or test_larger_leaf or test_parent_parameter or test_recomputed_reservation or compute_module_sizes or infer_auto_device_map) and not t0pp' -q
```

Linux, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. This validates actual CPU/meta model-size and device-map computation. GPU execution, checkpoint dispatch and the full repository suite were not run; the downloaded T0++ test was excluded.

## Scope and downstream dispatch limitation

This PR corrects maximum-layer sizing and the planner's reservation arithmetic. It does not change `dispatch_model` or its offload hooks; a planned direct-parameter placement does not by itself establish a runtime memory guarantee.

[JonnyFaeth's independent CPU/disk integration check](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/pull/4531#issuecomment-6834185084) on `afff12fe` reports that `dispatch_model` ignores the `parent.weight` entry as a non-submodule. Live CPU parameter storage reaches 908 bytes for an 850-byte budget, while the exact-parent control also exceeds that budget at 900 bytes. Numerical outputs still match the reference. These are forward-time tensor-storage counts, not RSS measurements or GPU OOM evidence. That direct-parameter dispatch limitation needs a separate follow-up; the sizing fix does not claim to resolve it.

## Before submitting

- [x] Read the contributor guidance and searched existing issues/PRs.
- [x] Updated the layer-definition docstring.
- [x] Added necessary regression tests and ran related existing tests.

Related patches #4344 (tied-parameter lookup), #4404 (nested buffer splitting), #3244 (balanced-memory distribution) and #3066 (fallback allocation) were checked for overlap. This change addresses maximum-layer sizing and reservation recalculation.

entries.title: Reserve balanced memory for the largest instance of each no-split class
entries.head: c100d247a46ab16429e58ff654fa641a4addc8f2
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`get_balanced_memory` records only the first instance of each `no_split_module_classes` class and stops once every class name has appeared. Instances of the same residual-block class can have different parameter sizes. A later, larger instance is then omitted from the buffer calculation, making the planned memory cap depend on module order and causing unnecessary CPU offload.

## Change

Keep the maximum size seen for each requested no-split class and inspect all instances. The existing mean-layer buffer, multiplier, memory ceilings, dtype accounting and low-zero policy remain in place.

A native regression uses four residual blocks of 64, 1,024, 1,024 and 64 bytes. With device budgets of 2,112 and 1,500 bytes, the original balanced cap is 1,428 bytes on the first device and the actual device-map planner offloads a block to CPU. The corrected cap allows the planner to place all four blocks on the two specified devices, with every parameter accounted for and both physical budgets respected.

## Validation

Exact source commit: `c100d247a46ab16429e58ff654fa641a4addc8f2`; original main: `f47439c1fb24721ea71ab98f9b512726b5a97828`.

[Successful native CPU/meta validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/accelerate/actions/runs/43308308588), Python 3.12.16 / PyTorch 2.9.1+cpu:

- Same 30 new regressions on unchanged main: **22 failed, 8 passed**.
- Fixed source: **30 new tests passed**.
- The entire existing `tests/test_modeling_utils.py` file: **38 passed, 10 skipped, 4 subtests passed** on both base and fixed source.
- New cases cover differently sized instances in multiple orders, multiple no-split classes, list/set/string inputs, planned FP16 and special FP64 dtypes, equal-sized and absent-class controls, low-zero budgets, non-contiguous device IDs, and the real `infer_auto_device_map` result.
- The mapping regression verifies complete parameter coverage, no split within residual blocks, no CPU/disk allocation and exact per-device parameter byte totals.
- Project-pinned Ruff 0.13.1 lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

The planner is executed with actual CPU/meta modules and explicit accelerator memory budgets; no accelerator availability is mocked. Actual GPU loading/execution, GPU peak memory and the full repository suite were not tested. Computing the buffer now visits all relevant size entries during planning.

## Prior work checked

I catalogued the complete 175-commit history of `modeling.py`, read the relevant original and later patches including #534, #583, #3244, #3776 and #4048, searched all-state balanced/no-split/buffer PRs, and checked all existing author PRs and fork branches. The largest-leaf proposal in #3244 changes a different part of the budget calculation and does not inspect later same-class no-split blocks.

entries.title: Delegate native optimizer hooks to the wrapped optimizer
entries.head: 53946e5cd4b5615ab9c9f8a10a141939f90dcd89
entries.published_body:
## Problem

An optimizer returned by `Accelerator.prepare()` inherits PyTorch's optimizer-hook registration API, but never initializes the hook registries that those inherited methods expect. All six registration methods raise `AttributeError`, preventing step hooks for gradient transforms or post-update bookkeeping and hooks used to customize checkpoint serialization/restoration.

## Changes

Delegate the six native hook-registration methods to the underlying optimizer, just as `state_dict`, `load_state_dict` and the actual update are delegated. Preserve native removable handles, `prepend` ordering and hook return values. Callbacks receive the underlying optimizer. Step hooks fire only for actual optimizer steps, so accumulation substeps and GradScaler overflow skips do not trigger them.

## Validation

Base: `f47439c1fb24721ea71ab98f9b512726b5a97828`.

- Identical 19 new native tests against unchanged main: **18 failed, 1 passed**. With the fix: **19 passed**.
- New tests plus existing optimizer tests: **20 passed, 1 skipped**. The existing GPU FP16 test is skipped on this CPU workspace.
- Real SGD and Adam trajectories match an independent unwrapped reference across accumulation factors 1, 2 and 3 with a hook that transforms gradients.
- Closure replacement, pre/post ordering, `prepend`, returned replacement dictionaries, native callback ownership and handle removal are exercised.
- `torch.save`/`torch.load` restores actual Adam moments and reproduces two subsequent updates. `Accelerator.save_state`/`load_state` also round-trips the model, optimizer moments and parameter-group learning rate through custom serialization hooks.
- A native CPU `torch.amp.GradScaler` skips an overflowing update; step hooks run exactly twice for the two successful updates.
- All repository pre-commit hooks applicable to the changed files and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_optimizer_hooks.py tests/test_optimizer.py -q
pre-commit run --files src/accelerate/optimizer.py tests/test_optimizer_hooks.py
```

Linux, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. GPU/XLA/FSDP execution and the full repository suite were not run. Existing optimizer-step return behavior and AMP exception handling are unchanged.

Full optimizer history, all-state issue/PR searches and all four existing user-fork branch heads were checked. The actual optimizer changes in #4246 add a different callback API and do not fix native hook registration.

entries.title: fix(fingerprint): resolve lazy tensor views before hashing
entries.head: a3effe550054d8487b831f31992bb6695847ff04
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The Torch tensor reducer calls `.numpy()` directly after detaching and moving the tensor to CPU. PyTorch rejects that conversion for views with a lazy conjugate or negative bit, including tensors returned by `tensor.conj()` and `tensor.conj().imag`. When a map transform captures such a tensor, fingerprinting falls back to a random value, so an unchanged transform recomputes the dataset instead of reusing its existing Arrow cache.

## Change

Resolve the detached tensor's conjugate and negative view bits before the existing NumPy conversion. Preserve the original object passed to `save_reduce`, so repeated references still share their reconstructed tensor. Keep the existing BF16 conversion and ordinary tensor paths.

## Validation

- 14 new native tests report **10 failed, 4 passed** on upstream, and **14 passed** after the change.
- Including the existing Torch tensor and generator fingerprint tests, **16 passed**.
- Tests cover complex64/complex128, strided views, exact logical values, pickle alias preservation, unchanged input storage/flags/gradient state, and ordinary int64/float32/BF16/complex128 controls.
- Real on-disk datasets exercise `Dataset.map` twice with a view captured by the transform: the second call reuses the same cache file and does not execute the transform again. Changing the underlying tensor values correctly changes the fingerprint and reruns the transform.
- Ruff checks, Ruff formatting checks and `git diff --check` pass.

This change is limited to CPU-tested dense tensor view serialization; it does not add sparse or quantized tensor serialization.

entries.title: fix(csv): honor parser modes that cannot iterate chunks
entries.head: 5e7b9d0dcb4327099f3f1cd6e42af7c11771f723
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The CSV builder always passes `iterator=True` and `chunksize` to pandas. This makes two existing configuration options unusable: `engine="pyarrow"` rejects the iterator argument, and `skipfooter` is unsupported by pandas' incremental reader. Both fail before yielding any training examples, including through `Dataset.from_csv` and streaming `load_dataset`.

## Change

For these two parser modes, read each file with pandas without iterator/chunksize options, then slice the resulting DataFrame into the requested Arrow batch sizes. Preserve a schema-bearing empty table for header-only inputs. Keep the existing incremental path for the default, C and ordinary Python parser modes, and keep pandas' error when an explicitly selected engine cannot parse the requested footer.

These parser modes necessarily materialize each input file in pandas before yielding Arrow batches; selecting the streaming Dataset API does not make their per-file parsing memory-bounded. Existing incremental modes retain their behavior.

## Validation

- 25 new native tests: **21 failed, 4 passed** on the upstream implementation; all 25 pass after the fix.
- New tests and the complete existing CSV module: **39 passed**. The 8 warnings are pandas' normal notice when it automatically selects the Python engine for `skipfooter`.
- Tests cover PyArrow, explicit and inferred Python footer handling; batch sizes 1, 2 and `None`; UTF-8 text; typed `Dataset.from_csv`; actual streaming `load_dataset`; header-only input; multiple files; and unchanged ordinary parser behavior.
- Ruff checks, Ruff formatting checks and `git diff --check` pass.

entries.title: fix(features): allow necessary copies in pandas array construction
entries.head: 2d73e5a4f38af00b57467eb7ae75a13e51140926
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Pandas extension-array construction uses `copy=False` to avoid unnecessary copies, but `PandasArrayExtensionArray._from_sequence` passes that flag to NumPy's strict no-copy constructor. On NumPy 2, constructing an ArrayXD pandas column from separate ndarray rows raises `ValueError: Unable to avoid copy while creating an array as requested`. Converting a contiguous input to a different requested payload dtype fails for the same reason.

## Change

Use `np.asarray` for the initial dense conversion so necessary stacking or dtype conversion is allowed. The existing final `cls(data, copy=copy)` still enforces an independent buffer when `copy=True`; same-dtype ndarray inputs can continue sharing storage when `copy=False`.

## Validation

- Added 17 tests for 2D/3D payloads, int32/float64, both copy settings, dtype conversion, contiguous and strided input storage, and existing empty/singleton/ragged behavior.
- The dense-row cases exercise `pd.array` to `DataFrame` to `Dataset.from_pandas` and verify exact reconstructed values.
- Unchanged upstream: **5 failed, 12 passed**.
- Fixed implementation with all 106 existing ArrayXD tests: **123 passed**.
- Ruff lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

This changes pandas sequence construction; NumPy's external `__array__` protocol is unchanged.

entries.title: fix(stratify): avoid overflowing class-count products
entries.head: b09aed557466e80782d09064974364343b37dd2b
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`approximate_mode` multiplies the integer class counts by the number of requested draws before converting the result to proportions. That intermediate product can overflow even when the individual counts, their sum, and the requested sample size are all valid int64 values. For example, counts `[4_000_000_000, 6_000_000_000]` and 8,000,000,000 draws currently produce `[-489348814, -734023222]` instead of `[3200000000, 4800000000]`.

## Change

Compute class proportions before multiplying by the number of draws. This matches the arithmetic order used by scikit-learn's corresponding allocation routine and keeps the existing floor, remainder ranking, and random tie-breaking logic.

## Validation

- Added 17 tests: six large-count cases compare int64/uint64 inputs against an independent exact `Fraction` allocation, eight small-count cases cover zero/full draws and the random stream after ties, one compares three complete splits with scikit-learn, and two exercise `Dataset.train_test_split` with real `ClassLabel` features.
- Unchanged upstream: **6 failed, 11 passed**.
- Fixed implementation, including both existing stratified Dataset tests: **19 passed**.
- Ruff lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

The large-count cases use small count vectors; they do not materialize or benchmark a billion-row dataset. This change prevents the intermediate integer product overflow and does not extend the range of the count sum or float64 precision.

entries.title: fix(parallel): restore outer backend contexts
entries.head: e8a958509998951cf92f4f232c0ef51072708d83
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Exiting an inner `parallel_backend` context always resets the selected backend to `None`, even when an outer backend context is still active. Subsequent operations inside the outer context silently use the default multiprocessing path. For example, a local callable that works with joblib's threading backend then fails to pickle after a nested context exits. Spark backend registration also happens before the `try/finally`, so a failed optional dependency import leaves the global selection changed.

## Changes

Save the previous backend and restore it when the context exits. Include Spark import and registration in the protected region so setup failures restore the outer selection as well. The backend configuration remains global; this change addresses nested context restoration, not concurrent thread isolation.

## Validation

- Added 14 native tests covering nested threading/sequential contexts, normal and exceptional exits, top-level controls, joblib backend validation errors, and the actual missing optional Spark dependency path.
- The new tests fail 10 cases and pass 4 on the unchanged upstream revision.
- With this change, the new tests and 37 existing `map_nested` cases pass: **51 passed**.
- The nested tests execute real `map_nested` calls with local closures before, during, and after the inner context.
- Ruff lint, Ruff formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

entries.title: fix(parallel): handle worker sentinels in automatic batching
entries.head: 0b87e2e5eabebe00b6e8951714aa00c648eac805
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`map_nested(..., batched=True, batch_size=None)` uses `num_proc` as a divisor when choosing the batch size. The existing serial sentinel `num_proc=0` therefore raises `ZeroDivisionError`, and joblib's `num_proc=-1` produces a negative batch size and raises `ValueError`. Nonpositive `batch_size` values have the same failure because they use this automatic path.

## Change

Use a positive count only for batch-size arithmetic while passing the original worker argument to the execution backend. For nonpositive worker arguments, the automatic batch contains the whole iterable, consistent with the documented full-batch setting. Positive worker counts and explicit positive batch sizes retain their existing boundaries.

## Validation

- Added 25 native tests for serial/threading/sequential execution, `None`/zero/negative automatic batch settings, empty and singleton inputs, nested training/validation inputs, positive worker batch boundaries, and explicit-batch controls.
- Unchanged upstream: **16 failed, 9 passed**.
- Fixed implementation and related existing mapping tests: **72 passed, 27 deselected**.
- Tests execute the real joblib backend and inspect actual batch contents; input data remains unchanged.
- Ruff lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

This fixes batch-size selection; it does not add negative-worker support to the default multiprocessing backend or change joblib's worker selection.

entries.title: perf(json): avoid shifting the schema traversal queue
entries.head: acc7c9a5e52bfd9ce34c32cd8fa9dad65f977217
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`find_mixed_struct_types_field_paths` uses a list as a breadth-first queue. Removing its first element with `pop(0)` shifts all remaining entries on every visit, adding quadratic queue-management work for wide JSON records.

## Changes

Use `collections.deque` and `popleft()` for the pending paths. The traversal order, detected paths, and input ownership stay the same.

## Validation

- Added 14 semantic controls for null/empty inputs, root handling, mixed nested values, literal field names, wide nested schemas, and native `Dataset.from_json` / streaming JSON loading. All 14 pass on both the upstream code and this change; this is a performance change.
- With the existing JSON parser module: **47 passed, 11 skipped**. The skipped cases require the optional `teich` dependency.
- Ruff lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

A local CPU benchmark builds inputs before timing, performs one warmup and five measured scans, and compares the resulting paths by SHA-256. Every output hash matches:

| Input | Before median | After median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1,000 flat fields | 0.785 ms | 0.801 ms |
| 10,000 flat fields | 11.444 ms | 9.409 ms |
| 50,000 flat fields | 206.961 ms | 130.515 ms |
| 10,000 nested fields | 49.440 ms | 45.665 ms |

The benefit is reduced queue overhead on wide inputs. The small case did not improve, and these measurements do not establish end-to-end dataset loading or training throughput.

entries.title: fix(features): recognize NumPy scalar indices in pandas arrays
entries.head: 546f58efcf57a76dc84ff557ccd58235d9097ec3
entries.published_body:
## Problem

An ArrayXD column converted to pandas treats a NumPy integer index as a nonscalar selection. `series.iloc[np.int64(1)]` and `series.iat[np.int64(1)]` return a `PandasArrayExtensionArray` wrapping the row instead of the row's ndarray. This loses the expected scalar shape/type and breaks downstream operations such as converting an embedding selected by `np.argmax` into a torch tensor.

## Change

Recognize NumPy integer scalars alongside Python integers in the extension array's scalar indexing branch. Slices, index arrays, and boolean masks keep the existing extension-array return path; no new production copy is introduced.

## Validation

- Added 26 cases covering native Dataset-to-pandas Array2D–Array5D columns, multiple payload dtypes, signed/unsigned NumPy indices, Python integers, negative indices, dynamic and empty row shapes, nonscalar selection controls, and out-of-bounds errors.
- An end-to-end case selects an embedding with `np.argmax`, converts a writable copy of that row with `torch.from_numpy`, and checks a hand-calculated projection.
- Unchanged upstream: **16 failed, 10 passed**.
- Fixed implementation plus all 106 existing ArrayXD tests: **132 passed**.
- Ruff lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

entries.title: fix(features): normalize non-native NumPy byte order
entries.head: db27ef286c5351924e4ae3a40c880e2fbdfacc36
entries.published_body:
## Problem

NumPy arrays can retain a non-native byte order after loading an NPY file or reading external binary data. The NumPy-to-Arrow conversion passes that dtype directly to Arrow, which raises `ArrowNotImplementedError: Byte-swapped arrays not supported`. This affects inferred scalar columns and multidimensional ArrayXD inputs, including read-only memory-mapped arrays.

## Changes

Normalize non-native NumPy dtypes to native byte order with a value-preserving `astype` before Arrow conversion. This changes the byte representation rather than relabeling the existing bytes. Native-order inputs keep the existing path, and the input array is never modified.

## Validation

- Added 42 cases covering signed/unsigned integers, float32/64, inferred and declared scalar features, Array2D through Array5D, reversed/strided/Fortran/read-only layouts, empty arrays, ragged Arrow storage, and ordinary Python-list controls.
- Native NPY integration opens a non-native file with `mmap_mode='r'`, builds a dataset, saves and reloads it, and checks exact feature values and a numeric projection. The source file remains byte-for-byte unchanged.
- Final regressions on unchanged upstream: **19 failed, 23 passed**.
- New tests plus the existing ArrayXD module: **148 passed**.
- Ruff lint, Ruff formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

The existing declared-uint64 overflow above int64 range and the ragged-null Python read path are separate issues; this change does not alter those paths. Full-range uint64 coverage here uses the inferred NumPy path, and the ragged-null check verifies the resulting Arrow storage.

entries.title: perf(batch): reduce grouping comparisons inside Arrow
entries.head: 7d1dd9bf999d56452449059f0b59b4c31edbde32
entries.published_body:
## Problem

When a `batch(by_column=...)` group spans input tables, the accumulation check converts an entire Arrow comparison column to a Python list just to call `any()`. This creates a temporary Python pointer for every input row, even though only one boolean result is needed.

## Changes

Reduce the existing null-aware comparisons with `pyarrow.compute.any` and convert only the scalar result to Python. Group boundaries, null semantics, accumulation, and output values stay the same.

## Validation

- Added 22 tests covering native `Dataset` and `IterableDataset` grouping, multiple keys, nullable/all-null columns, NaN keys, chunked Arrow columns, and Python allocation limits for long identical groups.
- On unchanged upstream: **20 passed, 2 failed**. The two failures are allocation-budget regressions; the numerical grouping controls already pass.
- With this change and the existing `batch_by_column` tests: **33 passed**.
- Ruff lint, Ruff formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

Local CPU measurements use preconstructed tables, one warmup, and five measured repetitions:

| Accumulated comparison rows | Before median | After median | Before Python peak | After Python peak |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1,000 | 0.036 ms | 0.030 ms | 17,064 B | 1,375 B |
| 100,000 | 0.552 ms | 0.065 ms | 1,601,192 B | 1,375 B |
| 1,000,000 | 5.011 ms | 0.337 ms | 16,448,936 B | 1,375 B |

A separate native `Dataset.batch` benchmark with 200,000 rows and 1,000-row input batches measured 14.042 ms before and 13.796 ms after, with identical serialized Arrow output hashes. That small end-to-end difference should not be read as a general throughput improvement. The substantial measured benefit is removal of the temporary Python comparison list, especially with larger input batches. Arrow's own comparison buffers are still needed and are outside the Python allocation figures.

entries.title: fix(unigram): apply sampling temperature once per token score
entries.head: 691dabb68ff22c5df5d414d49bbf90dcdfebd5f1
entries.published_body:
The full-lattice Unigram sampler multiplies the accumulated forward log weight by `theta` again at every node. Earlier token scores therefore receive extra temperature factors depending on path depth, although backward sampling uses `alpha[previous] + theta * token_score`.

Apply the temperature only to the current token score. The accumulated forward value already contains the scaled scores for every preceding path.

For a vocabulary where `a`, `aa`, `aaa`, and `aaaa` score -10, -20, -30, and -40, all eight segmentations of `aaaa` have total score -40 and must be equally likely at any temperature. The unchanged implementation assigns some paths frequencies near 0.1% instead of 12.5% when `alpha=0.5`.

Native Rust regression coverage includes this independently enumerated path distribution at alpha 0.1, 0.5 and 1, deterministic/empty controls, and low-score encoding through the actual `PipelineTokenizer` across repeated calls.

Validation at exact commit `691dabb68ff22c5df5d414d49bbf90dcdfebd5f1` on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:
- New regressions: 6 passed; restoring the upstream `lattice.rs` produces 2 failures and 4 passes.
- Existing Unigram unit tests: 20 passed.
- Rustfmt passed. Clippy with warnings denied reports the same two pre-existing `needless_range_loop` diagnostics on the original and patched sources (`word_cache.rs:147` and `lattice.rs:379`); this patch does not change those loops.

[Native baseline/patched run and logs](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43279871521). The workflow is on a separate validation branch. This change is limited to full-lattice sampling; `sample_nbest` is unchanged.

entries.title: fix(ctc): decode word boundaries with cleanup disabled
entries.head: 01e9c587e2acf292d5b5895d70ae8fa6a64deae2
entries.published_body:
`CTC` currently leaves word-delimiter tokens in decoded speech when `cleanup=false`. With `<pad>` as the blank and `|` as the delimiter, frame predictions `a a <pad> a | | b b <pad> b` decode to `aa|bb` instead of `aa bb`.

Move delimiter replacement outside the optional WordPiece punctuation cleanup. Repetition collapse and blank removal keep their ordering, and the cleanup-enabled path is unchanged.

The regression loads a complete canonical tokenizer JSON and uses `PipelineTokenizer::decode`. It covers custom and Unicode delimiters, Unicode words, punctuation with cleanup on/off, blank-separated repeats, and empty input.

Validation on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu with native Rust/Cargo, against exact patch commit `01e9c587e2acf292d5b5895d70ae8fa6a64deae2`:
- New integration tests: 4 passed; restoring the upstream decoder produces 3 failures and 1 pass.
- Existing CTC tests: 4 passed.
- Rustfmt and focused Clippy with warnings denied passed.

[Reproducible validation run](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43276644121). The validation workflow is isolated on a separate fork branch; it is not part of this PR.

entries.title: fix(unigram): normalize n-best weights before exponentiation
entries.head: 669dd2c81f7bcbc4458d0bcb927e209f549868d3
entries.published_body:
The n-best Unigram sampler exponentiates each complete path score directly. A sufficiently negative score shared by every candidate can underflow all weights to zero. `WeightedIndex` then fails and the existing fallback always returns the first path, although the relative path probabilities remain well defined.

Subtract the maximum log weight before exponentiation. This preserves every relative weight for finite scores and ensures that at least one candidate has weight one. The full-lattice sampling recurrence is unchanged.

The regression tests use a common prefix with scores 0, -2000 and -10000. Equal-score suffix paths must remain equiprobable regardless of this shared offset; unequal suffix scores are checked against an independently calculated logistic probability. Further tests exercise a canonical JSON tokenizer through the real `PipelineTokenizer`, as well as empty, single-candidate and zero-temperature controls.

Validation at exact commit `669dd2c81f7bcbc4458d0bcb927e209f549868d3` on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:
- New regressions: 4 passed. Restoring the upstream `lattice.rs` produces 3 failures and 1 pass.
- Existing Unigram unit tests: 20 passed.
- Rustfmt passed. Clippy with warnings denied reports the same two pre-existing `needless_range_loop` diagnostics on the original and patched sources (`word_cache.rs:147` and `lattice.rs:379`); this patch does not alter those loops.

[Native baseline/patched run and logs](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43280293002). The validation workflow is on a separate branch and is not part of this pull request.

entries.title: fix(split): preserve native mode when cloning pre-tokenizers
entries.head: 41c63e663873e0735beef74899520375a1886bb8
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Cloning a Split created for a native pre-tokenizer composition reconstructs it through Split::new. For DeepSeek's native composition, the component regexes are intentionally accepted without a general regex backend. A clone therefore panics in a build without fancy-regex. When fancy-regex is enabled, cloning an explicitly native Split instead silently switches its search implementation.

## Change

Reconstruct Search::Unavailable through Split::native. Literal and compiled-regex splits retain their existing construction path.

## Validation

Native Rust tests ran on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu against commit 41c63e663873e0735beef74899520375a1886bb8 in [this workflow](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43286040092):

- Without fancy-regex: the new tests fail 3 / pass 2 on unchanged upstream, then all 5 pass with the patch. The existing Split test also passes.
- With fancy-regex: the new tests fail 2 / pass 4 on upstream, then all 6 pass. The 3 existing Split tests pass.
- Tests include loading canonical DeepSeek JSON, cloning its actual pre-tokenizer, and constructing a usable PipelineTokenizer, plus Unicode literal, native-error, and compiled-regex controls.
- Rustfmt passes for the changed files.
- Strict Clippy is blocked in both upstream and patched builds by the same existing needless_range_loop diagnostic in word_cache.rs. The workflow checks that the diagnostic lists match; this is not a claim that strict Clippy passes.

The validation workflow lives on a separate fork branch and is not part of this PR.

entries.title: fix(unigram): widen aggregate training frequency counters
entries.head: c8101b0e09c53550c3aa3f4b9189fe878e82b182
entries.published_body:
Unigram training accepts a u32 count for each distinct word, but its character-frequency accumulator and total corpus-frequency accumulator are also u32. Valid per-word counts can overflow these aggregates. For example, "aa" occurring 3,000,000,000 times contributes 6,000,000,000 occurrences of "a"; a corpus containing several independently valid word counts can also exceed u32::MAX.

Accumulate these two quantities in u64 and convert to f64 at the existing probability calculations. The per-word input and serialized trainer types remain unchanged. This keeps weighted seed probabilities and the E-step normalization denominator valid without expanding the counted corpus.

The native regression suite checks hand-calculated seed probabilities, the weighted log-likelihood objective and expected counts, actual training from counted words, trainer serialization, Unicode characters, and equivalence to a small expanded corpus.

Validation at exact commit `c8101b0e09c53550c3aa3f4b9189fe878e82b182` on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:
- New regression tests: 6 passed. The original production source with the same test module gives 3 failures and 3 passes.
- Existing Unigram trainer tests: 5 passed.
- Rustfmt passed. Strict Clippy reports the same two pre-existing needless_range_loop diagnostics on the original and patched sources (word_cache.rs:147 and lattice.rs:379); the validation compares both results explicitly.

[Native baseline/patched run and logs](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43283917302). The validation workflow is isolated from this PR. The test corpus is represented by counts; no multi-billion-row dataset is materialized. Substring candidate scores, per-word counters and the diagnostic token counter are outside this change.

entries.title: fix(added-vocab): allocate IDs above sparse model vocabularies
entries.head: fdbaf41985934b2c66d8cdaf67063d0dabf5672a
entries.published_body:
The canonical JSON reader uses the number of model vocabulary entries as the starting ID for new added tokens. Sparse BPE, WordPiece and WordLevel vocabularies can already contain that ID: for example, {"<unk>": 0, "a": 2} assigns a newly added token ID 2, so decoding the original model token returns the added token instead.

Find the first ID above the highest model vocabulary ID before assigning new added tokens. Existing model tokens still reuse their own IDs, and vocabulary size continues to report the number of entries. Unigram's dense indexing is unchanged.

Keep the allocation cursor wide until a new ID is needed, then check that it fits u32. This allows the last available ID and returns an error when no further ID is available, rather than wrapping or overwriting a model entry. Registering an existing token at the ID limit remains valid.

Native regression coverage loads canonical JSON through the actual PipelineTokenizer and checks token lookup, encoded IDs, decoding, uniqueness, vocabulary size, and serialize/load round trips. It covers all three sparse model types, dense and empty controls, registration order, Unigram, and the WordLevel u32 boundary.

Validation at exact commit `fdbaf41985934b2c66d8cdaf67063d0dabf5672a` on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:
- 9 new tests passed; restoring both upstream implementation files produces 6 failures and 3 passes.
- 11 existing JSON reader tests and 14 existing added-vocabulary tests passed.
- Rustfmt passed. Strict Clippy is blocked by the same two pre-existing needless_range_loop diagnostics on the original and patched sources (word_cache.rs:147 and lattice.rs:379); the validation compares both results explicitly.

[Native baseline/patched run and logs](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43282863590). The validation workflow is isolated from this PR. No downloaded-model suite or 32-bit runtime was run.

entries.title: fix(pretokenizer): run children after the native DeepSeek prefix
entries.head: 9411811c8cc2eb27f1602d7662593af0948c8359
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The native DeepSeek optimization recognizes the first three members of a pre-tokenizer sequence, then returns immediately. Configured fourth and later non-identity pre-tokenizers are silently ignored. For example, appending `Digits(individual_digits=true)` still emits three-digit groups, which changes the resulting token IDs.

## Change

Keep the direct native path when the remaining members are identities. Otherwise, seed the existing sequential child loop with the native prefix's spans and execute the remaining members in order. This preserves the existing offset rebasing, output append, and scratch reuse behavior.

## Validation

Native Rust tests ran on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu against contribution SHA `9411811c8cc2eb27f1602d7662593af0948c8359`: [validation run](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43289111254).

- Nine new regression tests: the original source fails seven and passes two; the patch passes all nine in both `wordlevel` and `wordlevel,fancy-regex` builds.
- Existing pre-tokenizer tests: 21 pass without a regex backend and 23 pass with `fancy-regex`.
- Cases cover digit splitting, delimiter removal, Unicode span boundaries, multiple trailing children, output append/scratch reuse, error propagation, and canonical JSON through actual PipelineTokenizer encoding. Prefix-only, identity-tail, and ordinary-sequence controls remain unchanged.
- Changed Rust files pass rustfmt.
- Strict Clippy does not pass on either revision: both report the same existing `needless_range_loop` diagnostic in `tk-encode/src/utils/word_cache.rs`. The workflow compares these diagnostics explicitly.

This is a correctness change. No throughput improvement or Python-binding validation is claimed.

entries.title: fix(unigram): sample covered text without an unknown token id
entries.head: 58eb5c01f18ac667f45dae8c38cc5e6254965c08
entries.published_body:
## Problem

A Unigram vocabulary may omit an unknown-token ID when it covers the input. Deterministic encoding supports this configuration. Sampling instead checks every lattice node against unk_id.ok_or(...), so even known tokens raise MissingUnkId.

## Change

Compare Some(node.id) with the optional unknown ID. This matches the existing optimized path: known nodes remain ordinary pieces when no unknown ID is configured, and configured unknown spans retain their existing fusion behavior.

## Validation

[Native Rust validation on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu](https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43287236281) checks exact commit 58eb5c01f18ac667f45dae8c38cc5e6254965c08:

- 8 new regressions: unchanged upstream fails 6 / passes 2; the patch passes all 8.
- All 20 existing Unigram tests pass.
- Full-lattice and n-best sampling, Unicode token offsets, the actual PipelineTokenizer, switching from deterministic encoding, empty input, and configured unknown-token controls are covered.
- Rustfmt passes for changed files.
- Strict Clippy is blocked before and after by the same two existing needless_range_loop diagnostics in word_cache.rs and lattice.rs; the workflow verifies the matching diagnostics. Strict Clippy is not reported as passing.

The validation workflow lives on a separate fork branch.

## Scope

Only the unnecessary unknown-ID requirement while converting a covered sampled path to pieces changes. Sampling weights, vocabulary construction, and other out-of-vocabulary path behavior are unchanged.

entries.title: fix(unigram): preserve sampling settings in canonical JSON
entries.head: 8f2deb6d8295e1c0faa2410f210ffc9eae0c1087
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Serializing a configured Unigram model omits `alpha` and `nbest_size`; the reader also ignores these fields. Reloading a sampling tokenizer therefore silently switches to deterministic tokenization, disabling its subword sampling behavior.

## Change

Read and write the optional sampling settings, retaining explicit zeros. Existing files that omit them retain their deterministic defaults, and the writer omits unset fields. Invalid field types and nonfinite serialized temperatures return errors through the existing JSON contracts. Document the optional canonical fields.

## Validation

Native Rust tests on Ubuntu with Rust 1.100.0, checked out at the exact contribution SHA:

- 9 new regressions pass; restoring the unchanged upstream reader and writer gives 8 failures and 1 passing control.
- 42 existing serialization tests pass, with 1 existing ignored test.
- Cases cover optional/zero combinations, exact temperature bits, independent JSON field checks, missing/null defaults, actual PipelineTokenizer sampling after reload, single-best controls, malformed types, and nonfinite serialization errors.
- Changed Rust files pass rustfmt. Strict Clippy is blocked on both unchanged upstream and the patch by the same two pre-existing `needless_range_loop` diagnostics in `word_cache.rs` and `unigram/lattice.rs`.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43290673728

This changes configuration persistence; it does not change Unigram sampling formulas.

entries.title: fix(unigram): stabilize required-character finalization order
entries.head: af4f00f0148216afbdfb89d3a96b8ef628c7f87e
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Unigram finalization iterates required characters in hash-set order. Equal-score characters receive hash-dependent token IDs; required characters absent from the learned vocabulary also receive hash-dependent fallback penalties. Identical learned pieces can therefore be finalized into different vocabularies.

## Change

Visit required characters in a stable sorted order before assigning fallback penalties and applying the existing stable score sort. Special-token order, learned scores, candidate selection and EM updates retain their existing behavior. Freshly trained equal-score character IDs become stable; loading an existing model does not run this finalization step.

## Validation

Native Rust on Ubuntu with Rust 1.100.0, at the exact contribution SHA:

- 6 new tests pass. Restoring unchanged upstream gives 5 failures and 1 passing control.
- All 5 existing Unigram trainer tests pass.
- Fixed hash seeds are checked against explicit token-ID and fallback-score expectations. Tests also cover native repeated training, Unicode token offsets, unseen initial alphabets, requested special-token order/unknown ID and distinct-score controls.
- Changed Rust files pass rustfmt.
- Strict Clippy is blocked by the same two pre-existing `needless_range_loop` diagnostics in unchanged upstream and patched code (`word_cache.rs` and `unigram/lattice.rs`).

Run: https://github.com/Afloat16/tokenizers/actions/runs/43298508797

The scope is nondeterminism introduced by required-character iteration during finalization. This does not promise identical floating-point reductions across all parallel EM training configurations.

entries.title: Support NumPy output in DataCollatorForMultipleChoice
entries.head: cfb813eb70e312ff1a91a5726d52236b3827713c
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50675)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

`DataCollatorForMultipleChoice` documents `return_tensors="np"`, but dispatching to that backend currently raises `AttributeError` because `numpy_call` is missing. This blocks the documented multiple-choice preprocessing workflow when a NumPy batch is requested.

Share flattening, tokenizer padding and batch reshaping between the existing PyTorch path and the new NumPy path. Each backend constructs its own int64 labels. The existing `torch_call` entry point, input immutability and B × choices × sequence layout are preserved.

The regressions compare all batch fields against the PyTorch output for left/right padding, both label keys, longest/max-length/multiple-of padding, repeated calls and per-call backend overrides. A no-padding case checks the exact output arrays.

## Reproduction

This uses a local BERT vocabulary and the documented multiple-choice collator workflow:

```python
import numpy as np
from transformers import BertTokenizer, DataCollatorForMultipleChoice

tokenizer = BertTokenizer(vocab={"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "[CLS]": 2, "[SEP]": 3, "[MASK]": 4})
collator = DataCollatorForMultipleChoice(tokenizer, return_tensors="np")
batch = collator([{"input_ids": [[2, 3], [2, 1, 3]], "label": 1}])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(batch["input_ids"], [[[2, 3, 0], [2, 1, 3]]])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(batch["labels"], [1])
assert batch["labels"].dtype == np.int64
```

Validation:
- The new regressions against unchanged upstream source produce 13 failures for the missing NumPy method (12 parameterized subcases and one no-padding test).
- The complete native data-collator module passes: **85 tests and 22 subtests**, including the two multiworker DataLoader tests. The eight warnings come from existing Seq2Seq tensor construction and whole-word masking behavior.
- A separate `USE_TORCH=0` process verifies correct arrays and confirms that PyTorch is never imported.
- `make style` passes all five checks; `make fix-repo` passes all 18 checks.

[Reproducible native CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43279938090) checks out exact patch commit `cfb813eb70e312ff1a91a5726d52236b3827713c`. The validation workflow is kept on a separate fork branch. Tests use local tokenizer vocabularies without model or dataset downloads.

entries.title: Return a differentiable zero for all-ignored label smoothing
entries.head: f1af5a0d1993eb58304db4ebe61daec35ba4a132
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50665)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

# What does this PR do?

When every target is ignored, `LabelSmoother` divides two zero sums by a zero active-token count. This returns NaN for both causal and unshifted smoothing, including when Trainer supplies an explicit zero count.

Replace only a zero reduction denominator with one. Ignored labels still contribute zero and the loss keeps its autograd connection. Positive counts, including fractions produced by parallel normalization, keep their existing scale. Two regressions cover empty supervision and positive external counts in the existing Trainer data test file.

## Reproducer on main

This ran on main `158f872ebb33a59f992f69a3abccc6472c548c3f` with a default GPT-2 configuration (124,439,808 parameters), without downloading a checkpoint:

```python
import torch
from transformers import GPT2Config, GPT2LMHeadModel
from transformers.trainer_pt_utils import LabelSmoother

model = GPT2LMHeadModel(GPT2Config())
input_ids = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3, 4]])
loss = LabelSmoother()(
    model(input_ids), torch.full_like(input_ids, -100), shift_labels=True
)
print(loss.item())  # main: nan; with this patch: 0.0
loss.backward()
```

The patched loss requires gradients and backward leaves all parameter gradients finite. This is a correctness fix for batches with no contributing labels, not a speed claim.

## Validation

- The new regression exercises shifted/unshifted labels with an inferred count, integer zero, tensor zero, and a positive external count. Before the fix, six subcases fail with NaN and the two positive-count controls pass. After the fix, all eight subcases pass and produce exactly zero logits gradients.
- `PYTHONPATH=src PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 RUN_SLOW=1 python -m pytest tests/trainer/test_trainer_data.py::TrainerLabelSmoothingTest -q -p xdist.plugin -p pytest_env.plugin`: **4 passed, 20 subtests passed**, including both existing tests. Twelve positive-count controls cover integer and fractional Python/tensor counts, shifted and unshifted targets, and compare both loss and gradients with PyTorch cross entropy with label smoothing.
- `make style`: all five checks pass. `git diff --cached --check` passes.
- `make fix-repo`: all 18 applicable checks pass. `utils/tests_fetcher.py --print_dependencies_of src/transformers/trainer_pt_utils.py` completes successfully. A final `make style` passes all five checks, and the staged tree remains identical to the published commit. The complete test suite and GPU/distributed execution were not run.

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. Searches for this single-label all-ignored case found no existing issue or equivalent PR; the proposed multi-label branch in #48713 addresses a different path.

## Who can review?

Trainer maintainers.

entries.title: Honor absolute scheduler minimums for each parameter group
entries.head: 6cb160b49beefcb922bc7f0b158094be1000ca74
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50678)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## Problem

The polynomial and cosine-minimum schedule factories normalize absolute learning rates with `optimizer.defaults["lr"]`. Parameter groups may override that default. As a result, `lr_end` or `min_lr` does not produce the requested absolute endpoint, even for one custom group. Restoring an optimizer with a different constructor default can also change its remaining schedule.

For two groups starting at 3e-5 and 5e-5, an optimizer default of 1e-3 and a requested minimum of 1e-6, the cosine scheduler currently finishes at 3e-8 and 5e-8.

## Change

Build the existing LambdaLR factors separately for each group's initial learning rate, using the same `initial_lr` fallback as LambdaLR. Apply this to polynomial decay and both cosine-with-minimum factories. Relative `min_lr_rate` retains its existing proportional behavior; zero-rate groups remain frozen. Validate polynomial endpoints against each positive initial group rate.

The LambdaLR interface and state-dict format are retained. Both `last_epoch` and state-dict restoration now use the recorded initial group rates rather than the new optimizer constructor default.

## Reproducer

This runs actual optimizer updates and needs no downloaded model or dataset:

```python
import math
import torch
from transformers.optimization import get_cosine_with_min_lr_schedule_with_warmup

model = torch.nn.Linear(2, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(
    [{"params": [model.weight], "lr": 3e-5},
     {"params": [model.bias], "lr": 5e-5}],
    lr=1e-3,
)
scheduler = get_cosine_with_min_lr_schedule_with_warmup(
    optimizer, num_warmup_steps=2, num_training_steps=10, min_lr=1e-6
)
for _ in range(10):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    model(torch.ones(2, 2)).square().mean().backward()
    optimizer.step()
    scheduler.step()
print(scheduler.get_last_lr())
assert all(math.isclose(lr, 1e-6) for lr in scheduler.get_last_lr())
```

Unchanged main prints `[3.0000000000000004e-08, 5.0000000000000004e-08]` and fails the assertion. This change prints `[1e-06, 1e-06]` and passes.

## Validation

Exact patch commit: `6cb160b49beefcb922bc7f0b158094be1000ca74`; base: `acf8004ec93d3d3195ea4945c693ff1c8959374e`.

- The new tests on the original implementation produce **16 failures** (including six resume subcases), with five parent tests passing.
- Full `tests/optimization` and `tests/trainer/test_trainer_optimizers.py`: **65 passed, 32 skipped, six subtests passed** on both local CPU and GitHub-hosted Ubuntu. The hosted run uses Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.9.1 CPU.
- Three native Trainer cases run ten SGD updates with independently configured weight/bias groups. The unit cases compare each group's entire trajectory against a separate single-group schedule and exercise both checkpoint-resume routes, frozen groups, relative minimums and endpoint validation.
- `make style` (five checks), `make fix-repo` (18 checks), and `git diff --check` pass.

[Native original/patched execution and logs](https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43283294717). Its workflow is on a separate validation branch. GPU/distributed execution and the full repository suite were not run.

entries.title: Resolve Trainer optimizer groups by parameter identity and name
entries.head: d7b21da91ac1f4aae5276869762853508475ed00
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50700)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## Problem

`Trainer.get_optimizer_group(parameter)` uses Python list membership, which invokes tensor equality. Looking up a matrix parameter in a later optimizer group can raise an ambiguous tensor truth-value error. Distinct scalar parameters with equal values can instead select the wrong group. The documented string-name argument is not resolved to a parameter.

## Change

Resolve parameter names with the model's native `get_parameter` method and match group members by object identity. Preserve the existing all-groups result when the argument is omitted or a supplied parameter is not present in the optimizer.

## Validation

Native PyTorch 2.14.0 CPU with the repository's normal test configuration:

- 16 new tests cover every weight and bias by object and name, tied parameter names, equal-valued scalar parameters, foreign parameters, and invalid names.
- Original source: 15 failures and 1 pass. Patched source: all 16 pass; both existing optimizer-inspection tests also pass.
- Real two-layer models run two SGD updates for float32 and float64. Setting the returned second group's learning rate to zero freezes only that layer, while the first layer continues updating.
- Ruff 0.15.9 checks and formatting pass.

Exact production head: `d7b21da91ac1f4aae5276869762853508475ed00`.
