entries.title: Batch array labels before Seq2Seq tensor conversion
entries.head: 708763e7fe0c2627bf2305442bd324d571e82187
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50680)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## Problem

`DataCollatorForSeq2Seq` pads NumPy and CPU-tensor labels into a list of arrays, then passes that list directly to `torch.tensor`. This traverses the arrays element by element, emits PyTorch's slow-conversion warning, and adds work to every training batch. These labels are handled separately from tokenizer padding, so they do not use BatchEncoding's existing bulk conversion.

## Change

For the already padded array-label path, combine the arrays into one int64 NumPy batch before the existing tensor constructor. Keep the Python-list path unchanged. Retaining `torch.tensor` also preserves the original default-device behavior and output ownership.

The production change is two added lines. Padding values and side, label aliases, output dtype, NumPy output, decoder-input preparation and input immutability retain their behavior.

## Native pipeline benchmark

The workload iterates a real Arrow-backed `datasets.Dataset` through a PyTorch DataLoader (`num_workers=0`), applies dynamic padding to multiples of eight, and calls the native decoder-input preparation of a default-config T5 model (60,506,624 parameters). It measures the complete batch preparation path, including Arrow formatting and source-token collation. Model forward/backward and data construction are outside the timed region.

GitHub-hosted Linux, AMD EPYC 7763, Python 3.12.16, PyTorch 2.9.1+cpu, NumPy 2.5.4, Datasets 5.2.0; two Torch threads. Three fresh before/after process pairs each run one warmup pass and five measured passes over 48 batches. The table uses the median of those three per-process medians.

| Batch / source / target | Dataset format | Before ms/batch | After ms/batch | Time reduction |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 / 128 / 128 | numpy | 4.610 | 4.023 | 12.7% |
| 32 / 128 / 128 | torch | 5.091 | 4.550 | 10.6% |
| 32 / 128 / 128 | python | 3.699 | 3.682 | 0.5% |
| 32 / 256 / 512 | numpy | 9.038 | 6.720 | 25.6% |
| 32 / 256 / 512 | torch | 9.455 | 7.191 | 23.9% |
| 32 / 256 / 512 | python | 7.675 | 7.663 | 0.1% |
| 8 / 512 / 2048 | numpy | 5.608 | 3.396 | 39.4% |
| 8 / 512 / 2048 | torch | 5.741 | 3.513 | 38.8% |
| 8 / 512 / 2048 | python | 4.763 | 4.730 | 0.7% |

The unchanged Python-list controls vary by less than 0.7% in this hosted run. A separate local AMD EPYC 9V45 / PyTorch 2.15 CPU run also reduced long-label preparation time, while its short-label and list controls showed more noise. These are batch-preparation timings, not end-to-end training throughput or GPU measurements.

[Reproducible benchmark source](https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/blob/d4f32181e9a3482a093ff1c7eea2ab4cffbb6f79/validation/hf_seq2seq_collation_benchmark.py) and [paired execution, raw measurements and artifact](https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43288377129) are on a separate validation branch, outside this PR.

## Correctness and quality

Exact patch commit: `708763e7fe0c2627bf2305442bd324d571e82187`; base: `acf8004ec93d3d3195ea4945c693ff1c8959374e`.

- Original source with the new equivalence tests: **12 passed, 24 subtests passed**. They protect behavior; this is a performance change and they are not claimed to fail before it.
- Patched complete collator module, including both multiworker loaders, in native CI: **86 passed, 34 subtests passed**.
- Tests cover left/right, longest/max-length/multiple/no padding, int32 and strided NumPy labels, strided Torch labels, repeated calls and storage isolation, the label alias, NumPy output and a non-CPU default-device context.
- Real T5 forward/backward and two SGD updates have exactly matching batches, losses, every parameter gradient and resulting parameters against the Python-list reference.
- Every before/after benchmark output hash agrees.
- Local relevant tests pass; `make style` (five checks), `make fix-repo` (18 checks), dependency inspection and `git diff --check` completed.

The full repository suite and GPU/distributed execution were not run.

entries.title: Pad tiny distributed length groups to every rank
entries.head: d6a9829826927f13543ccc3e93a74ba2cde0aae3
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50701)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## Problem

`DistributedLengthGroupedSampler` pads by copying its index list only once. When the dataset is smaller than half the number of ranks, this does not fill `total_size`, so iteration fails its length assertion. An explicitly empty lengths list also reaches a maximum operation on an empty tensor.

## Change

Repeat the shuffled length-grouped indices as many times as required to fill all ranks, following the padding behavior of PyTorch's `DistributedSampler`. Return an empty index list before grouping explicitly empty lengths. Preserve the existing ordering and `drop_last` behavior.

## Initial validation

Native PyTorch 2.14.0 CPU with the repository's normal test configuration:

- 43 new tests cover dataset sizes 0, 1, 2, 3, and 7; replica counts 1, 2, 3, and 8; both `drop_last` settings; deterministic iteration across two epochs; and empty explicit lengths.
- Original source: 15 failures and 28 passes. Patched source: all 43 pass, along with all 13 existing sampler tests.
- A real three-process Gloo DDP job trains on one example for two epochs. Every rank completes two SGD steps, all ranks finish with identical parameters, and updates match a native single-process reference.
- Targeted Ruff 0.15.9 checks and formatting pass.

The empty-input coverage uses `lengths=[]`; automatic length inference from an empty dataset is outside this change.

Initial sampler-fix validation at `29f8350bd70881f6badf4a4d62d6e58cbc7b9238`:
https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43310764584

## Test-launch follow-up

Current head: `d6a9829826927f13543ccc3e93a74ba2cde0aae3`. This follow-up changes only the two test files; the production sampler implementation is unchanged from the initial validation above.

- Use the repository's existing `execute_subprocess_async` helper with the same explicit Python/module arguments, retain the zero-exit assertion with both output streams, and print a deterministic rank-0 completion summary. This addresses the new test's B603 gate finding without suppressions or security-check configuration changes.
- Keep each worker bounded by a 180-second `faulthandler` watchdog through initialization, training, and process-group cleanup; cancel it after cleanup. This is a worker execution deadline, not a deadline covering interpreter imports and launcher startup.
- Exact-head native validation on PyTorch 2.14.0+cpu: **56 passed** (43 new cases and 13 existing sampler cases), including the real three-rank Gloo/SGD test.
- With the worker deadline temporarily shortened to five seconds, separately blocking initialization, training, and cleanup made the real three-process launcher exit with status 1 in 7.99, 7.99, and 7.75 seconds. The original candidate files were restored and checked afterward.
- Bandit 1.9.4 with the gate's flags reports zero blocking findings. Ruff 0.15.9 checking and formatting pass for all three PR files.

[Exact-head native and timeout evidence](https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43399955236/job/131800043739): the validation step passed. The fork run's final full-repository `make style` step fails on existing Ruff findings: the original and candidate trees produce identical 84-finding reports (46 auto-fixable, 38 remaining). None of the unrelated automatic formatting changes is included in this commit.

The current [upstream PR CI Security Gate passed](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/actions/runs/43400213055), including Bandit. [Upstream PR CI](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/actions/runs/43400217022) is now waiting for maintainer approval under the repository's first-contribution policy.

entries.title: Expand CFG negative prompts with returned generation sequences
entries.head: 3bf25ca148b65b52f3c6849d86c3084205a03c5c
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50702)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## Problem
`generate()` expands the conditional input batch for multiple returned sequences, but keeps `negative_prompt_ids` and `negative_prompt_attention_mask` at the original batch size. Classifier-free guidance then fails on either its first model call or its next cached step when `num_return_sequences > 1`.

## Change
Repeat negative prompt IDs and their optional attention masks using the same expansion factor and ordering as the conditional inputs, before constructing the logits processors. The caller's tensors remain unchanged.

## Validation
Add 36 native tiny-GPT2 generation cases covering batches of one and two, one and three returned samples, guidance scales 0 and 1.5, cache on/off, explicit masks, mask-only inputs, and implicit negative prompts. Compare all four generated-token steps, scores, and returned sequences against a manually expanded input batch using identical random seeds.

- Original source: 18 failures and 18 passing controls.
- Patched source: all 36 new cases pass, plus both existing CFG logits-processor cases.
- Ruff check and format pass.
- The models are constructed locally; no downloaded model or mocked model output is used.

Exact production commit: `3bf25ca148b65b52f3c6849d86c3084205a03c5c`.

Native CPU validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43399313262

This change covers negative-prompt batch expansion for multiple returned samples.

entries.title: Fix NumPy conversion of cached float8 Trainer predictions
entries.head: bf9a3cbe64372541b9be46b691f033301e6fc1b8
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50705)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

# What does this PR do?

Fixes evaluation and prediction when `preprocess_logits_for_metrics` returns FP8 tensors to reduce the size of cached logits. The hook is documented as running before prediction caching, but `nested_numpify` currently only promotes BF16. NumPy conversion of the cached FP8 tensors raises `TypeError: Got unsupported ScalarType Float8_e4m3fn`.

Extend that existing promotion to single-byte floating-point tensors at the NumPy boundary. FP8 tensors can remain in their compact dtype during caching; the resulting NumPy arrays use FP32. Ordinary floating-point and integer conversion paths remain unchanged.

## Reproducer

This fails on main `41f9d3992023970fb5a463e70d56232506c80fbc` and succeeds with this change, using the default GPT-2 configuration and the real Trainer on CPU:

```python
import tempfile
import torch
from transformers import GPT2Config, GPT2LMHeadModel, Trainer, TrainingArguments

model = GPT2LMHeadModel(GPT2Config())
rows = [{"input_ids": torch.tensor([1, 7, 3, 9, 4, 8, 6, 2]) + i} for i in range(3)]
for row in rows:
    row["labels"] = row["input_ids"].clone()

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as output_dir:
    trainer = Trainer(
        model=model,
        args=TrainingArguments(
            output_dir=output_dir,
            use_cpu=True,
            per_device_eval_batch_size=2,
            eval_accumulation_steps=1,
            report_to=[],
        ),
        preprocess_logits_for_metrics=lambda logits, labels: logits.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn),
    )
    predictions = trainer.predict(rows).predictions
    assert predictions.shape == (3, 8, 50257)
```

## Regression test and validation

The single added regression in the existing Trainer evaluation test file reuses `get_regression_trainer`. Its 14 subcases cover four FP8 formats plus BF16/FP32/FP64 controls, with and without per-step CPU accumulation. It checks both nested prediction outputs, labels, metrics and evaluation/prediction loss parity with a partial final batch.

- Original source: eight FP8 subcases fail; six dtype controls pass.
- Patched source: all 14 subcases pass.
- Four existing evaluation/prediction tests pass.
- The separate default-config GPT-2 run verifies every returned quantized logit against native model output and checks the metric and labels.
- Repository `make style` passes.

[Native validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43404959034) tests exact commit `bf9a3cbe64372541b9be46b691f033301e6fc1b8` with PyTorch 2.14 CPU. This validation does not claim FP8 distributed-collective support or a change to model quantization accuracy.

entries.title: fix: Preserve outer signal suspension during bulk task deletion
entries.head: 0f828731e70bab5ae2ca026995a3b97235c60f02
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Fixes #10034.

The signal suspension context unconditionally reconnects every listed receiver. A nested `Task.delete_tasks_without_signals()` call can resume an outer operation's paused summary callbacks before that operation finishes. A receiver absent before entry is also incorrectly registered on exit.

## What changed

Keep a per-entry list of receivers that were actually disconnected, and restore only that list. A stack preserves ownership for nested entries, including reuse of one context instance. Dispatch UID handling and ordinary receiver reconnection are unchanged.

## Testing

Native locked dependencies (`uv sync --frozen --group test`), Python 3.12 and SQLite on Ubuntu, at the exact contribution SHA:

- 16 new regressions pass. Unchanged source gives 12 failures and 4 passing controls.
- All 55 existing core tests pass.
- Tests use real Django Signals and actual Task queryset deletions with ProjectSummary counters. They cover registered/absent receivers, nested separate/shared contexts, exception unwinding, one-shot iterable entries, reused contexts and unrelated senders.
- Project-pinned Ruff 0.15.1 check and format pass.

Run: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43296890638

## Acceptance criteria

- A nested bulk task deletion leaves an outer signal suspension active until the outer context exits.
- Normal callbacks resume once the context that disconnected them exits.
- Receivers absent on entry remain absent afterward.
- An inner exception does not prematurely reconnect an outer context's receiver.

## Scope

No database schema or public API changes. This patch changes context bookkeeping through Django's native connect/disconnect methods. PostgreSQL and concurrent sharing of one context instance across threads were not tested; this does not add transaction-like recovery for an exception during context entry.

entries.title: Fix loss weighting for short iterable evaluation batches
entries.head: bbfc2fe3c40a2d017f52934a6cb0d43aeee4710c
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50708)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## What does this PR do?

Use each observed evaluation batch size when expanding its mean loss before gathering.

With an unknown-length iterable dataset and `accelerator_config={"dispatch_batches": False}`, the final batch can be shorter than the configured batch size. Its mean loss is currently repeated for a full batch. Accelerate cannot trim this unknown-length loader by a known dataset remainder, so the tail is overweighted in both `evaluate()` and `predict()`.

The existing configured-size fallback remains for inputs whose batch size cannot be inferred. Gathering, accumulation, and the reduction of model losses are unchanged.

## Reproduction and validation

Native CPU validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43406792756

- New regression in the existing iterable Trainer suite: original code has **2 failing and 10 passing subcases**; the fix passes all **12 subcases**. These cover actual `evaluate()`/`predict()`, an independent MSE reference, dispatch enabled/disabled, accumulation enabled/disabled, and batch sizes 1, 3, and 8 for seven examples.
- Four existing evaluation/prediction tests pass, including the existing iterable tests.
- A separate real workflow uses an unmodified default `GPT2Config()`, `GPT2LMHeadModel`, `Trainer`, and the same Hugging Face `Dataset` converted with `to_iterable_dataset()`. With batch size 3 and seven examples:

| Loader | Original loss | Fixed loss |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Map-style, dispatch disabled | 9.6250963211 | 9.6250963211 |
| Iterable, dispatch disabled | 9.5590667725 | 9.6250963211 |
| Iterable, dispatch enabled | 9.6250963211 | 9.6250963211 |

The GPT-2 check uses locally initialized weights and verifies evaluation aggregation; it is not a model-quality benchmark. Validation ran on CPU, without distributed or GPU claims.

Commands:
```bash
python -m pytest tests/trainer/test_trainer_data.py::TrainerDynamicShapesAndIterableTest::test_iterable_evaluation_loss_uses_actual_batch_size -q
python -m pytest tests/trainer/test_trainer_data.py::TrainerDynamicShapesAndIterableTest::test_evaluation_iterable_dataset tests/trainer/test_trainer_data.py::TrainerDynamicShapesAndIterableTest::test_predict_iterable_dataset tests/trainer/test_trainer_evaluation.py::TrainerEvaluationTest::test_evaluate tests/trainer/test_trainer_evaluation.py::TrainerEvaluationTest::test_predict -q
make style
```

Full `make style` passes, with 5,108 files unchanged.

## Related work

This is a standalone reproduction. The existing batch-size fix in #16763 selected the configured total batch size for data parallelism. The Accelerate migration in #24028 removed the old final truncation of losses and delegated gathering to Accelerate; this patch instead makes each local loss expansion match the batch that produced it. Related evaluation-loop changes and current open/closed PRs were checked for the same fix.

entries.title: fix: preserve sliced and combined querysets during batch iteration
entries.head: 1b3c60f52c0d8aea720f2fe35d21674188a05b73
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10038.

Primary-key batching adds a filter to the original queryset. Django rejects this for slices and combined queries (UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT), so valid selections fail before they can be processed. Re-selecting primary keys also rewrites some projected combined queries.

## Changes

Use bounded offset pages for sliced and combined querysets. This preserves their existing limits, ordering, selected values and UNION ALL multiplicity. The existing primary-key path and aggregate fallback retain their behavior.

The fallback does not introduce server-side cursors, preserving the motivation for #8259's PgBouncer transaction-pooling compatibility. OFFSET cost can grow for large combined queries; correctness for these previously failing queries is the objective.

## Testing

Exact SHA `1b3c60f52c0d8aea720f2fe35d21674188a05b73`, Python 3.12 and locked native dependencies, on both SQLite and PostgreSQL 16:

- Each database passes 25 new cases and all 6 existing iterator cases.
- Restoring unchanged upstream on each database gives 19 failures and 6 passing controls.
- Tests cover sliced annotations/values, nonzero offsets, empty limits, four set operations, UNION ALL duplicates, combined values with a slice, invalid batch sizes and ordinary-query controls.
- The real Data Manager column-update function changes exactly the requested limited task selection.
- SQL observations check bounded LIMIT pages.
- Pinned Ruff 0.15.1 lint and formatting pass.

Run: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43301342700

## Acceptance criteria and scope

Supported Django slices and set-operation queries can be iterated in batches without unsupported filter calls, with the tested limits and result semantics preserved.

No schema migration or feature flag is required. As with the existing batching helper, this does not provide a transactional snapshot when rows are concurrently added, removed or reordered.

entries.title: fix: preserve empty common-data-column intersections across import batches
entries.head: bed8cea6f91e60a040c94d347ef58142e5a99551
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10036.

Both intersection steps in `ProjectSummary.update_data_columns` treat an empty set as uninitialized. Later tasks can therefore resurrect columns that are absent from earlier tasks, making column-summary metadata depend on task order and import batch boundaries. Empty batches also discard a populated common-column list.

## Changes

Use a distinct uninitialized sentinel for the current batch. Distinguish a fresh summary from an existing empty intersection using existing column counts and, when those counts are empty, the number of persisted tasks relative to the incoming batch. All existing import, storage and task-save callers persist their batch before updating the summary; full recalculation passes all tasks.

An empty batch preserves the current field values and still follows the existing save path, so full recalculation on an empty project persists its explicit cache reset.

## Testing

Native Django SQLite database, Python 3.12 and locked repository dependencies at exact SHA `bed8cea6f91e60a040c94d347ef58142e5a99551`:

- 19 new tests pass. Unchanged upstream has 11 failures and 8 passing controls.
- All 55 existing core tests pass.
- Real task save signals, persisted import-style batches, six row permutations, four batch partitions, prior empty-data tasks, empty batches, and populated/empty project recalculation are covered.
- Column counts and intersections are compared with independent set/Counter calculations.
- Pinned Ruff 0.15.1 lint and formatting pass.

Run: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43300292035

## Acceptance criteria and scope

The common-column intersection stays empty after a missing column is observed, independent of the tested row orders and batch boundaries. Empty batch updates preserve the summary, and empty-project recalculation clears persisted cached columns.

There is no schema migration or feature flag. This changes column-summary metadata only; it does not add concurrency guarantees or change annotation counters. PostgreSQL has not been exercised by this test run.

entries.title: fix: detect CSV delimiters outside quoted header fields
entries.head: ef338e5da49ba613e7860d1900b48bc27e2ed4f7
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10042.

CSV separator detection counts punctuation inside quoted header fields. A comma-separated file with a header such as `"context;one;two;three"` can therefore be read as semicolon-separated, and vice versa. This can reject otherwise valid task imports or change their columns.

Count commas and semicolons outside quoted fields in the first logical header record. Preserve the existing semicolon-if-more-frequent rule and comma fallback. Track field starts so literal quotes inside unquoted fields keep their existing meaning; also handle escaped quotes, embedded newlines, and the initial UTF-8 BOM.

## Tests and acceptance criteria

- Both delimiters retain the original header names and task values, including quoted punctuation and multiline headers.
- Escaped quotes, unquoted literal quotes, UTF-8 BOM, single-column and empty-header cases are covered.
- Native FileUpload and streaming readers return identical expected data.
- Real import API requests persist the expected Task dictionaries.
- Exact tested commit: `ef338e5da49ba613e7860d1900b48bc27e2ed4f7`.
- SQLite and PostgreSQL16 each pass 24 new cases and 20 existing CSV/TSV API cases.
- Original source: 15 failures and 9 passing controls on each database.
- Ruff0.15.1 lint and format checks pass.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43305826080

## Scope and risks

This retains the existing two-candidate frequency heuristic and its comma tie-breaking rule. It does not attempt to infer arbitrary CSV dialects or uniquely resolve ambiguous headers. The test suite checks the backend import paths; no frontend behavior is changed.

entries.title: fix: preserve apostrophes in inline JSON imports
entries.head: 967977d2c7e0e1cca0612e2e481642bf4351f11f
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10040.

Valid inline JSON in the form-encoded `url` field can contain apostrophes in text or object keys. The shared parser currently replaces every apostrophe before parsing, so content such as `don't` becomes invalid JSON. The synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming loaders then incorrectly take the download-URL path.

Parse the original JSON first and use the existing single-quote normalization only as a fallback after a parse failure. The file-import paths retain the original uploaded bytes.

## Tests and acceptance criteria

- Valid JSON preserves apostrophes, escaped double quotes, backslashes, Unicode, and nested values.
- Legacy single-quoted helper inputs and invalid-input `None` behavior are preserved.
- Native form parsing plus all three import loaders produce the expected tasks and unchanged uploaded file bytes.
- Exact final commit: `967977d2c7e0e1cca0612e2e481642bf4351f11f`.
- SQLite and PostgreSQL16 each pass 17 new tests and 6 existing import/file-size controls.
- On the original implementation, the new suite has 7 failures and 10 passing controls on each database.
- Ruff0.15.1 lint and format checks pass.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43304481562

## Scope and risks

The change is limited to deciding whether an input is inline JSON. URL validation, external downloads, task-count rules, and the existing legacy fallback are unchanged. Validation uses real database and local file-import paths; it does not involve an external download service.

entries.title: fix: accept long leading whitespace in streaming JSON imports
entries.head: 8fce0827c6980b02722bb11b3c470568bf7f521d
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10046.

The streaming JSON reader inspected only the first 4,096 bytes when selecting the array or object parser. Valid JSON with a longer whitespace prefix therefore failed import before either parser ran.

Scan successive bounded blocks until the first non-JSON-whitespace byte or EOF, then seek back to the beginning and use the existing parser. This keeps the existing handling of arrays, objects, invalid input, and upload metadata.

## Tests and acceptance criteria

- Native file uploads and both file/async loaders accept valid prefixes across the 4,096-byte boundary, including a 65,536-byte prefix.
- Batch contents, metadata, and file bytes remain unchanged.
- Empty input and non-JSON whitespace continue to raise validation errors.
- Exact tested commit: `8fce0827c6980b02722bb11b3c470568bf7f521d`.
- SQLite and PostgreSQL 16 each pass 21 new cases and 10 existing streaming import cases.
- Original source on each database: 12 failures and 9 passing controls.
- Ruff 0.15.1 lint and format checks pass.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43310332585

## Scope and risks

The prefix scan uses one 4,096-byte block at a time. The existing object parser and its materialization behavior are unchanged; this does not claim fully streaming object imports.

entries.title: fix: process every file in repeated multipart upload fields
entries.head: f0783c10eacf7c7857ebff179d77ff9cc729d1d3
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10044.

Django's multipart file mapping can contain multiple uploaded files under one field. Iterating its items returns only the final value, so earlier uploads are omitted from task creation and from extension/total-size validation.

Add one iterator that expands native MultiValueDict lists and keeps the existing values behavior for ordinary mappings. Use a fresh iterator in each of the two validation and two import entry points.

## Tests and acceptance criteria

- Every file in repeated or mixed multipart fields contributes its own expected tasks and FileUpload record.
- The total-size limit applies to all files, and unsupported extensions in either position are rejected before persistence.
- Ordinary single-value mappings and empty mappings retain their behavior.
- Native DRF multipart requests cover synchronous loading, FileUpload preparation, and the real import API.
- Exact tested commit: `f0783c10eacf7c7857ebff179d77ff9cc729d1d3`.
- SQLite and PostgreSQL 16 each pass 18 new cases and 6 existing import validation cases.
- Original source: 11 failures and 7 passing controls on each database.
- Ruff 0.15.1 lint and format checks pass.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43307508940

## Scope and risks

This changes traversal of uploaded file values, not parsing of individual files, URL downloads, or task formats. Each validation/import operation creates its own iterator and does not consume file contents during validation.

entries.title: Prevent half-precision overflow when reducing label smoothing losses
entries.head: 70f2d58479c7f204648bfad1a67a08435d453e72
entries.published_body:
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:start -->
[![🤗 Transformers CI](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Transformers%20CI-333333?style=flat)](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/pytest-observability-by-pr/pytest-observability-branch?var-pr=50699)
<!-- ci-dashboard-badge:end -->

## Problem

`LabelSmoother` already sums the uniform smoothing term in float32, but the NLL term is still reduced in the logits dtype. With sufficiently many valid tokens, an FP16 sum overflows even though the normalized loss is finite. BF16 accumulation also loses avoidable precision before normalization. This affects label smoothing over long token batches produced by half-precision models.

## Change

Accumulate the NLL term in float32 for FP16 and BF16 inputs. Preserve float32 and float64 reduction precision, label shifting, ignored-token masking, and the caller-provided full-batch denominator.

## Validation

Native PyTorch 2.14.0 CPU, repository test configuration:

- 30 new tests cover FP16/BF16 reductions, inferred and external integer/tensor counts, shifted labels, ignored labels, smoothing factors 0 and 0.1, and float32/float64 controls.
- Original source: 26 failures and 4 passes.
- Patched source: all 32 tests in `TrainerLabelSmoothingTest` pass.
- Real FP16 and BF16 tiny GPT-2 models each complete two SGD updates. Losses match an independent reference using native unreduced NLL with float32 accumulation; all parameter gradients and updated parameters match exactly.
- Ruff 0.15.9 checks and formatting pass.

Exact production head: `70f2d58479c7f204648bfad1a67a08435d453e72`.
https://github.com/Afloat16/transformers/actions/runs/43305917064

entries.title: fix: derive URL import filenames from the resolved path
entries.head: 0e1901aed38f406f993ecfc48d33efd65572e339
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Direct URL imports derive the filename from the entire URL. A valid URL such as `https://host/tasks.json?token=example` therefore gets the unsupported extension `.json?token=example`. A slash in the query can also replace the basename and send structured data down the asset-import path. Redirected responses already parse the URL path, so equivalent direct and redirected resources behave differently.

## Change

Derive the filename from the decoded path of the resolved response URL for both cases, then take its basename. The request still uses the complete original URL, including its query parameters. Existing address, extension and size validation remain in place.

Fixes #10052.

## Validation

Native tests ran against both SQLite and PostgreSQL with the repository's locked dependencies:

- 26 new tests passed on each database; the same tests against the original source produced 14 failures and 12 passes.
- 10 existing import-validation controls passed on each database.
- Ruff checks and formatting checks passed.

The regressions use a local HTTP server and the real request/import paths. They cover direct and redirected JSON/CSV URLs, query strings and fragments, percent-encoded filenames, the authenticated import API, both project-import parser modes, unsupported extensions and the size limit. A separate control verifies that enabled SSRF protection still rejects the local address before a request is made.

[Exact-commit validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43402323705) tests commit `0e1901aed38f406f993ecfc48d33efd65572e339`.

## Scope

This changes filename selection and parser dispatch. It introduces no setting, migration or UI change. Download buffering is unchanged.

entries.title: fix: clean intermediate ZIP archives after synchronous export
entries.head: b79fb42eee772e026ce84890de0ca8cf65b6ef62
entries.published_body:
## Reason for change

Closes #10049.

Synchronous exports with multiple output files create an intermediate ZIP beside the managed output directory. The function then copies that ZIP into the returned temporary file. Cleaning the conversion directories and closing the returned file leaves the intermediate archive behind, so repeated exports accumulate disk usage.

Create the intermediate ZIP inside the separately managed input directory, while continuing to archive only the converter's output directory. The returned file remains an independent temporary copy with the same public filename and contents.

## Tests and acceptance criteria

- Successful COCO/YOLO exports leave only the returned temporary file; closing it removes the final temporary artifact.
- Empty, one-task, and three-task exports preserve actual archive contents, category labels, COCO boxes, and YOLO values.
- Repeated exports do not accumulate archives, and two concurrently open returned files have independent lifetimes.
- Single-file JSON behavior and input task data remain unchanged.
- Exact tested commit: `b79fb42eee772e026ce84890de0ca8cf65b6ef62`.
- SQLite and PostgreSQL 16 each pass 11 new cases and all 36 existing export-media cases.
- Original source on each database: 9 failures and 2 passing controls.
- Ruff 0.15.1 lint and format checks pass.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43400018800

## Scope and risks

This fixes orphan ZIP files after successful synchronous exports. It does not change persistent snapshot storage, media download authorization, or the existing temporary-directory helper's exception behavior. The archive is created outside its input tree, so it cannot include itself or the converter input JSON.

entries.title: fix: normalize upload suffix case before parser selection
entries.head: bc366894e486ab8d74194c4ab0a51f3acd2b6027
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Uploaded files are accepted by the existing case-insensitive extension checks, but `FileUpload.format` retains the suffix's original case. Parser selection compares that value with lowercase format names. As a result, a valid `tasks.JSON`, `tasks.CsV` or `tasks.TSV` can fail import or be treated as an asset instead of structured task data.

## Change

Normalize the format suffix to lowercase where `FileUpload.format` exposes it. This gives synchronous imports, streaming imports and format filters the same format value while retaining the stored filename and file contents.

Fixes #10050.

## Validation

[Native validation of the exact commit](https://github.com/Afloat16/label-studio/actions/runs/43402380605) passed with the repository's locked dependencies on SQLite and PostgreSQL 16:

- 29 new cases passed on each database. The same cases against the original source produced 20 failures and 9 passes.
- 10 existing import controls passed on each database.
- Ruff lint and formatting passed.

Coverage includes lowercase, uppercase and mixed-case suffixes for JSON, CSV, TSV, TXT, HTML, HTM and XML; the authenticated import API persists all rows from JSON/CSV/TSV; synchronous and streaming parser paths agree. Explicit TXT/CSV file-as-asset imports remain supported. Tests also verify that the stored filename's case and bytes are preserved.

Tested commit: `bc366894e486ab8d74194c4ab0a51f3acd2b6027`.

## Rollout and scope

No migration or new setting is required. This normalizes format metadata at the existing dispatch boundary; it does not rename uploaded files.

entries.title: Normalize continuous truncated lognormal mixture densities
entries.head: 43b9e64c0a2ce099049e7ba1c760f3925bbb4682
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`LGMM1` samples its normal component in `[low, high)` and then exponentiates it. `LGMM1_lpdf` computes the corresponding mixture acceptance probability, but its continuous branch does not divide by it. The returned density therefore integrates to the acceptance probability instead of one. The quantized branch already applies this normalization.

For a standard lognormal restricted to `exp(-1) <= x < exp(1)`, the continuous density currently integrates to approximately 0.682689 rather than 1.

## Change

Subtract `log(p_accept)` from the continuous mixture log density, matching the existing quantized branch and the distribution sampled by `LGMM1`. Bounds remain in log space. Unbounded densities keep `p_accept = 1`.

## Validation

- Nine new regression cases: base code has 7 failures and 2 passing controls.
- Fixed code: 19 tests pass across the new module and the existing `TestLGMM1Math` / `TestQLGMM1Math` classes.
- Independent references use SciPy lognormal component densities, weighted normal-CDF acceptance probabilities, and numerical integration over the bounded support.
- Coverage includes scalar, vector and matrix outputs, mixed components, unbounded densities, and quantized masses to prevent double normalization.
- Ruff 0.15.18 lint/format and `git diff --check` pass.

This corrects probability normalization. It does not establish faster optimization or improved objective values; in a single variable's comparison the normalization term is constant across candidates. The full test suite was not run.

entries.title: Compute Gaussian mixture normalizers in log space
entries.head: 0199f05f75082a1303d125b2a0cfa5047bad033d
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`GMM1_lpdf` computes `sqrt(2 * pi * sigmas**2)` before taking the logarithm of its mixture coefficient. Squaring a finite standard deviation around `1e154` or above can overflow. Valid Gaussian log densities consequently become NaN, and TPE can no longer compare its mixture scores correctly for large finite uniform search ranges.

For example, a zero-mean normal with standard deviation `1e200` has a finite log density of approximately -461.436 at zero; the current implementation returns NaN.

## Change

Compute the same coefficient as `log(weights) - log(sigmas) - 0.5 * log(2*pi) - log(p_accept)`. This avoids the intermediate squared scale and division before taking logs. The Mahalanobis term, existing sigma floor, quantized branch, and truncation acceptance calculation are unchanged.

## Validation

- Fourteen new regression cases: base code has 10 failures and 4 passing ordinary-scale controls.
- Fixed code: 16 tests pass including the existing `TestGMM1Math` cases.
- Independent SciPy normal log-density/logsumexp references cover mixed components, bounded/unbounded densities, scalar/matrix outputs, and scales 1, 1e154 and 1e200.
- Native `fmin`, `Trials`, and TPE tests compare the 12-step suggestion trajectory for an equivalent uniform search at scales 1, 1e155 and 1e200.
- Ruff 0.15.18 lint/format and `git diff --check` pass.

This addresses overflow in the Gaussian mixture normalizer. It does not claim to resolve every extreme-tail or truncation-CDF cancellation case, nor demonstrate better objective values or general optimization speed. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: Include uncertain competing trials in average best error
entries.head: 76256d9d051daad940bb5a8701869e53279e2b96
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`Trials.average_best_error` estimates each successful trial's chance of having the lowest loss, then weights its `true_loss` by that probability. Before sampling, however, it discards trials whose observed losses exceed the lowest observed loss by three standard deviations, using only that lowest-loss trial's variance.

This ignores other trials' uncertainty: a higher observed loss with large variance can still have a substantial chance of being best. When the lowest-loss trial has zero variance while another trial is uncertain, the strict cutoff selects an empty array and the probability calculation raises `ValueError`.

## Changes

Apply the existing `pmin_sampled` calculation to all successful trials whenever any loss has nonzero variance. Keep the all-deterministic shortcut and failed-trial filtering.

This removes an invalid truncation assumption, at a cost: sampling now uses all successful trials. Its time and sample-array memory scale with **N successful trials times the existing 1,000 samples**. This change does not claim a speedup.

## Validation

Base: `9834314879c09c13e0b8e93eb678408ba46441a8`.

Eight new cases produce **4 failed, 4 passed** on unchanged master and **8 passed** with the fix. Two Gaussian losses with means 0 and 1 and variances `1e-6` and 100 have an analytically computable probability of being best. With true losses 4 and 10, the expected weighted result is about 6.761; the original cutoff returns 4. With a zero-variance best trial, the original code raises on the empty array. Tests compare to the independent Gaussian-difference CDF with a Monte Carlo tolerance, covering native `Domain` and default extraction, failed results and the all-deterministic control.

`PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest hyperopt/tests/unit/test_average_best_error.py -q`: **8 passed**. Repository-pinned Ruff 0.15.18 lint and changed-file formatting, and `git diff --check`, pass.

Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5 and SciPy 1.17.0. The full repository suite and optimization-convergence benchmarks were not run.

entries.title: Handle deterministic predictions in Gaussian expected improvement
entries.head: b8870be44ec3a8f6bca578eb6086f8f99e8bb51a
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`EI_gaussian` and `logEI_gaussian` divide by the predictive standard deviation. A zero-variance prediction is deterministic, but the helpers currently return NaNs or raise floating-point errors even when the expected improvement has a finite, known value. `logEI_gaussian` already accepts nonnegative variances in its validation.

## Changes

Handle zero-variance entries as point masses: expected improvement is `max(mean - threshold, 0)`, and log expected improvement is its logarithm, or negative infinity when no improvement is possible. In mixed arrays, pass the remaining entries through the existing positive-variance implementation. Preserve scalar results and float64 precision when float32 inputs are mixed with deterministic entries.

## Validation

Base: `9834314879c09c13e0b8e93eb678408ba46441a8`.

- Ten new regression/control cases: **9 failed, 1 passed** on unchanged master.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest hyperopt/tests/unit/test_criteria.py -q`: **14 passed** with the fix, including the existing empirical/analytic and extreme-tail checks.
- Deterministic predictions below, at and above the threshold are checked under `np.errstate(all="raise")`; mixed arrays also exercise a positive-variance entry. Float32 controls compare the retained positive-variance result exactly to the original scalar calculation.
- Repository-pinned Ruff 0.15.18 lint and formatting, and `git diff --check`, pass.

Tested with Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5 and SciPy 1.17.0. The full repository suite and optimizer convergence benchmarks were not run. This change fixes the acquisition helpers' mathematical boundary behavior; it does not change TPE's sampling algorithm.

entries.title: Ignore unsuccessful trial losses when constructing sampler history
entries.head: 4b339129a45349c0bfa899f36c5c42105d7731ff
entries.published_body:
## Problem

TPE and annealing both state that new, running, or failed evaluations receive infinite loss. In practice, both paths read any numeric `loss` without checking the result status. A failed evaluation that retains a low loss can therefore become a preferred point for subsequent suggestions. This also contradicts the expected behavior described in #609.

## Changes

Read an observed loss only for `STATUS_OK` results. Other statuses use the existing infinite-loss path. Trials remain in the history with their existing ordering, and their result dictionaries are not modified. Annealing uses the domain's status accessor consistently with its loss accessor.

## Validation

- Added deterministic tests using native `Trials` and actual TPE/annealing suggestions. For fail/new/running/suspended results, supplying a low loss must produce the same next suggestion as omitting that invalid loss.
- Added successful-result controls confirming that valid losses still affect the next suggestion.
- Before the change: 8 new failures and 2 passing controls. After the change: all 10 new tests pass; together with the existing annealing smoke cases, 18 tests pass.
- Ruff checks, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

This corrects how result status affects sampling. It does not claim improved convergence on a benchmark or change early stopping and loss-threshold handling.

entries.title: Preserve small positive values in quantized loguniform TPE
entries.head: 0b2be04d2c7a07a6e766aba348f832c3fbc42e4a
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Two absolute EPS floors distort quantized loguniform search spaces below 1e-12. The lognormal CDF replaces all such inputs, including zero, with 1e-12; for mu=-30 it consequently returns about 0.991 even at zero. Quantized mixture bins can then receive zero probability, producing -inf likelihoods and NaN candidate scores. The qloguniform posterior also raises all small observations to EPS instead of the distribution's lower bound.

## Change

Compute the CDF using the actual nonnegative input: log(0) naturally gives -inf and therefore CDF zero, within the existing divide-warning guard. Retain negative-input validation and the existing sigma floor. For qloguniform observations, keep the exp(low) floor but use the smallest positive representable float solely to protect against exp(low) underflow.

Both corrections belong to the same preservation of small search-space values. Fixing only the CDF does not restore the search trajectory because the posterior observation floor still changes the fitted mixture.

## Validation

- 15 new regressions: upstream base 9 failed, 6 passed.
- Fixed tests plus all 8 existing TestQLGMM1Math cases: 23 passed.
- SciPy references cover CDF values including zero and small positives, and bounded/unbounded quantized mixture bin probabilities.
- Native fmin/TPE/Trials runs produce the same normalized 12-step trajectory for equivalent qloguniform spaces at scales 1, 1e-15, and 1e-100.
- Zero-observation controls include an exp(low) that actually underflows, preserving a finite logarithm floor.
- Ruff 0.15.18 lint/format and git diff --check pass.

The qlognormal posterior's separate observation-floor heuristic and extreme-tail CDF cancellation are unchanged. The trajectory check is a deterministic regression on equivalent spaces, not a general convergence or model-quality benchmark.

entries.title: Preserve zero-density tails in mixture log reductions
entries.head: dd6208b10eb84d27349209e55a5da54d60c34981
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The manual max-shift in logsum_rows subtracts -inf from -inf when every component has zero representable density. This turns a valid log likelihood of -inf into NaN. Positive-infinity rows have the same invalid subtraction. With ordinary mixture sigmas of 1 or 2, a finite far-tail sample such as 1e155 already reaches the first case; the normalization coefficients themselves remain finite.

## Change

Use scipy.special.logsumexp along the existing row axis. SciPy is already a required dependency. Finite rows, sample shape, and the surrounding mixture/TPE formulas are preserved, while extended-real rows retain their correct results.

## Validation

- Seven new regressions: upstream base 6 failed, 1 passed.
- Fixed regressions plus the existing Gaussian and lognormal mixture math tests: 11 passed.
- Explicit row-sum references cover zero/infinite mass, finite values, and an empty sample batch.
- Gaussian-mixture tails are checked against independent SciPy normal log densities reduced with NumPy logaddexp.
- Native fmin/TPE/Trials runs continue from finite initial observations at +1e155 and -1e155 with invalid floating-point operations configured to raise.
- Ruff 0.15.18 lint/format and git diff --check pass.

This addresses the row reduction, separately from #969's Gaussian normalization coefficients. Overflow of an unrepresentably large squared distance can still produce infinity, correctly corresponding to log density -inf. Arbitrary invalid inputs or an undefined -inf-minus--inf likelihood ratio are not repaired by this change. No optimization-speed or general convergence claim is made.

entries.title: Use the category axis when constructing annealing batch probabilities
entries.head: 5a0f2e9a4e63750b5f504f359e790d47c4b6a66c
entries.published_body:
## Problem

When annealing proposes a batch for a categorical parameter, its prior probabilities are a matrix with one row per active trial. hp_categorical currently uses p.size as the number of categories. For a batch of two with three categories this allocates six empirical counts, then tries to combine shape (6,) with probabilities of shape (2, 3). Native anneal.suggest_batch therefore fails with a broadcasting ValueError once categorical observations exist.

## Change

Use p.shape[-1] for the count vector and its empty-value fallback. Preserve the existing batch-shared empirical frequencies, prior shrinking formula, and sampling behavior. This concerns construction of the probability matrix; the stochastic sampler's separate one-dimensional-probability shape handling is unchanged.

## Validation

- 8 new tests on the upstream base: 5 failed, 3 passed.
- Fixed tests plus the existing pchoice tests: 17 passed on CPU.
- Hand-calculated prior/empirical mixtures after four observed configurations are checked against native NumPy draws, including the following RNG value, for uniform and nonuniform priors and several batch sizes.
- A real conditional search space passes through anneal.suggest_batch and space_eval. Single-item and empty-history controls preserve the existing behavior.
- Ruff lint/format and git diff --check pass.

This makes the existing batch proposal path usable. It does not change the annealing algorithm or demonstrate a convergence improvement. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: Preserve multidimensional categorical sample shapes
entries.head: 08c7259a47746f71372df3b14b0d286909a403ad
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The one-dimensional probability-vector branch of categorical accepts a tuple size, but flattens it to an integer before calling NumPy's multinomial sampler. It then asserts that the returned array has the original multidimensional shape. Requests such as size=(2, 3), size=(2, 1, 3), and multidimensional shapes containing zero fail with AssertionError, including through pyll.stochastic.sample.

## Change

Pass the normalized size directly to multinomial, which already supports multidimensional sample shapes. The existing category-index conversion then produces the requested shape. Keep the scalar/default convention of returning shape (1,), the one-dimensional path, and the separate per-row probability branch.

## Validation

- 14 new tests on the upstream base: 9 failed, 5 passed.
- Fixed tests plus the existing stochastic and pchoice tests: 28 passed on CPU.
- An independent flattened multinomial draw, reshaped to the requested dimensions, verifies the sample values and the next RNG draw. Controls cover empty dimensions, scalar/integer/vector sizes, deterministic category indices, input immutability, a native stochastic expression graph, and per-row probabilities.
- Ruff lint/format and git diff --check pass.

This restores categorical shape support. It does not change the category distribution or demonstrate an optimization-convergence improvement. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: Avoid calling the early-stop callback twice per iterator step
entries.head: 0a3b8fdb8b1eb6ac4a4f567af026ed8ca787d019
entries.published_body:
## Problem

FMinIter.__next__ calls run, which already invokes early_stop_fn and updates its state, then invokes the callback again for the same trial. Stateful patience counters advance twice: a callback configured to stop after four evaluations stops the iterator after only two. A one-time True decision can also be lost if the second call returns False.

## Change

Record the early-stop decision made inside run and let __next__ consume it without another callback invocation. An iterator that has stopped does not schedule more evaluations when next is called again. An explicit run resets the flag, retaining a way to resume deliberately. Keep the existing max_evals, timeout, loss-threshold, and asynchronous polling policies.

## Validation

- 10 new tests on the upstream base: 9 failed, 1 passed.
- Fixed tests plus the two existing early-stop tests: 12 passed on CPU.
- Native FMinIter/Domain/Trials cases check callback counts and arguments, one-time True decisions, repeated next after stopping, and explicit resumption.
- The built-in no_progress_loss callback follows the same evaluation count and seeded trial values through iteration and public fmin for two patience settings.
- Controls cover a callback that never stops and an iterator without a callback.
- Ruff lint/format and git diff --check pass.

The once-per-evaluation assertions cover synchronous execution. This removes the extra iterator callback; it does not redesign how asynchronous run invokes callbacks while polling, or change other stopping criteria. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: Preserve LAMB update options when resuming from checkpoints
entries.head: e8670aa247380670a8eaf6f3181684e65f47174f
entries.published_body:
## Problem

LAMB's `clamp_value`, `adam`, and `debias` options are stored only as optimizer attributes. They are absent from `state_dict()`, so a normal checkpoint restore can silently change the update rule when the new constructor uses different options.

For example, after three native CPU steps with `clamp_value=0.1`, saving and loading the optimizer state into a default constructor changes the next first-coordinate value from approximately **4.99422** to **4.91188**. The `adam` and `debias` flags independently produce divergent continuation as well.

## Change

Include the current global options in a `lamb_options` checkpoint entry and restore them after the base optimizer loads its parameter groups and moment state. Legacy checkpoints without the entry keep the constructor's options. The public global attributes and update equations retain their current behavior.

The regression suite performs actual `torch.save` / `torch.load` round trips and compares four subsequent steps against uninterrupted training. It covers each option separately, the combined options, one and two parameter groups, overriding conflicting constructor settings, old checkpoint dictionaries, and options changed during training.

## Validation

Native CPU validation with Python 3.12.14 and PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New tests: **10 failed / 4 passed before; 14 passed after**.
- Existing LAMB selection: **7 failed / 1 passed before and after**; with new tests, **7 failed / 15 passed**. The seven retained failures are `tests/test_optimizer.py::TestOptim::test_optimizer[Lamb_0]` through `[Lamb_6]`, all at the pre-existing snapshot comparison in `_test_state_dict` (line 205). Native `load_state_dict` shares moment tensor storage with the input checkpoint in this PyTorch version; subsequent steps mutate the input tensors. The preceding resumed-parameter comparisons pass, as does the existing neural-network case.
- Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check` pass for the changed files.

This validation covers optimizer state dictionaries on CPU. It does not cover CUDA, the historical CI version matrix, whole-optimizer pickling/deepcopy, or unrelated optimizers.

entries.title: Preserve AdaBound initial rates across added groups and checkpoints
entries.head: 2a5635e395da99e8a46c967e502eb9d5c4d1842d
entries.published_body:
## Problem

AdaBound keeps its initial learning rates in a constructor-only `base_lrs` list. This breaks two ordinary training workflows:

- A parameter group added during progressive unfreezing is silently skipped by `zip(param_groups, base_lrs)`, so its parameters never update.
- The initial rates are absent from `state_dict()`. Loading a checkpoint into an optimizer constructed with different rates changes the final-bound scaling and the continued training trajectory. Copying an optimizer also drops the list and makes the next step fail.

## Change

Store each group's initial rate in its serialized `base_lr` field, initialize it when a group is added, and rebuild the existing `base_lrs` list when state is restored. Older checkpoints remain loadable: their constructor's initial rates are retained when available. The update equations are unchanged.

The regression tests compare added groups with independent optimizers and compare continued training after actual `torch.save` / `torch.load` with uninterrupted training. They cover AdaBound and AMSBound, explicit and inherited added-group rates, multiple groups, learning-rate changes, different constructor rates on resume, legacy checkpoints, and deepcopy.

## Validation

Native CPU validation with Python 3.12.14 and PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New regression suite: **10 failed / 2 passed before; 12 passed after**.
- Existing AdaBound selection: **7 failed / 4 passed before and after**; together with the new tests, **7 failed / 16 passed**. All seven retained failures are `tests/test_optimizer.py::TestOptim::test_optimizer[AdaBound_0]` through `[AdaBound_6]`, at the pre-existing saved-state comparison in `_test_state_dict` (line 205). In this PyTorch version, loaded moment tensors share storage with the input checkpoint; subsequent steps change those tensors, violating the test's snapshot-immutability expectation. The preceding resumed-parameter comparisons pass. The three benchmark cases and neural-network case pass.
- Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check` pass for the changed files. The repository-pinned Flake8 4.0.1 cannot start on Python 3.12 because it uses the removed entry-points mapping API; its pycodestyle and pyflakes components were run directly.

This validation does not cover CUDA, the historical CI version matrix, or unrelated optimizers.

entries.title: Initialize MADGRAD state lazily from each parameter group
entries.head: f9570ad675c5915762f2fd949bc625116ef84cd0
entries.published_body:
## Problem

MADGRAD creates parameter state only during construction and uses the constructor's global momentum value. A group overriding momentum from zero to a positive value has no `x0` and fails on its first step. A group added later during unfreezing has no accumulators and fails with `KeyError: grad_sum_sq`.

## Change

Initialize the accumulators when each parameter first receives a gradient, using its effective parameter-group momentum. This covers both constructor overrides and `add_param_group()`, while preserving the existing group step counters and update equations. Sparse-gradient compatibility checks still run before initialization.

## Validation

Native CPU tests with Python 3.12.14 and PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New suite: **9 failed / 6 passed before; 15 passed after**. Tests compare independent optimizers for momentum overrides and added groups, cover explicit and inherited learning rates and weight decay, perform real `torch.save` / `torch.load` continuation, and train a newly added sparse Embedding.
- Existing MADGRAD selection retains **7 failed / 4 passed** before and after. The seven existing `TestOptim::test_optimizer[MADGRAD_0..6]` failures are the saved-state snapshot comparison in `_test_state_dict` at line 205: native checkpoint loading shares tensor storage and subsequent steps mutate the input checkpoint. The preceding resumed-parameter comparisons and the three benchmark cases plus neural-network case pass.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

The scope is state initialization for constructor groups and newly added groups. Changing an already trained group's momentum mode, CUDA, and the historical CI matrix are outside this validation.

entries.title: Preserve the SWATS momentum buffer during SGD updates
entries.head: 2155681b316f95e8a5449707254747a98c731748
entries.published_body:
## Problem

After SWATS switches to SGD, the local gradient aliases the momentum buffer. Multiplying that direction by `1 - beta1` also scales the saved buffer, so the next step uses a different momentum recurrence. The Nesterov branch additionally loses the distinction between the current gradient and the accumulated velocity.

For constant unit gradients, beta1=0.9 and lr=0.1, three SGD steps from 1.0 currently end near 0.95929 instead of the normalized-momentum result 0.9439.

## Change

Keep the buffer as `u = beta1 * u + gradient`, form the Nesterov direction from the current gradient and that buffer, and apply `1 - beta1` only in the final step coefficient. Adam-phase calculations and the phase-switch criterion are unchanged.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New native tests: **10 failed / 2 passed before; 12 passed after**. The independent oracle is `torch.optim.SGD` with learning rate scaled by `1 - beta1`; cases cover zero/nonzero momentum, Nesterov, weight decay, a natural automatic phase switch, and real checkpoint continuation.
- All **4 existing SWATS convergence tests** in `test_basic.py` and `test_optimizer_with_nn.py` pass after the change; these also passed on the base revision.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

Validation is limited to the listed CPU tests; it does not claim the full optimizer suite or CUDA coverage.

entries.title: Support strided parameters in AdamP and SGDP projections
entries.head: 7d0c28d394df79f58e9cf1f435abce02f2c32d6e
entries.published_body:
## Problem

AdamP and SGDP flatten parameter/gradient tensors with `view` when computing channel and layer projections. Valid transposed weights and channels-last convolution weights can therefore fail during an optimizer step with the incompatible-size-and-stride error.

## Change

Use `reshape` in the two flattening helpers in both optimizers. These flattened tensors are read for norms and dot products; the original perturbation and parameter tensors still receive the updates. Projection formulas and parameter layout are preserved.

The same helper defect affects both optimizers, so they are fixed together.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New native tests: **12 failed / 4 passed before; 16 passed after**. Transposed and channels-last parameters are trained against contiguous copies, with and without Nesterov momentum and with projection disabled/enabled. Every update matches the reference and parameter strides are retained.
- All **8 existing AdamP/SGDP convergence tests** in `test_basic.py` and `test_optimizer_with_nn.py` pass after the change; these also passed on the base revision.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

Validation covers the listed CPU layouts and convergence cases. It does not claim CUDA or the full historical CI matrix.

entries.title: Key RAdam cached step sizes by their hyperparameters
entries.head: 0a017f50f9011084e8b32cfa28d3bfac3451fc4c
entries.published_body:
## Problem

RAdam caches a learning-rate-dependent step size using only the parameter's step counter. Groups with the same betas can share that cache, so a later group can use the first group's learning rate. A parameter receiving its first gradient after a learning-rate change can also reuse a stale entry. Iterable groups with different betas have the same problem when they bypass the list-only constructor setup.

With learning rates 0.01 and 0.1, the second parameter's first coordinate becomes approximately 0.997 instead of 0.970 for a gradient of 0.3.

## Change

Key each cache entry by every scalar that determines its value: step, beta1, beta2, and learning rate. The update equations and cache size are unchanged. Old checkpoints with integer-only keys naturally miss and recompute their entries.

## Validation

Native CPU tests with Python 3.12.14 and PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New suite: **8 failed / 6 passed before; 14 passed after**. Grouped training is compared step by step with independent optimizers, across list/generator inputs, different betas, both learning-rate orders, delayed gradients, rectified and early steps, and old cache entries.
- Existing RAdam selection retains **7 failed / 4 passed** before and after. The seven existing `TestOptim::test_optimizer[RAdam_0..6]` failures are the saved-state snapshot comparison in `_test_state_dict` at line 205: loaded moment tensors share storage with the input checkpoint and subsequent steps mutate them. The preceding resumed-parameter comparisons and the three benchmark cases plus neural-network case pass.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

CPU validation does not cover CUDA or the historical CI matrix. The repository's RAdam deprecation warnings remain unchanged.

The earlier #103 separated buffers for constructor lists with different betas; it did not include learning rates in the cache key or cover generator groups and delayed gradients.

entries.title: Accumulate Shampoo mode statistics before preconditioning
entries.head: cff7891eae17729df921fc7da16d4ee08d5942a3
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Shampoo updates a mode's Gram matrix and immediately applies its inverse factor to the gradient. The next mode then accumulates statistics from an already preconditioned gradient. All mode statistics should instead use the same gradient before any inverse factors are applied.

For gradient [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and epsilon=0.5, the second-mode statistic becomes approximately [[0.968, 0.364], [0.364, 1.227]] instead of [[10.5, 14], [14, 20.5]]. This changes subsequent preconditioning and parameter updates.

## Change

Accumulate and refresh all mode factors first, then apply the factors to the gradient. The cached-factor update frequency, momentum/decay preparation, and existing matrix-power exponent are preserved.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New tests: **6 failed / 5 passed before; 11 passed after**. Independent tensor contractions compute each raw-gradient Gram matrix; eigendecomposition supplies an update oracle. Cases cover scalar through four-dimensional parameters, two factor-refresh frequencies, several steps, and actual checkpoint continuation.
- The existing **Shampoo neural-network convergence test passes** before and after.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

The separate open #548 changes the matrix-power exponent. Its full diff was checked; this patch addresses the input statistics and retains the current exponent so the fixes remain separate concerns. CPU validation does not cover CUDA or the full historical CI matrix.

entries.title: Warm up Apollo groups toward their own learning rates
entries.head: 1c8eb55b9296f6fae92f68d79ba90db18d36eecf
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Apollo initializes `base_lr` in the shared defaults from the constructor's global learning rate. A parameter group with its own `lr` therefore warms up toward a different rate from the one it will use after warmup. Newly added groups inherit the same incorrect target.

For a group with lr=0.1 and global lr=0.01, warmup=2 and init_lr=0.001, two unit-gradient steps from 1.0 produce approximately 0.9935 instead of the independent-optimizer result 0.9485.

## Change

Initialize `base_lr` when each group is registered, after defaults have been applied, using that group's effective `lr`. Explicit group `base_lr` values are preserved. The warmup schedule and update equations are unchanged.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New tests: **5 failed / 10 passed before; 15 passed after**. Grouped trajectories match independent optimizers for list/generator inputs, different rate orders and warmup lengths, newly added groups, and explicit base rates preserved through actual checkpoint restoration.
- The existing **Apollo neural-network convergence test passes** before and after.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

Validation covers the listed CPU cases; CUDA and the full optimizer test suite were not run.

entries.title: Preserve precision in NovoGrad gradient norm accumulation
entries.head: e9e3c740e13b1b8806c7999ad3fdb547e5b39263
entries.published_body:
## Problem

NovoGrad always creates its scalar second moments in the default floating dtype and squares gradients before selecting an accumulation dtype. Float64 gradient norms can therefore overflow or underflow when copied into float32 state, while FP16 gradients can overflow or underflow during the square itself. For example, nonzero gradients of magnitude 2000 in FP16 produce an infinite norm and no parameter update.

Float64 checkpoint restoration also changes the scalar-state dtype through PyTorch's native casting rules, so continued training can differ from uninterrupted training.

## Change

Keep float64 norm state for float64 parameters and float32 norm state otherwise, including the AMSGrad maximum. Convert gradients to that accumulation dtype before squaring. The default float32 update formula is unchanged.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New tests: **22 failed / 4 passed before; 26 passed after**. An independent double-precision norm checks float64 range, FP16 overflow/underflow, bfloat16, float32 controls, gradient averaging, and AMSGrad. Actual float64 checkpoint continuation matches uninterrupted training exactly.
- All **4 existing NovoGrad convergence tests** pass before and after.
- Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check` pass for changed files.

This covers CPU normalization and float64 checkpoint continuation. Half-precision checkpoint loading retains PyTorch's existing state-casting policy; this patch does not add master-state restoration. CUDA and the full optimizer suite are outside the validation scope.

entries.title: Synchronize Lookahead slow weights after each k fast steps
entries.head: 523e7700df266a7354a7b1f8177ad49b5ea9bd9f
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Lookahead captures its first slow weights after the first inner update and synchronizes at fast steps 1, k+1, 2k+1, and so on. The first synchronization is a no-op, and later interpolation uses the wrong initial weights and cadence.

## Change

Capture slow weights before the first fast step, then synchronize after every completed block of k fast steps. Initialization remains lazy, so model weights loaded after optimizer construction are captured correctly. Closure results and the inner optimizer's momentum state are preserved.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu:

- New native tests: **13 failed / 6 passed before; 19 passed after**. A closed-form geometric-series oracle checks constant-gradient SGD with and without momentum across k=1/2/5 and alpha=0/0.5/1, including partial blocks and weights loaded after construction. A quadratic closure checks both returned losses and the synchronized parameter value.
- All **4 existing Lookahead convergence tests** pass before and after.
- Changed files pass Black 23.3.0, isort 5.9.3, pycodestyle, pyflakes, and `git diff --check`.

The scope is slow-weight initialization and update cadence. The existing modern-PyTorch state_dict-hook compatibility problem is unchanged and is not presented as passing checkpoint coverage. CUDA and the full historical CI matrix are outside this validation.

entries.title: Allow fine-tuning with zero learning-rate warmup
entries.head: 5b83003c23a587803a27f707ac532dd077c670ad
entries.published_body:
## What does this PR do?

Fixes #2395.

All five fine-tuning scheduler factories construct a LambdaLR that evaluates `step / warmup_steps` immediately. Choosing `warmup_steps=0` therefore raises ZeroDivisionError before training starts, even though disabling warmup is supported by TrainArgs.

Return the existing cosine scheduler directly when warmup is zero. It starts at the configured learning rate and decays over `max_steps`. Positive warmup keeps its existing LambdaLR/SequentialLR path. The same two-line guard applies to LoRA, legacy LoRA, full fine-tuning, adapter, and adapter v2.

## Validation

- 20 native regression cases across all five entry points: upstream base 10 failed / 10 passed; patch 20 passed.
- Check every step against the closed-form warmup/cosine schedule and verify actual SGD parameter updates for two parameter groups.
- A real `torch.save`/`torch.load` optimizer/scheduler round trip exactly matches uninterrupted subsequent parameter updates. Both zero and positive warmup are covered.
- `python -m pytest tests/test_finetune_lr_scheduler.py tests/test_args.py -q`: 21 passed, including the existing TrainArgs test.
- Applicable Python pre-commit hooks, including pinned Ruff 0.15.9, passed, along with compileall and `git diff --check`.
- Initializing the full pre-commit set was blocked by npm's `EALLOWGIT` restriction for the Prettier Node environment. Prettier does not match these Python files; the applicable hooks were run individually without changing hook configuration or npm policy.
- CPU validation with Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu, and Lightning 2.6.6. No GPU fine-tuning or full repository suite result is claimed.

entries.title: Train wrapped LoRA biases for lora_only policy
entries.head: 9d7e33c2600802dbe3e884eade98da0ed883d488
entries.published_body:
Fixes #2403

## Problem

`mark_only_lora_as_trainable(model, bias="lora_only")` leaves the standard LoRA layers' biases frozen. After LoRA moved to composition, the biases live on `m.linear.bias`, while this selector still checks `m.bias`. The requested policy consequently produces no bias gradients or optimizer updates.

## Changes

Select the wrapped linear bias on `LoRALinear`, including its `LoRAQKVLinear` subclass. Keep the base weights and unrelated module biases frozen. The existing `none` and `all` policies, bias-free layers and rank-zero wrappers retain their behavior.

## Validation

Base: `5341568a65e918a85cb284fac038de2157eebf3f`.

- Identical 27 new native cases on unchanged main: **6 failed, 21 passed**. With the fix: **27 passed**.
- New cases plus selected existing LoRA layer replacement, merge, GQA/MHA, index, convolution, initialization and legacy checkpoint tests: **148 passed, 1 skipped**. The skipped test requires CUDA/bitsandbytes.
- Real linear, MHA and selectively enabled GQA layers are checked against an independent explicit parameter-selection reference. Two SGD updates compare outputs, input gradients, all parameter gradients and final weights, while verifying frozen parameters remain unchanged.
- A small native LoRA GPT is trained for two steps under each bias policy. Bias-free and rank-zero wrappers, and unrelated linear biases, provide controls.
- All applicable Python pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_lora_bias_policy.py tests/test_lora.py \
  -k 'bias_policy or layer_replacement or lora_merge or mqa_gqa or lora_ind_correctness or compare_conv1d or merged_status or init_weights or load_legacy_state_dict' -q
```
