- Tests cover default and custom out-of-vocabulary ignore IDs, default and custom padding values, and both explicit and implicit target masks. They check equality with the unpadded loss, the actual IDs seen by the embedding, unchanged caller inputs, and finite backward gradients.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 MKL_NUM_THREADS=2 python -m pytest tests/test_xval_ignore_index.py tests/test_x_transformers.py -q -k xval`: **9 passed, 237 deselected**.
- `git diff --check` passed.

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. This is a focused XVal test run; the full repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

entries.title: Apply sequence lengths to continuous embedding pooling
entries.head: ec0f00ba4a26bbce60698a3cafabf81bc4652f2e
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`ContinuousTransformerWrapper` saves its pooling mask before converting `lens` to a boolean mask. With lengths supplied, attention sees the correct padding mask but average pooling still receives `None`, so padded outputs change both the pooled embedding and its gradients. An empty sequence can also produce a nonzero embedding.

## Change

Retain the original sequence mask after converting lengths, before adding memory-token mask entries. The pooled output then uses the same valid sequence positions as attention and excludes the memory tokens already removed from the output.

## Validation

Base: `b840af1a56690c08cb246a53c6582d39e52cb64b`.

- Thirteen new native tests: **5 failed, 8 passed** before; **13 passed** afterward.
- Compare a padded batch to independent unpadded per-row Encoder calls, including input gradients, explicit-mask/no-mask controls, zero/two memory tokens, projected outputs, returned embeddings, and an empty-length example.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 python -m pytest tests/test_continuous_pool_lengths.py tests/test_x_transformers.py::test_continuous_transformer_external_projects tests/test_x_transformers.py::test_caching_when_inputs_not_include_past_continuous -q`: **15 passed**.
- Ruff on the new tests and `git diff --cached --check` pass; staged and published Git trees match.

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. The complete suite and GPU/distributed execution were not run. This is separate from the earlier masked-mean helper shadowing fix in #359, which is already present in this base.

entries.title: Apply sequence-start masks to continuous attention
entries.head: d4fc48e7d484a12bbb6ea58b978b3dadc3b84d7f
entries.published_body:
## Problem

ContinuousTransformerWrapper accepts seq_start_pos and uses it for absolute positions, but does not mask the preceding padding from attention. Valid continuous-token predictions and gradients therefore depend on left-padding values, and cached decoding can include those padding keys.

## Change

Build the sequence-start mask in the input-token domain and combine it with an existing mask before prepending memory or external embeddings. Align it with the actual cached keys and selected queries, retain explicit KV-mask constraints including external memory, and use the returned-query mask for average pooling.

## Validation

- 41 native regression cases on the unchanged base: **33 failed, 8 passed**. With the patch: **41 passed**.
- Compare valid outputs and input gradients with individually unpadded Encoder/Decoder calls, for absolute and rotary positions. Padding gradients are exactly zero.
- Existing explicit-mask behavior, memory tokens, external memories, prefixed inputs, explicit key masks, and prefix pooling have focused controls.
- Full-sequence and appended-input KV caching cover cache ages zero, one and two. An independent attention-probability assertion verifies that explicitly masked historical prefix/body positions remain blocked.
- New cases plus the existing continuous hybrid-cache and external-projection tests: **43 passed**.
- Ruff on the new regression module and git diff --cached --check pass. Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu; the full repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

Related #382 changes rollout cut selection/history, and #413 adjusts discrete generation windows. Their patches do not add masking to this continuous-wrapper input path.

entries.title: Avoid copying output projections during next-latent KL training
entries.head: 81439399781ab0f8b4250b64a6a875147a685fff
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Next-latent KL training deep-copies the vocabulary projection on every forward pass. The standard linear head does not need a copy: the auxiliary objective only needs to stop gradients into its weights while retaining gradients into the rollout states. Tied-embedding heads are callables rather than modules, so the current `.parameters()` call also raises `AttributeError` for that supported configuration.

## Change

Use a functional projection with detached weights and bias for ordinary linear heads, and the detached token embedding plus the existing scale for native tied heads. Keep the existing copied-module path for custom modules and Linear subclasses, preserving their forward behavior.

## Validation

- 21 native regression cases compare losses and every model parameter gradient against an independent frozen-head reference. Coverage includes linear, tied, MLP, biased linear and overridden Linear heads, one/three rollout steps, and padded/unpadded inputs.
- Upstream base: 5 failed, 16 passed. With the change: 21 passed.
- New cases plus all six existing next-latent cases: 27 passed on CPU.
- A real torch.profiler regression verifies removal of the 4 MiB vocabulary-weight clone for a 32768 by 32 projection.
- Separate native CPU allocation measurements at 4096 by 16, 32768 by 32 and 65536 by 64 projection sizes preserve the exact reported losses. The largest individual operator allocation changes from 256 KiB / 4 MiB / 16 MiB to 128 KiB / 1 MiB / 2 MiB respectively. These are individual allocation sizes, not total process peak memory.
- Ruff for the new test module and git diff --cached --check pass. The complete repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

The timing samples were mixed, so this change claims removal of the redundant projection allocation and restoration of tied-head training, without a general throughput claim.

entries.title: Allow test-time adaptation with frozen base parameters
entries.head: fe2e093f870fca277d07e7a93f03473b238c5f7f
entries.published_body:
## Problem

TTT initializes its per-example fast weights by repeating the base parameters. If those parameters are frozen, the copies also have requires_grad=False, and the first adaptation step fails in torch.autograd.grad. This affects both training forward calls and generation with a frozen pretrained model or a frozen adapted layer.

## Change

Enable gradients on the repeated fast weights. The original parameters keep their values and requires_grad settings. When a base parameter is trainable, its existing graph connection is preserved for end-to-end training.

## Validation

- 12 native Decoder/TransformerWrapper/XLAutoregressiveWrapper cases: upstream base 8 failed, 4 passed; patched branch 12 passed.
- Covers fully frozen bases, a frozen adapted layer, an unfrozen control, optional episodic memories, real generation and forward/backward under an outer no_grad context.
- Losses, greedy tokens and adapted weights match an independent native reference with gradients enabled only on the reference's adaptation source.
- Fast weights actually change, base parameter values remain unchanged, frozen source gradients stay absent, and gradients of trainable base parameters match the reference.
- Ruff on the regression module and git diff --cached --check pass. CPU validation used PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. The complete repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

entries.title: Apply each distinct test-time training mapping once
entries.head: 3a4ae22b62dce3320a2316673390448bab7648b2
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Low-rank TTT paths automatically add a source-to-target mapping. If the same module is also listed in ttt_module_paths, the mapping appears twice. The wrapper instances are deduplicated but the update mappings are not, so the same gradient and weight decay are applied repeatedly. Explicit repeated paths and equivalent string/pair forms have the same effect.

## Change

Deduplicate the normalized source/target pairs while preserving their order. Different targets for the same source remain distinct. This gives each configured mapping one update per inner step, including automatically registered low-rank memories.

## Validation

- 20 native Decoder/TransformerWrapper/XLAutoregressiveWrapper cases: upstream base 16 failed, 4 passed; patched branch 20 passed.
- Explicit one-step SGD and weight-decay references cover repeated paths, string/pair aliases, low-rank overlap, and a shared-source/different-target control.
- Both create_graph modes and optional episodic memories are exercised.
- Real two-chunk training with redundant and unique configurations produces the same loss and every model parameter gradient.
- Ruff on the regression module and git diff --cached --check pass. CPU validation used PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. The complete repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

This corrects the number of adaptation updates; it does not change the optimizer formula or claim a measured model-quality gain.

entries.title: Return differentiable zero for empty training targets
entries.head: 1cb08d3b6b4b354b876076140c1c64c6e15770b5
entries.published_body:
## Problem

An autoregressive batch can contain no supervised targets after the next-token shift, ignored labels, or the per-example length mask. The regular token loss, loop-exit loss and continuous next-embedding loss currently average empty selections and produce NaN. This can invalidate an otherwise usable accumulated training step.

## Change

Normalize the summed token loss by a valid-target count clamped to one. For loop-exit and continuous losses, keep the existing mean when valid elements exist and use a differentiable empty sum otherwise. Fully unsupervised batches now contribute zero loss and finite zero gradients.

## Validation

- 22 new cases on the upstream base: 18 failed, 4 passed.
- Patched cases plus the existing looped-transformer test: 23 passed on CPU.
- Real Decoder/TransformerWrapper training covers ignored labels, length-one masks and one-token inputs with looped training, mixture-of-softmax output or continuous prediction enabled.
- Nonempty controls compare the loss and every parameter gradient to native cross-entropy/NLL and L1 references.
- A real FP16 continuous-head case whose elementwise sum overflows verifies that the existing finite mean and finite gradients are preserved.
- Ruff on the regression module and git diff --cached --check pass. PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu; the complete repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

entries.title: Align auxiliary training losses with text after prepended embeddings
entries.head: 96939cc3f6d1d15680b1d04cdc56138ff869c3d7
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Prepended embeddings are removed from the main language-model logits before computing the next-token loss, but remain in the continuous prediction tensors and looped decoder caches. With a nonempty prefix, the auxiliary predictions no longer align with the text labels: joint continuous prediction raises a mask-shape error, and looped training raises a prediction/target batch-size mismatch.

## Change

Remove the same prefix from the continuous predictions and initial embeddings, as well as the per-loop prediction and exit logits. Apply the existing next-token shift afterward. Calls without a prefix retain their current behavior and loss normalization.

## Validation

- Sixteen native Decoder/TransformerWrapper/AutoregressiveWrapper regression cases cover ordinary and looped training, continuous prediction enabled/disabled, prefix lengths zero/two, and ignored text targets.
- Baseline: **6 failed, 10 passed**. With the patch: **16 passed**.
- Independent references calculate per-loop cross-entropy, hazard/survival weighting, exit BCE and the continuous L1 objective, then compare losses, all model gradients and prefix gradients.
- New cases plus the existing looped-wrapper regression: **17 passed**. The full repository test suite was not run.
- Ruff on the new regression module and `git diff --cached --check` pass.

CPU validation with PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. This repairs prefix-conditioned training loss alignment; it does not claim a measured model-quality or throughput gain.

entries.title: Prevent half-precision Muon normalization from zeroing finite updates
entries.head: 6ad9c8e0475755b16f3e24b787f26a037ca5b33c
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Muon normalizes each batched gradient matrix in its input dtype. A matrix can have finite float16 elements but a norm above 65504; that norm becomes infinity and the entire Newton-Schulz update becomes zero. This silently skips test-time adaptation even though the original gradient is finite.

## Change

Compute float16 normalization with a float32 norm and division, then restore the input dtype before the Newton-Schulz iterations. Other dtypes, shapes, coefficients, iteration count and the non-matrix SGD path retain their existing behavior.

## Validation

- 20 new cases: unchanged base 8 failed, 12 passed; patched branch 20 passed.
- Tall, wide and multi-batch half matrices cover large and ordinary scales, zero/five iterations, finite nonzero updates, input ownership and a double-precision normalization reference.
- Float32/float64/bfloat16 controls preserve the existing output exactly; zero and non-matrix controls are included.
- A real half-precision RMSNorm Decoder with a scaled next-token objective exercises both create_graph modes. Its matrix norms overflow in half while every gradient element remains finite. Adapted fast parameters match the reference, and the subsequent native forward/backward remains finite.
- Ruff on the regression module and git diff --cached --check pass. CPU validation with PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu; GPU and the complete repository suite were not run.

The training regression uses RMSNorm. Native CPU half LayerNorm double-backward at large loss scales has a separate NaN limitation; this change does not claim to solve general second-order half-precision stability or to change the Newton-Schulz iteration arithmetic.

entries.title: Preserve hidden states and apply the full mixture output head
entries.head: 61043c7db334bd1e1bdb31a37b0a47e224d8b9e1
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Mixture-of-softmax projection replaces the decoder hidden tensor with its expanded mixture components. Returning embeddings then either raises on an unassigned logits variable or returns a rank-four tensor; continuous next-embedding prediction receives the same expanded tensor and training fails on incompatible targets.

Looped training also bypasses the mixture and sigsoftmax transformations when recording per-loop predictions. With mixture_of_softmax enabled, the autoregressive wrapper consequently applies NLL to raw linear scores instead of the declared log probabilities.

## Change

Keep the full output projection in one helper, used by final and per-loop predictions. Mixture expansion stays local to that projection, so returned hidden states and continuous predictions keep their decoder dimensions. Embedding-only returns skip logit transformations and initialize the optional logits value explicitly.

## Validation

- 25 new native cases: upstream base 19 failed, 6 passed; patched branch 25 passed.
- Including the existing looped-transformer regression: 26 passed on CPU.
- Two/four mixture components, ordinary output heads, sigsoftmax, embedding return modes, prepended embeddings and continuous-head training are covered.
- Direct weighted-probability references check final and per-loop predictions. A separate exit-weighted NLL calculation verifies the real training loss and every model parameter gradient.
- Ruff on the regression module and git diff --cached --check pass. PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu; the full repository suite and GPU execution were not run.

entries.title: Preserve histogram probability mass in entropy calibration
entries.head: 7ea94334d49d7cf39e7f3f953b0c054c3205b086
entries.published_body:
### Description

Correct reconstruction of a quantized histogram when evaluating entropy-calibration thresholds:

- Store reconstructed bucket averages in floating point instead of truncating them into the integer histogram dtype.
- Expand the final quantized bucket over its complete interval, including the remainder bins already accumulated into that bucket.
- Distribute each bucket's mass only over the originally occupied histogram bins.

These changes make the reconstructed distribution preserve the quantized bucket mass and original support. Candidate threshold enumeration, outlier handling, smoothing, KL selection, and threshold dtypes retain their existing behavior.

### Motivation and Context

Integer truncation and incomplete expansion can change the distribution compared by KL divergence, selecting an incorrect clipping interval. The regression cases use independent Python bucket reconstruction to check mass conservation and support, then exercise real CPU calibration, persisted calibration data, static quantization, and quantized inference.

For the fixed integration fixture, correcting histogram reconstruction changes the stored UINT8 activation scale from `16/255` to the independently expected `13/255`. This is a correctness result for that fixture, not a claim of a general model-accuracy gain.

### Validation

- Built the Release CPU runtime from this exact PR commit using the official `tools/ci_build/build.py` on Ubuntu 24.04 / Python 3.12. The [source-build job](https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43299831579/job/131467712087) completed compilation and produced the wheel.
- The [successful native validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43304990254) consumes that exact source-built wheel and checks its source commit and installed calibration source bytes: **27 passed, 17 subtests passed**, including the existing calibration module.
- Restoring the original calibration implementation in the same runtime reproduces **1 failing test method and 10 failing subtests**; the other controls pass. The follow-up validation corrects source-package shadowing during the first job's pytest collection.
- Ruff lint, Ruff formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

Validation covers the CPU calibration/quantization paths above; the full C++ and GPU suites were not run.

entries.title: Prevent range overflow in blocked quantization
entries.head: 8554dd5683f4d6e492d38b530d6d4f14755680f5
entries.published_body:
### Description
Blocked quantization computes the difference between the maximum and minimum weights in the input dtype. Opposite-sign float16 weights near 60000, or float32 weights near 2e38, overflow that subtraction even though the resulting scale is representable. Infinite scales then corrupt the quantized weights.

Promote both range endpoints to float64 before subtracting them. The final scale still uses the weight dtype, and the existing zero-point, symmetry, clipping, block layout and degenerate-range rules are retained.

### Validation
- Added 8 unittest methods with 40 subcases covering float16/float32, both axes, int8/uint8, symmetric/asymmetric ranges, same-sign symmetric ranges, read-only noncontiguous weights, and ordinary/small/zero-range controls.
- An independent Python-float calculation checks every block's scale and zero point.
- Native CPU blocked DequantizeLinear and actual static QDQ quantization followed by MatMul verify finite persisted scales and inference results. Graph optimization is disabled for these integration checks.
- New tests plus existing quantization utility and block-size tests: **25 methods passed, 183 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original implementation yields **28 failing subtests**, 8 completed methods and 12 passing subtests.
- Ruff lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43400845218

The runtime was built with the official CPU Release build.py/CMake path from commit 8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80, whose C++ sources match base a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7. This run installs that built wheel, verifies the matching native-source baseline, and overlays the complete quantization Python package from this exact patch with byte-for-byte checks and a SHA-256 manifest. It uses ordinary native imports. This is targeted Linux CPU validation, not a GPU or full C++ test-suite result.

### Motivation and Context
Finite weight ranges should produce finite scales when those scales fit in the original dtype. This fixes the blocked helper's intermediate range subtraction; it does not change the quantization algorithm or claim a general model-accuracy improvement.

entries.title: Normalize negative axes in blocked quantization helpers
entries.head: a798a04dfbdddb08181903bc7d73923ca97dd2b3
entries.published_body:
### Description
Both `compute_scale_zp_blocked` and the blocked path of `quantize_onnx_initializer` accept an axis but use its original value when enumerating the other dimensions. For a rank-2 weight and axis -1 or -2, that enumeration includes both dimensions, so valid input fails while reshaping the weights.

Normalize a negative axis immediately after indexing the selected dimension. This preserves the existing out-of-range-axis validation and makes the remaining layout calculations use the same axis as NumPy. Scale computation, rounding, clipping, per-channel quantization and the rank-2 restriction are unchanged. The main QDQ quantizer already normalizes its axis; this fixes the two lower-level entry points.

### Validation
- Added 7 unittest methods with 50 subcases: positive/negative-axis equality across float16/float32, int8/uint8, symmetric/asymmetric ranges and block sizes; quantized initializer contents; read-only noncontiguous inputs; invalid-axis and existing rank/per-channel controls.
- Native CPU DequantizeLinear followed by MatMul, with optimization disabled, checks both negative axes against independently reconstructed weights.
- New and existing `test_quant_util.py` / `test_qdq_block_size.py`: **24 methods passed, 193 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the exact original implementation yields **46 failed subtests**, 7 completed methods and 4 passing subtests. Failures occur in parameter calculation, initializer packing, noncontiguous-input and native integration cases.
- Ruff lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43308384299

The runtime was built with the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake path from commit 8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80, whose C++ sources match base a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7. This run installs that built wheel, verifies the unchanged native-source baseline, and overlays the complete quantization package from this exact patch with byte-for-byte checks and a SHA-256 manifest. It uses ordinary native imports. This is targeted Linux CPU validation; it does not claim GPU or the full C++ test suite.

### Motivation and Context
Negative axes are an existing supported way to identify tensor dimensions. Equivalent positive and negative values should produce identical blocked quantization parameters and initializers, including when these helpers are called directly.

entries.title: Vectorize byte packing for four-bit quantized weights
entries.head: d8596d3fe7a5b0d548e52a97f2252111035b1879
entries.published_body:
### Description

Packing INT4/UINT4 weights currently runs a Python iteration for every pair of elements. Add a NumPy bitwise path for bytes and bytearray inputs, writing the low and high nibbles into the destination bytearray.

The layout, odd-length zero padding, return type and input ownership are unchanged. Other sequences retain the original element-wise path, including noncontiguous and non-byte memoryviews.

### Validation

- Seven new unittest methods cover all signed/unsigned nibble pairs, empty/odd/even lengths, bytearray ownership, strided/reversed/signed/wider buffer inputs, explicit nibble order and persisted INT4/UINT4 initializer bytes.
- Native CPU DequantizeLinear followed by MatMul checks actual quantized initializers against independently reconstructed float16/float32 weights.
- New and existing quantization utility tests: **16 methods passed, 163 subtests passed**.
- The same new tests pass on the original helper: **7 methods, 32 subtests**. This is a performance improvement; the original packing outputs are already correct.
- Ruff lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Exact-source native validation and benchmark: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43401492131

### Measured helper performance

One warmup and five timed calls per case, with median time reported. Input construction is outside the measured region. Peak Python/NumPy allocations are measured separately with tracemalloc; packed output hashes match in every case.

| Input elements | Original median | Patched median | Original peak | Patched peak |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 | 0.002233 ms | 0.005738 ms | 73 B | 978 B |
| 4,096 | 0.298420 ms | 0.006619 ms | 2,261 B | 5,134 B |
| 1,000,000 | 74.687110 ms | 0.519886 ms | 500,213 B | 1,001,038 B |
| 8,000,000 | 571.160013 ms | 7.104263 ms | 4,000,213 B | 8,001,038 B |

The shifted odd-element array adds temporary storage of roughly half the input length. Tiny inputs are slower, as shown above. These results concern this packing helper only, not end-to-end quantization throughput or model accuracy.

The native runtime comes from the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake build at 8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80. Its C++ sources match base a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7. The validation installs that built wheel and overlays the complete quantization package from this exact patch, verifying every Python file byte-for-byte and recording a SHA-256 manifest. Tests use normal native imports. This is targeted Linux CPU validation, not GPU execution or the full C++ suite.

entries.title: Fix numerical stability of distribution calibration moments
entries.head: 8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80
entries.published_body:
### Description

Compute distribution-calibration histogram moments in float64 before converting the resulting mean and standard deviation back to the histogram dtype:

- Form bin midpoints after promotion, so finite float16 endpoints do not overflow during addition.
- Apply the existing signed-power transform in the promoted dtype.
- Compute the second central moment directly, avoiding the overflow, underflow, and cancellation in `E[x²] - E[x]²`.

The change preserves the histogram's output dtype, signed-power convention, empty-histogram behavior, and zero variance of a single occupied bin.

### Motivation and Context

Finite float16/float32 histograms can currently produce infinite, zero, or NaN standard deviations even when the correct result is representable. This propagates into distribution calibration ranges and FP8 quantization scales.

The regression tests compare histogram moments with independently expanded observations and exercise real CPU MatMul calibration, persisted calibration data, and static FP8 quantization. They cover midpoint overflow, squared-moment overflow/underflow, cancellation, signed powers, and control cases.

### Validation

- Built the Release CPU runtime from this exact source commit with the official `tools/ci_build/build.py` entry point on Ubuntu 24.04 / Python 3.12. The [source-build job](https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43296543822/job/131456261228) completed compilation and produced the wheel.
- The [successful native validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43303231831) downloads only that source-built wheel, verifies its source commit and installed `calibrate.py` bytes, and runs the new tests together with `test_calibration.py`: **31 passed, 15 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original `calibrate.py` into the same native runtime reproduces **7 failing test methods and 6 failing subtests**; the remaining controls pass. The initial build job's test-collection path was corrected in the linked follow-up validation.
- Ruff lint, Ruff formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.

Validation is limited to the CPU calibration/quantization paths above. This does not claim support for arbitrary extreme float64 powers or a general model-accuracy improvement; the full C++ and GPU suites were not run.

entries.title: Preserve captured subgraph dependencies in quantization graph utilities
entries.head: ff57d2442bf826c42f0dd70c96b1e6b7001447e1
entries.published_body:
### Description

The quantization ONNXModel utilities only consider a node's explicit inputs. Values captured by an If or Loop subgraph are consequently missing from topological dependencies and unused-constant analysis. A valid model can be reordered so a capture precedes its producer, or lose a constant/initializer used only inside a subgraph.

Collect lexical dependencies recursively from GRAPH and GRAPHS attributes, including graph outputs that directly reference an outer value. Subtract each subgraph's formal inputs, dense/sparse initializers and local node outputs so local names correctly shadow outer values. Use this input set for both topological sorting and constant cleanup. Seed sorting from graph inputs and both dense and sparse root initializers, using each sparse initializer's `values.name`.

This addresses one missing-dependency problem in both consumers. It does not reorder subgraph-internal nodes or change the separate transformers.OnnxModel implementation.

### Validation

- Ten new unittest methods cover native If/Loop execution, nested captures, save/reload, captured constants and initializers, local-name shadowing, duplicate explicit inputs, missing/cyclic capture rejection, and sparse-only captures.
- New and existing model graph tests on `ff57d2442bf826c42f0dd70c96b1e6b7001447e1`: **13 methods passed and 13 subtests passed**, with no skips.
- The two sparse-capture methods exercise four subcases: both If branches and Loop trip counts 0 and 2. They execute valid models on the native CPU runtime, sort/save/reload them, retain the sparse initializer without a dense duplicate, and check the resulting values.
- Restoring the helper from the preceding PR head `16f7f332eac743749ade445f8cecc7f2d4d688b2` in the same runtime makes all four sparse subcases fail with `Graph is not a DAG`. The runner reports `4 failed, 2 passed, 8 deselected`: the four failures are subcases across the two selected methods.
- The GRAPHS attribute control checks dependency ordering only; no custom operator execution is claimed.
- Repository `lintrunner` initialization, changed-file formatting and lint, remote Ruff checks, and `git diff --check` passed.

[Exact-source native CPU validation and parent comparison](https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43408398837). The earlier lexical-capture comparison is retained in [the preceding validation run](https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43401505086).

The native runtime is the unchanged wheel from the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake build at `8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80`. Its C++ sources match base `a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7`. The validation installs that built wheel and overlays the complete quantization package from the exact patch, verifying all 60 Python files byte-for-byte and recording a SHA-256 manifest. Tests use normal native imports on the hosted Ubuntu runner. This is targeted Linux CPU validation, not GPU execution or the full C++ suite.

Local native imports were blocked before testing by this host's executable-stack policy; the native results above come from the linked hosted run.

### Motivation and Context

Control-flow subgraphs use ONNX lexical scoping. Graph transformations must retain and order those dependencies just as they do explicit node inputs.

entries.title: Handle scalar and empty tensors in integer quantization helpers
entries.head: be74e3b96032bfdc7060e1a91625de54d1bf773f
entries.published_body:
### Description

Integer `compute_data_quant_params` uses `len(data)` to decide whether an array contains values. This raises on a zero-dimensional tensor and misclassifies empty shapes such as `(2, 0)` as nonempty, leading to invalid reductions or inconsistent override handling.

Use `data.size` for the three element-count checks. Scalars now follow the same quantization calculation as a one-element vector. Empty integer tensors use the existing identity scale/zero-point defaults regardless of which dimension is empty, while preserving their shape.

### Validation

- Seven new unittest methods cover FP16/FP32, INT4/UINT4/INT8/UINT8/INT16/UINT16, symmetric/asymmetric settings, explicit hard-coded scale/code expectations, range overrides, minimum range, readonly inputs and invalid-argument controls.
- A native CPU `DequantizeLinear + Add` model consumes the scalar quantized initializer after ONNX save/reload.
- New and existing quantization utility tests: **16 methods passed, 279 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original helper produces **1 failing method and 123 failing subtests** (pytest reports 124 failures), with 6 completed methods and 25 passing subtests.
- Ruff 0.12.12 lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43402852485

The runtime was built using the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake process at `8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80`. Its C++ sources match base `a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7`. This Python-only validation installs that built wheel, overlays the complete quantization package from this exact commit, and verifies byte equality and hashes before normal native imports. It does not claim a separate C++ rebuild for this Python-only change.

### Motivation and Context

The public array helpers should determine emptiness by total element count. This change is limited to integer quantization; FLOAT8's separate statistics path is unchanged. Some higher-level initializer callers already flatten their inputs, so this is not a claim that every static quantization entry point previously rejected scalars. No model-quality or throughput improvement is claimed.

entries.title: Use wide accumulation for FLOAT8 weight statistics
entries.head: 5c574563ff5a3707345cd40f507e4c0cdbfb438f
entries.published_body:
### Description

FLOAT8 weight quantization computes the input standard deviation in the weight dtype. Finite FP16/FP32 weights can therefore produce an infinite or zero scale when the intermediate squared deviations overflow or underflow. The resulting codes can collapse or contain NaNs even when the final scale is representable.

Accumulate the standard deviation in float64 for FP16/FP32 input weights, then cast the final scale back to the original weight dtype. Other direct-helper input dtypes retain NumPy's existing default statistics/result dtype. The codebook reference distribution and zero-variance policy are unchanged.

### Validation

- Eight new unittest methods cover large and small nonconstant weights, independent `math.fsum` standard-deviation references, quantized FP8 codes, ordinary values/options, readonly strided inputs, zero variance and six other direct-helper input dtypes.
- Native CPU `DequantizeLinear + Add` inference consumes the saved/reloaded FP32-weight quantization result, with persisted scales and codes checked independently.
- New and existing quantization utility tests: **17 methods passed, 161 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original implementation produces **19 failing subtests**, with 8 completed methods and 11 passing subtests. These include finite large/small inputs as well as FP16 rounding controls.
- Ruff 0.12.12 lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43406537495

The runtime was built using the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake process at `8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80`. Its C++ sources match base `a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7`. This Python-only validation installs that built wheel, overlays the complete quantization package from this exact commit, and verifies byte equality and hashes before normal native imports.

### Motivation and Context

This repairs the direct FLOAT8 weight-statistics path. Histogram calibration, the codebook distribution, integer quantization and constant-weight policy keep their existing behavior. The tests establish numerical correctness for the covered FP16/FP32 scales; they do not measure end-to-end model accuracy or throughput.

entries.title: Preserve parent node properties during quantization subgraph traversal
entries.head: 0bceda4c8362cd68a0593cac842957d60363c7e2
entries.published_body:
### Description

Quantization's initializer-cleanup and Gemm-replacement passes reconstruct every parent node that contains graph attributes. That reconstruction drops the parent's domain, overload, documentation, metadata and graph-attribute metadata. A valid custom-function call can consequently become an unregistered default-domain operator.

Both passes already modify their GraphProto arguments in place. Recurse directly into the existing GRAPH and GRAPHS attributes and retain the original parent NodeProto. Initializer cleanup and Gemm replacement inside those graphs continue to run.

### Validation

- Seven new unittest methods exercise custom ONNX functions, overload dispatch, nested standard If nodes, repeated graph attributes, all non-graph node properties, actual inner-graph transformations and ordinary nodes.
- Native CPU inference checks the original and transformed custom-function models, including saved/reloaded models and both branch choices.
- New tests plus the existing ONNXModel tests: **10 methods passed, 16 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original implementation produces **14 failing subtests**, with 7 completed methods and 2 passing subtests.
- Ruff 0.12.12 lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43409044245

The runtime was built using the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake process at `8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80`. Its C++ sources match base `a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7`. This Python-only validation installs that built wheel, overlays the complete quantization package from this exact commit, and verifies byte equality and hashes before normal native imports.

### Motivation and Context

This preserves model semantics and metadata during the two recursive passes. Repeated GRAPHS attributes receive structural coverage; native execution covers valid custom-function and standard control-flow models. This change does not alter subgraph dependency sorting or measure model accuracy or throughput.

entries.title: Honor 16-bit overrides when upgrading FLOAT8 quantization opsets
entries.head: d9c51010d378330a4aeb9c3d7a9f4fdbba4866c4
entries.published_body:
### Description

A FLOAT8 quantization request can also contain INT16 or UINT16 tensor overrides, which require opset 21. For an input model at opset 17 or 18, the FLOAT8 branch currently wins first and upgrades only to opset 19. Mixed QDQ models then receive incompatible operator domains and can fail native model loading.

Let the existing 16-bit requirement take precedence over the FLOAT8-only upgrade. This is a one-condition change; blocked quantization, newer opsets, and other version rules retain their existing order.

### Validation

- Six new unittest methods cover direct and nested 16-bit overrides, direct TensorProto type inputs, ordinary upgrade rules, and preservation of the caller's source model.
- Eight real `quantize_static` models and two `get_qdq_config` models use supported FLOAT8 defaults with per-tensor 16-bit overrides. Tests check persisted opsets, domains and types, ONNX model validation, saved-model CPU inference, and an independent ONNX ReferenceEvaluator.
- New tests plus the existing quantization-utility tests: **15 methods passed, 167 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original implementation produces **1 failing method and 20 failing subtests** (pytest reports 21 failures), with 5 completed methods and 16 passing subtests. Failures include native loading of the incorrectly upgraded mixed models.
- Ruff 0.12.12 lint/format and `git diff --check` passed.

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/onnxruntime/actions/runs/43412825667

The runtime was built using the repository's official CPU Release build.py/CMake process at `8dea1194e974fa07b1d2f07a190949c3a92cab80`. Its C++ sources match base `a8246c0d094f1ab0d6bf236228e5e67683321cd7`. This Python-only validation installs that built wheel, overlays the complete quantization package from this exact commit, and verifies byte equality and hashes before normal native imports.

### Motivation and Context

The public integration tests use per-tensor overrides; validation of top-level mixed quantization types is unchanged. Native CPU inference disables graph optimization to exercise the saved QDQ graph directly. This fixes version selection and model validity without claiming a general quantization-accuracy or throughput improvement.

entries.title: Avoid quadratic list copying in the autologging metrics queue
entries.head: d537881b2c3d26be4e3faaf16b7d3c510a2b7199
entries.published_body:
### Related Issues/PRs No linked issue. ### What changes are proposed in this pull request? Preparing a queued metrics flush performs repeated list copying twice: grouping a run's metrics concatenates an ever-growing list, and removing each snapshot item repeatedly shifts the queue's remaining elements. These costs grow quadratically when a busy background logger accumulates a large queue. Append metrics to each run's list and delete the captured queue prefix in one operation. Producers only append; the flush lock excludes other removals. Deleting exactly the captured prefix therefore preserves metrics appended after the snapshot. Run order, per-run metric order, duplicates, and the queue object's identity are retained. A local benchmark times the complete `flush_metrics_queue` call with `MlflowClient` mocked to exclude network and storage work. Five repetitions per size produced these median CPU times: | Queued metrics | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | 500 (normal flush threshold) | 0.288 ms | 0.137 ms | | 10,000 (backlog) | 55.594 ms | 0.469 ms | | 50,000 (backlog) | 1,690.063 ms | 1.871 ms | These measurements isolate queue preparation on one machine; they are not end-to-end training or server benchmarks. The larger rows characterize backlog handling, not the usual 500-item queue. ### How is this PR tested? - [x] Existing unit/integration tests - [x] New unit/integration tests - [x] Manual tests `pytest -p pytest_mock -p pytest_timeout tests/utils/test_metrics_queue.py tests/utils/test_autologging_utils.py -q`: 10 passed. The seven new controls cover empty and large grouping, object identity/order, duplicate entries, and metrics appended by another thread while a flush is logging. All ten also pass on the baseline; this is a performance change with behavior-preservation checks. Pinned Ruff, Clint, character normalization, and `git diff --check` pass. The complete repository suite was not run. Full pre-commit initialization is blocked in this environment by npm's `EALLOWGIT` restriction on the Prettier environment; Python checks were run directly. entries.title: Prevent numeric overflow in regression `sum_on_target`
entries.head: 6d1ec610ae49ed6517332fafd446b6c5dc719509
entries.published_body: ### Related Issues/PRs Relates to #27729. That change corrects weight normalization for `mean_on_target`; this change fixes arithmetic precision in target accumulation. ### What changes are proposed in this pull request? Promote targets and sample weights to float64 before multiplication and summation in `_get_regressor_metrics`. NumPy can otherwise retain a narrow input dtype during arithmetic: summing uint8 targets `[200, 210]` reports 154, and applying uint8 weights `[2, 3]` reports 262 instead of 1030. Small signed integers can wrap negative, float16 accumulation can become infinite, and float32 can discard small contributions. The promoted calculation preserves the intended weighted sum and does not modify caller inputs. It also supplies the correct sum to the existing unweighted mean calculation. Values remain subject to float64 precision; this is not arbitrary-precision arithmetic. ### How is this PR tested? - [x] New unit/integration tests 18 new tests: 14 failed and 4 passed on the upstream base; all 18 pass with this change. They use independently calculated Python-float sums, cover integer/float dtypes, list and Series inputs, input immutability, and native `mlflow.models.evaluate` runs whose corrected sums are verified after persistence. Ruff 0.16.8, Clint, character normalization, and `git diff --check` pass. The broad legacy evaluator test module requires unavailable PySpark, so the full evaluator suite was not run. The complete pre-commit hook set could not be installed because npm rejected a Prettier dependency under its Git-install safety policy; the listed direct Python checks were executed. ### Does this PR require documentation update? - [x] No. ### Does this PR require updating the [MLflow Skills](https://github.com/mlflow/skills) repository? - [x] No. ### Release Notes #### Is this a user-facing change? - [x] Yes. entries.title: Compute mean BCa acceleration without quadratic jackknife samples
entries.head: 4d70d5066b326a5a2922fc2c2c71a6c1a455addb
entries.published_body:
### Related Issues/PRs Relates to #26396, which introduced paired evaluation comparisons. ### What changes are proposed in this pull request? The BCa interval for the mean currently uses SciPy's generic jackknife. For N paired rows, that constructs and reduces N leave-one-out samples, adding quadratic work beyond the bootstrap resampling. For the mean, the jackknife influence values are proportional to each observation minus the sample mean. Compute the acceleration from those centered second and third moments in linear time. Normalize the deviations before taking powers, retain SciPy's mid-rank bias correction, and apply the same BCa quantile adjustment to the original 10,000 seeded bootstrap means. The seed, resample count, batching, confidence level, and percentile fallback remain unchanged. An undefined BCa interval reuses the percentile interval from the same bootstrap distribution. ### How is this PR tested? - [x] Existing unit/integration tests - [x] New unit/integration tests - [x] Manual tests The 20 new numerical controls and the real constant-sample fallback control all pass on the original implementation. After this optimization, the complete comparison module plus the new controls pass: **78 tests**. The controls compare directly with native SciPy BCa jackknife intervals for small, normal, skewed, tied, binary, and negative-stride samples at three confidence levels. They also exercise the paired-comparison entry point and verify that inputs are unchanged. The fallback test uses actual undefined acceleration instead of a mocked bootstrap return. Local CPU timings, with one warmup and five timed repetitions per implementation and sample size, using the same lognormal data, 10,000 resamples, NumPy 2.5.4, and SciPy 1.18.1: | Paired rows | Original median | New median | | --- | ---: | ---: | | 1,000 | 35.15 ms | 32.42 ms | | 10,000 | 451.15 ms | 273.31 ms | | 25,000 | 1,963.62 ms | 760.50 ms | The largest bound difference in these benchmark cases is 1.56e-15. These are local confidence-interval timings, not end-to-end model or training measurements. The 10,000-by-N resampling cost remains.
