entries.head: 4a777b1d8af433e0c26f1d8433e39b071f245544
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The shipped math reward function calls `grade_answer`, whose integer normalization converts answer strings to binary floats before rounding. Distinct answers above the exact float-integer range can collapse to the same value:

```python
grade_answer("9007199254740993", "9007199254740992")  # True on main
grade_answer("9007199254740992.5", "9007199254740992")  # True on main
```

This awards a positive training reward to an incorrect answer. Negative values and scientific notation are affected as well.

## Change

Use Decimal for integer recognition and rounding, preserving the existing `1e-7` near-integer tolerance and finite-float input range. Remove the two private float helpers after checking that they have no remaining callers. Existing answer-format and symbolic-comparison rules are unchanged.

## Validation

- 19 regression cases execute the real grader and `examples/python/math_reward_func.py`, checking rewards, scores, and reported accuracy: 6 failed / 13 passed on the upstream base; all 19 pass with the fix.
- The complete reward-shaping test file passes, including its 34 existing cases.
- The repository suite has the same 16 pre-existing environment failures before and after the patch: every `test_pretrain_targets_and_gradients_follow_valid_next_tokens` case is blocked while a `datasets.map` multiprocessing manager creates a Unix socket (`PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted`). The unchanged base has 205 passing tests; the patch has 224.
- `python -m compileall -q openrlhf examples tests`, Black, isort, and `git diff --check` pass.
- CPU validation with real PyTorch 2.15.0, Transformers 5.15.0, DeepSpeed 0.19.6, SymPy, and pylatexenc; no GPU training run is claimed.

The historical math-grading PRs concerning symbolic equivalence, boxed answers, tuple delimiters, and units address separate behavior; this change only fixes precision lost during numeric normalization.

entries.title: Normalize consecutive thousands groups in math reward answers
entries.head: c616b1ee69f1b806844fe2a108756ab60730aa41
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The shipped math reward function rejects correctly formatted numbers with consecutive thousands groups. For example, `grade_answer("1,234,567,890", "1234567890")` returns False and the example reward function assigns zero.

The comma-stripping regex consumes the digit before each separator and the character after its three-digit group. One substitution can combine neighboring groups into a six-digit run; later loop iterations cannot match the remaining separator.

## Change

Match only the separator, using lookbehind and lookahead for the same surrounding digit conditions. All adjacent matching separators can then be removed in one substitution, eliminating the loop.

This retains the existing local formatting rule; it does not introduce general validation of thousands-separated numeric strings. Tuple separators and malformed group controls keep their existing behavior. All regression values are within the exact integer range of binary floats, so this is independent of numeric-precision changes.

## Validation

- 25 cases call the real `grade_answer` and shipped `examples/python/math_reward_func.py`, checking rewards, scores, and accuracy. The upstream base has 8 failures / 17 passes; the patch passes all 25.
- Covers positive and negative values, decimals, tuples, units, one to five digit groups, plain numbers, and separators that should remain.
- Full repository suite: unchanged base 205 passed / 16 environment failures; patch 230 passed / the same 16 failures. The failing `test_pretrain_targets_and_gradients_follow_valid_next_tokens` parameterizations cannot start a `datasets.map` multiprocessing manager because creating its Unix socket raises `PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted`.
- Compileall, Black, isort, and `git diff --check` pass.
- CPU validation; no GPU training run is claimed.

Searched prior PRs and issues for comma handling and checked the full file history; no equivalent fix was found.

entries.title: Align custom metric columns with their input rows
entries.head: 24a5e68f716f21b03c41b44cda246e49481a941f
entries.published_body:
### Related Issues/PRs Related to #25799, which aligned the logged evaluation table, and #11156, which sliced input columns during first-row metric validation. Neither change aligned the columns passed to a custom metric. ### What changes are proposed in this pull request? Model outputs correspond to input rows by position, but their pandas indexes can differ from the input index. A custom metric that combines predictions or targets with an input column currently triggers pandas label alignment. Reordered labels can silently produce the wrong metric; disjoint or duplicate labels can produce extra scores and fail artifact logging. Give the copied prediction/target columns and auxiliary output columns the input's row labels before passing them to modern column-argument metrics. Also slice auxiliary outputs during the first-row validation pass, matching the prediction and input slices already used there. The legacy `(eval_df, builtin_metrics)` signature retains its existing DataFrame index contract. Nullable integer values and dtypes are preserved, and neither the caller's input DataFrame nor model output is modified. ### How is this PR tested? - [x] New unit/integration tests The final 17-case regression module gives **11 failures and 6 passes on the original source**, and **17 passes after the fix**. The tests use native `mlflow.models.evaluate`, real callable models, and SQLite tracking. They check the returned metric, the persisted run metric, and the evaluation table for matching, disjoint, reordered, duplicate, string, and MultiIndex row labels. Both single-output regression and generic multi-output evaluation are covered. Hand-computed per-row scores expose the silent misalignment independently of the implementation. Additional controls verify nullable `Int64` values, the legacy two-argument metric signature, unchanged inputs and model outputs, and the existing rejection of empty regression data and inconsistent prediction counts. The four warnings in the focused run are existing integer-input schema warnings. Ruff 0.16.8, Clint, character normalization, and `git diff --check` pass. The full MLflow suite, PySpark-dependent evaluator module, and remote tracking stores were not run. ### Does this PR require documentation update? - [x] No. ### Does this PR require updating the [MLflow Skills](https://github.com/mlflow/skills) repository? - [x] No. ### Release Notes #### Is this a user-facing change? - [x] Yes. Keep custom metric predictions, targets, input columns, and auxiliary outputs aligned by evaluated row. #### What component(s), interfaces, languages, and integrations does this PR affect? Components - [x] `area/evaluation`: MLflow model evaluation features, evaluation metrics, and evaluation workflows #### How should the PR be classified in the release notes? Choose one: - [x] `rn/bug-fix` - A user-facing bug fix worth mentioning in the release notes #### Is this PR a critical bugfix or security fix that should go into the next patch release?
What is a minor/patch release? - Minor release: a release that increments the second part of the version number (e.g., 1.2.0 -> 1.3.0). Minor releases are expected to contain larger changes, such as new features and improvements. Non-critical bug fixes and doc updates can be included as well. By default, your PR should target the next minor release. - Patch release: a release that increments the third part of the version number (e.g., 1.2.0 -> 1.2.1). Patch releases are typically only performed when there has been a major regression or bug in the latest release. For the sake of stability, your PR should not be included in a patch release unless it is a critical fix, or if the risk level of your PR is exceedingly low.
- [ ] This PR is critical and needs to be in the next patch release - [x] This PR can wait for the next minor release

entries.title: Keep fully masked loss reductions and gradients finite
entries.head: 6721b9503c98c8da6c3fd164ab39ce20f7c1b337
entries.published_body:
## Problem

A batch with no valid supervision/actions makes `aggregate_loss` divide by zero in both token-level and sequence-level modes, including when global normalizers are supplied. Losses and gradients become NaN. PPO's masked KL and clipping metrics also become NaN. In float16, a fully masked row can poison an otherwise valid sequence-level batch because `1e-8` underflows to zero.

## Changes

Replace only exactly zero reduction denominators with one, so empty masks produce a differentiable zero contribution. Preserve all positive normalizers, including values below one produced by gradient-accumulation normalization, and preserve the existing nonempty sequence formula. Keep unmasked means and NaNs at valid tokens unchanged.

## Validation

Base: `26494490bc237f6c3af62dab6117e6bbb0a78dba`.

- The same 44 new cases on unchanged main: **29 failed, 15 passed**. With the fix: **44 passed**.
- Entire loss-aggregation test module: **58 passed**.
- Real `Linear`/log-softmax graphs with SFT, clipped value, PPO and GSPO losses produce zero gradients and unchanged SGD parameters for empty masks. Python and tensor global normalizers and local reductions are covered.
- Four-microbatch accumulation with a single valid token verifies that the legitimate `0.25` global normalizer is preserved, including the optimizer update. A local empty shard with a positive global count matches the unsharded loss and gradients under DP averaging algebra.
- Float16, float32 and float64 mixed empty/nonempty rows; weighted masks; all reduction axes; and valid NaNs provide regression controls.
- Full repository run in the same environment: unchanged main **204 passed, 17 failed**; patched **248 passed, the same 17 failed**. Sixteen failures are all parameterizations of `test_pretrain_targets_and_gradients_follow_valid_next_tokens`: the workspace denies the Unix socket used by the datasets multiprocessing manager. The remaining failure is `test_save_model_lora_tied_embeddings_zero3`, where PEFT 0.18.1 expects `.get` on the existing `_TinyConfig` fixture. That failure also reproduces separately on unchanged main.
- All repository pre-commit hooks applicable to the changed files and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_loss_aggregation.py -q
python -m pytest -q
pre-commit run --files openrlhf/models/loss.py openrlhf/models/utils.py tests/test_loss_aggregation.py
```

Linux, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. Tests use the repository's existing loader for the real loss/utilities modules; numerical outputs are not mocked. No GPU, multi-rank process group, or full RL training run was performed. The repository suite is not completely green for the reasons above.

Existing history and all-state PR/issue searches were checked. #1240 handles invalid values at masked positions, #1216 changes distributed loss aggregation interfaces, and #1360 handles incomplete accumulation windows; none repairs these zero denominators. This change retains their separate scope.

entries.title: Preserve episode counts when concatenating unequal experience batches
entries.head: 773b2aa2784f0361dbe2b4ff1f48acbb771ac73e
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`concat_experiences` sends every tensor through sequence padding. For a per-episode tensor with shape `(B,)`, its only dimension is the batch dimension, so concatenating unequal batch sizes pads smaller batches with artificial zero-valued episodes. For example, combining batches of two and one produces four rewards but only three sequence rows. Episode metrics become misaligned and subsequent `split_experience_batch` can fail.

## Change

Concatenate one-dimensional per-episode tensors directly along the batch dimension. Continue using the existing right-padding path for step-wise sequence/action tensors. The recursive merge also preserves the length of one-dimensional tensor metrics in `info`.

The scope is concatenation of batched experiences, including unequal batch sizes. The separate single-sample `make_experience_batch` path is unchanged.

## Native validation

Exact source commit: `773b2aa2784f0361dbe2b4ff1f48acbb771ac73e`; original main: `26494490bc237f6c3af62dab6117e6bbb0a78dba`.

[Successful CPU before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/OpenRLHF/actions/runs/43305640708), Python 3.12.16 / PyTorch 2.9.1+cpu:

- Identical 17 new tests on unchanged main: **14 failed, 3 passed**.
- Fixed source: **17 new tests and all 3 existing experience tests passed**, **20 passed** in total.
- Unequal, equal and empty component batches; different sequence widths; all episode fields; recursive metrics; metadata and input preservation; and concat → split → rebatch are checked against independently padded sample references.
- Native CPU Linear/SGD and Linear/Adam training performs three updates with sample-aligned features and rewards, comparing losses, gradients, parameters and optimizer state with an independent reference.
- Black 26.5.1, isort, autoflake and `git diff --check` passed.

The new tests import the actual public experience module and tensor utilities. The three pre-existing tests retain their upstream fixture behavior. Full PPO/DeepSpeed/Ray training, GPUs and multi-rank execution were not run. Validation workflow files are isolated on a separate fork branch.

## Prior work checked

All-state concat/merge/episode-padding searches, the complete five-commit history of `experience.py`, the relevant prior PR patches including #1299 and #1307, and all pre-existing fork branches were checked. The earlier balancing and selection changes do not correct one-dimensional tensor padding.

entries.title: Initialize packing configuration for Actor model instances
entries.head: f644edc44b24a66ba2382d474b2762bbdc4dbf90
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`Actor` accepts either a pretrained-model name or an existing `nn.Module`. The constructor only initializes `packing_samples` in the string-input branch, although `forward` reads it for both input types. Passing an existing causal language model therefore raises `AttributeError: 'Actor' object has no attribute 'packing_samples'` before normal policy inference or training.

## Change

Initialize the packing configuration in the common constructor path. Existing module instances and their parameter identities are preserved, and the pretrained-name path receives the same value as before.

## Validation

Exact source: `f644edc44b24a66ba2382d474b2762bbdc4dbf90`; upstream base: `26494490bc237f6c3af62dab6117e6bbb0a78dba`.

[Successful native CPU before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/OpenRLHF/actions/runs/43404655917), Python 3.12.16, PyTorch 2.9.1+cpu and Transformers 4.57.1:

- Identical 18 new tests on the unchanged base: **18 failed**, all on the missing packing attribute.
- Fixed source: **18 new tests plus both existing Actor entropy tests passed**, **20 passed** total.
- A real TinyGPT2 model covers action log probabilities, full log probabilities, raw model outputs, entropy, two temperatures, left/right padding and preservation of the supplied module.
- SGD and AdamW perform three real updates, including a model/optimizer checkpoint round trip after the first update. Losses, gradients, parameters and optimizer state are compared with the independent Transformers model calculation.
- Both values of the packing flag are checked at construction. Packed FlashAttention/ring execution is outside this CPU validation.
- Black 26.5.1, isort 9.0.0a3, autoflake 2.3.3 and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest -q tests/test_actor_module_instance.py tests/test_actor_entropy_temperature.py
```

The tests reuse the existing Actor CPU import fixture, which substitutes unavailable optional backend imports and runs entropy eagerly. The actual Actor forward, Transformers model, tensor calculations and optimizers execute normally. No GPU, DeepSpeed, packed-attention, compiled execution or complete repository suite is claimed. The validation workflow is on a separate fork branch.

## Prior work checked

All-state Actor/packing/module-input searches, the complete 93-commit Actor history, related patches including #1115, #1178 and #1209, the user's existing PRs and every pre-existing fork branch were checked. The original packing assignment is specific to the string constructor path; the prior FSDP and from-config work does not initialize this attribute for supplied module instances.

entries.title: Batch length-penalty reward updates
entries.head: e2686ee519b511a4b5d037e168511665a9615165
entries.published_body:
## Summary

DAPO and ProRL length penalties currently extract one Python scalar for every sample, then update rewards in Python. This makes reward shaping expensive for large rollout batches.

This change computes each penalty mask and reward update in a batch, keeping one scalar extraction per experience for the returned sample count. The overlong formula retains the original Python floating-point calculation before rounding penalties to the reward dtype. The in-place reward tensor, selected-sample counts, fractional buffers, negative fixed rewards, integer assignment casts, and untouched values are preserved.

## Validation

Exact source: `e2686ee519b511a4b5d037e168511665a9615165`, based on `26494490bc237f6c3af62dab6117e6bbb0a78dba`.

[Native CPU before/after run](https://github.com/Afloat16/OpenRLHF/actions/runs/43418881621) uses Python 3.12, official PyTorch 2.9.1+cpu, and Transformers 4.57.1.

- **50 new tests pass.** The unchanged source passes 48 semantic controls and fails the two profiler regression tests: each helper extracts 256 scalars for two 128-sample experiences; the change extracts two.
- Tests import the public Experience and penalty functions normally. They cover FP16/BF16/FP32/FP64 rewards, noncontiguous views, fractional/zero/negative buffers, fixed and scaled penalties, absent/empty flags, NaN/infinity controls, signed zero, and integer rewards.
- Four real GPT-2 training cases compare three SGD/AdamW steps, gradients, parameters, optimizer state, and disk checkpoint continuation against independently specified reward values.
- The existing multiturn truncation tests pass: **24 passed, 32 deselected**.
- `compileall`, Black, isort, and autoflake pass.
- The complete existing suite was also attempted on both sources. Both stop at the same five collection errors: `test_dataset_utils.py` and `test_pretrain_loss_mask.py` need `datasets`; `test_kl_estimator_gradient.py`, `test_loss_aggregation.py`, and `test_reward_shaping.py` need `deepspeed`. These results do not establish full-suite compatibility.

## Measured cost

A single CPU thread, five timed invocations per size, real Experience objects, both penalty helpers, and identical reward hashes/counts before and after:

| Samples | Before median | After median | Before / after |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.0115 ms | 0.0342 ms | 0.34x |
| 64 | 0.2637 ms | 0.0361 ms | 7.30x |
| 4,096 | 16.8356 ms | 0.0600 ms | 280.41x |
| 32,768 | 209.4488 ms | 0.6199 ms | 337.88x |

The benchmark uses response lengths `arange(batch_size) % 8193`, a 4096-token buffer at a maximum of 8192, and every third sample marked truncated. The smaller three cases have no overlong samples; the 32,768-sample case includes 16,380 overlong and 10,923 truncated samples. Reward cloning is outside the timed section. The benchmark source and raw measurements are in the validation branch/run artifacts.

Batching adds linear temporary tensors, including FP64 length arithmetic, and is slower for the single-sample case shown above. These are CPU helper measurements; GPU timing and full distributed PPO throughput have not been measured.

entries.title: Stabilize selective log probabilities without retaining vocabulary buffers
entries.head: 3378c344009614dc0d8f49c2f0642abee96bb4bf
entries.published_body:
## Problem

The float32/float64 fallback in `log_probs_from_logits` subtracts a large `logsumexp` result from the selected logit. A shared logit offset can erase the normalizer in that subtraction and also corrupt its gradient. For seven equal float32 logits at 1e8, the existing fallback returns 0 instead of -log(7).

## Change

Normalize each existing 1,024-token chunk with `log_softmax` before gathering the selected labels. Non-reentrant checkpointing includes both operations, so backward recomputes a chunk instead of retaining an additional full-vocabulary output for every token. The unused single-caller logsumexp helper is removed. The FlashAttention path, lower-precision path, temperature behavior, invalid-label checks and empty-batch gradients are preserved.

## Validation

- Exact upstream base: `26494490bc237f6c3af62dab6117e6bbb0a78dba`.
- Native CPU regression file: 10 failures / 34 passes before; 44 passes after.
- Repository commands: `python -m compileall -q openrlhf examples tests` passes; `python -m pytest -q` reports 247 passed and 2 skipped. Black, isort and autoflake checks pass.
- Covers FP32/FP64 values and analytic gradients, signed common offsets, noncontiguous inputs, 1,024-token boundaries, empty batches, FP16/BF16 controls, nonfinite rows, invalid labels and saved-tensor storage.
- Four local GPT2 training cases compare three SGD updates, including saved optimizer/model restoration, against a stable double-precision reference evaluated on the actual rounded input logits.
- Native packages: Torch 2.9.1+cpu, DeepSpeed 0.19.6, Transformers 5.15.0, Python 3.12. The complete numerical source module is loaded directly with real dependencies; no functions or dependencies are stubbed. FlashAttention, full Actor execution, GPU and distributed training were not run.

## Memory and timing

One CPU runner, two threads, one warmup and five timed iterations, random float32 logits:

| Shape | Forward only median | Forward + backward median | First-step process peak RSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 32 × 512 | 0.231 → 0.324 ms | 0.457 → 0.773 ms | 493,768 → 501,104 KiB for backward |
| 4,097 × 8,192 | 65.921 → 56.563 ms | 512.248 → 483.824 ms | 1,018,448 → 927,084 KiB for backward |

The larger backward case saves no additional vocabulary buffer (extra saved storage 16,388 → 0 bytes, excluding input storage). Checkpoint bookkeeping adds overhead to small batches; these are local helper measurements, not an end-to-end RL throughput claim. The benchmark verifies ordinary-input values and sampled gradients before comparing timings.

Native evidence: https://github.com/Afloat16/OpenRLHF/actions/runs/43421276254

entries.title: Support INT16 per-group and per-channel fake quantization
entries.head: 8d29c54ba128b48cb705e7695a8de00261179607
entries.published_body:
## Summary

`IntxFakeQuantizeConfig(torch.int16, ...)` accepts per-group and per-channel granularities, but their forward path selects legacy helpers that assert the bit width is at most 8. Consequently, a valid INT16 QAT configuration fails on its first training forward pass with `AssertionError: Unsupported n_bit 16`.

Use the existing generic affine qparam-selection path for INT16, as is already done for INT32. This retains each mapping type and the dynamic/static update policy without changing lower-bit paths.

## Validation

Base `a724e78b166c828a81d858b029daf4e4f4011a27`; patch `8d29c54ba128b48cb705e7695a8de00261179607`.

- The same 14 new cases: **14 failed before; 14 passed after**.
- Related fake-quantization and range-learning tests: **34 passed, 224 deselected**.
- Covers per-group/per-channel quantization, all three mapping types, dynamic and cached qparams, and repeated forward/backward passes.
- Independently calculated qparams and native `torch.fake_quantize_per_channel_affine` provide the reference. Outputs match exactly. Gradient clipping masks match exactly, with a relative tolerance of two float32 epsilons for the decomposition's multiply/divide rounding.
- A real two-layer classifier trains for three momentum-SGD updates through the public `quantize_(..., QATConfig(...))` API for both granularities; checkpoint restoration reproduces outputs exactly.
- Native CPU Inductor `torch.compile(..., fullgraph=True)` forward/backward matches eager execution.
- Repository-pinned Ruff 0.11.6 checks/formatting and `git diff --check` pass.

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 python -m pytest test/quantization/test_qat.py -k 'int16_group or fake_quantize_per or fake_quantizer or qat_range_learning' -q
```

Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. Validation uses the current Python implementation and native PyTorch CPU kernels; optional GPU kernels and the full repository suite were not run.

## Related changes

#4884 adds INT16 configuration support and per-tensor coverage. #4924 extends the generic INT32 path for asymmetric activation ranges. Neither enables the INT16 per-group/per-channel forward path. Checked the fake-quantizer history, current PR catalog and all-state related PR/issue searches for an existing fix.

entries.title: Preserve frozen and shared meta parameters during QAT module swaps
entries.head: df5b76c2210d9d67e9e14115f84c1af02999f849
entries.published_body:
## Problem

QAT's Linear and Embedding module-swap helpers skip assigning the original parameters when the model is on the meta device. They return newly created trainable parameters instead. This loses `requires_grad=False` and parameter sharing: preparing a meta model with a frozen layer, materializing it on CPU and taking an optimizer step updates that supposedly frozen layer.

## Change

Reuse the original weight and bias Parameter objects when preparing and converting meta modules, matching the existing CPU behavior. Registering a Parameter does not copy tensor storage, so the meta-device exclusions and their data-copy warning are unnecessary.

This preserves sharing across these module swaps; it does not change PyTorch's separate materialization or checkpoint assignment semantics.

## Validation

Base `a724e78b166c828a81d858b029daf4e4f4011a27`.

- The identical 20 new cases: **12 failed, 8 passed** before; **20 passed** after.
- New cases plus related module-swap, prepare/convert, bias and meta tests: **28 passed, 21 skipped, 215 deselected**. Skips are existing hardware-dependent tests.
- Direct prepare and convert tests cover CPU/meta, float32/bfloat16, frozen/trainable weights, opposite bias trainability, and tied Linear/Embedding weights.
- Public `quantize_(..., QATConfig(...))` tests prepare a meta network, optionally convert it, materialize it with `to_empty(device="cpu")`, and perform three native momentum-SGD updates. Frozen Linear/Embedding parameters remain bit-identical with no gradients, while the later trainable layer changes.
- Repository-pinned Ruff 0.11.6 checks/formatting and `git diff --check` pass.

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 python -m pytest test/quantization/test_qat.py -k 'module_swap_preserves_parameter_identity or meta_frozen_layer or quantize_api_prepare or qat_api_convert_no_quantization or fake_quantized_linear or fake_quantized_embedding or quantizer_meta_weights or qat_linear_bias or activation_calibration_config_supports_meta_device' -q
```

Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. Distributed/GPU execution and the complete repository suite were not run.

## Related work

#1415 and #1540 introduced the meta exclusions in the prepare and convert helpers. #4887 adds a separate calibration flow, and #4863 changes tied-embedding range learning. The file histories and all-state meta/parameter/QAT searches contain no equivalent parameter-preservation fix.

entries.title: Avoid retaining autograd graphs during MSE observer calibration
entries.head: c5bafe82a631837cb2f462901c2e51cf0a825a8d
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`AffineQuantizedMSEObserver.line_search` detaches inputs when computing the initial range, but scores candidate ranges against the original input. When that activation requires gradients, the candidate losses build an autograd graph across the whole search even though the scores only select calibration ranges and are never backpropagated. This can retain many activation-sized intermediates during calibration inside a training forward.

## Change

Disable autograd while selecting calibration ranges. `forward` still returns the original input object, preserving the surrounding model's gradient path. The separately callable `loss_fn` remains differentiable.

## Validation

Base: `a724e78b166c828a81d858b029daf4e4f4011a27`.

- The same nine new cases: **8 failed and 1 control passed before; all 9 passed after**.
- Entire observer test module: **26 passed**.
- Covers per-tensor/per-axis observation, float32/bfloat16, repeated observation and `run_once`, exact qparams against a no-grad reference, input identity, unchanged outer gradients and differentiability of standalone `loss_fn`.
- A real two-layer classifier with the observer trains for three momentum-SGD steps. Outputs, all gradients and model parameters match a reference classifier without an observer exactly.
- Ruff 0.11.6 checks/formatting and `git diff --check` pass.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 python -m pytest test/quantization/test_observer.py -q
```

### Local resource measurement

For a float32 activation of shape `(128, 2048)` and 32 candidate ranges, autograd saved **224 intermediate tensor references before and 0 after**. Their aggregate logical size was 100,728,832 bytes; this is not a count of distinct storage allocations.

In separate native CPU processes, peak process RSS was **453,048 KiB before and 322,700 KiB after**. The corresponding pre-calibration process peaks were 308,792 and 309,140 KiB. These RSS figures include the complete Python/PyTorch process.

A same-process paired range-search timing check (two CPU threads, two measurement rounds) gave original medians of 17.690 and 11.127 ms, versus patched medians of 6.438 and 6.590 ms. This shared CPU measurement is specific to the calibration helper, not an end-to-end training-speed claim. Selected scales and zero points are exactly equal between original and patched runs.

Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. GPU execution and the full repository suite were not run.

Checked all-state MSE/observer/autograd/memory searches, the observer file history including the original #2508 implementation, and the existing fork branches. No equivalent calibration-graph fix was found.

entries.title: Ignore empty batches before updating MSE observer calibration
entries.head: f0f6d28e312ab505fbe2a08de50d3e37e46643f4
entries.published_body:
## Summary

An empty input currently reaches `AffineQuantizedMSEObserver.line_search`, whose empty-input return is a tensor rather than a pair of bounds. Empty shapes such as `(0, 8)` raise during tuple unpacking. Shape `(2, 0)` instead silently installs empty bounds and marks the observer calibrated; with `run_once=True`, the next nonempty input is then skipped.

Return the original empty tensor before updating the MSE observer's ranges or calibrated flag. Previously calibrated ranges remain intact across empty batches.

## Validation

Native CPU PyTorch 2.14.0, with the repository's normal test configuration:

- 26 new cases cover three empty shapes, per-tensor and per-axis calibration, and both `run_once` settings.
- Against the unmodified source: 20 fail and 6 pass.
- With this change: all 43 tests in `test/quantization/test_observer.py` pass, including the 17 existing tests.
- A real two-layer network processes an empty batch followed by two nonempty batches. Outputs, parameter gradients, and three SGD updates match the reference network exactly.
- Ruff 0.11.6 checks and formatting pass.

entries.title: Compute half-precision MSE calibration losses in float32
entries.head: f1cca771be688284f1015db6f8d5e5ff8541e03b
entries.published_body:
## Summary

MSE calibration currently computes subtraction, squaring, and reduction in the input dtype. For FP16 inputs, candidate reconstruction errors can underflow to zero, so the search accepts an excessively narrow clipping range. Large residuals can also overflow before reduction.

Promote both operands to float32 when both are FP16 or BF16, before subtraction and squaring. Float32, float64, and mixed inputs containing a higher-precision operand retain their existing arithmetic. Autograd remains connected through the casts.

## Measured effect

On native CPU PyTorch 2.14.0, calibrating four rows of 1,024 FP16 values spanning -0.004 to 0.004 with 64 candidates:

- Original reconstruction MSE: `2.75132255e-8`.
- Patched reconstruction MSE: `8.24749991e-11`.
- The patched result equals the independently evaluated best candidate, a 333.6-fold reduction in this example.

Per-tensor and per-axis calibration both reproduce this result. This measures reconstruction error for the stated calibration input; it does not establish end-to-end model accuracy or a speed improvement. The change uses float32 temporary tensors during low-precision loss evaluation.

## Validation

- 16 new native tests cover small and large residuals, FP16/BF16 gradients, float32/float64 preservation, and exhaustive clipping-candidate comparisons.
- Unmodified source: 12 fail and 4 pass.
- Patched source: all 33 observer-module tests pass, including the 17 existing cases.
- Ruff 0.11.6 checks and formatting pass.

Exact production head: `f1cca771be688284f1015db6f8d5e5ff8541e03b`.

entries.title: Fix AMSGrad maximum dispatch for low-bit optimizer states
entries.head: 9e0beae00fd32dfb34fe173cacd97f22bbfc356a
entries.published_body:
## Summary
Low-bit Adam and AdamW accept `amsgrad=True`, but their first update fails when the running maximum is an `OptimState4bit`, `OptimState8bit`, or `OptimStateFp8` tensor: none of these subclasses implements `aten.maximum.default`.

Register `maximum` with the existing read-only dequantizing dispatch handler for all three state formats. The operation returns a regular FP32 tensor, allowing the existing Adam update to compute the denominator in FP32 and copy the maximum back into the quantized state.

## Validation
- Add 18 dispatch cases covering each format, FP32/BF16 appearance, and quantized operands on either or both sides; verify exact dequantized results and unchanged packed operands.
- Add 12 actual `nn.Linear` training cases covering Adam/AdamW, all three state formats, and FP32/BF16. Compare four backward/update steps with native PyTorch AMSGrad, including a falling-gradient sequence that must preserve the earlier maximum.
- Serialize and reload actual model/optimizer state after step two, then verify the next two updates against uninterrupted training.
- All 30 new cases fail on the original source; the patched source passes all 59 selected tests, including 29 existing cases.
- Ruff check and format pass.

Native CPU validation of the exact production commit:
https://github.com/Afloat16/ao/actions/runs/43398462913

entries.title: Preserve Conv2d semantics when replacing pointwise convolutions
entries.head: 2cb2497e32703910b9998c90886bcf44eb0e4322
entries.published_body:
## Problem
The 1x1 Conv2d-to-Linear helper replaces convolutions whose stride, padding, or groups cannot be reproduced by a pointwise linear operation. It also assumes batched NCHW inputs, recreates frozen weights as trainable parameters, resets evaluation mode, and discards a replacement when the convolution itself is the root module.

## Change
- Retain convolutions with non-unit stride, nonzero padding, or groups.
- Use channel-axis moves that work for both CHW and NCHW inputs.
- Preserve the weight's `requires_grad`, the original bias object, and module training mode.
- Return the replacement so callers can use `model = swap_conv2d_1x1_to_linear(model)` for a root convolution. Nested replacements continue to happen in place.

The equivalent `same` and `valid` padding modes remain supported for 1x1 kernels.

## Validation
28 new native cases cover:
- Three actual SGD steps through a two-convolution model, comparing outputs, input gradients, parameter gradients, and updates with the original Conv2d model.
- Batched/unbatched inputs, optional biases, frozen weights, and training/evaluation mode.
- Retaining spatial/grouped convolutions with default and custom filters.
- Root replacement followed by actual INT8 weight-only quantization and inference.

Original source: 26 failures, 2 passing controls. Patched source: all 28 new cases pass, plus 4 existing quantization-flow tests; one existing unsupported CPU case is skipped. Ruff checks and formatting pass.

Production commit: `2cb2497e32703910b9998c90886bcf44eb0e4322`.
Native CPU validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/ao/actions/runs/43401804602

entries.title: Restore scalar learning rates when loading low-bit optimizer checkpoints
entries.head: 49d23b3410c6870bab011b5f6d9e4b3c1e3d927b
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Low-bit Adam optimizers convert scalar learning rates to tensors when parameter groups are added, but `load_state_dict()` restores parameter groups through `__setstate__` and skips that conversion. Loading a normal PyTorch Adam/AdamW checkpoint, or a low-bit checkpoint whose learning rates were serialized as scalars, leaves a float learning rate and makes the next optimizer step fail.

## Change

Apply the existing FP32 scalar-to-tensor learning-rate normalization during state restoration. Existing tensor learning rates keep their dtype and device.

## Validation

Exact commit: `49d23b3410c6870bab011b5f6d9e4b3c1e3d927b`.

36 new native CPU cases cover all six public low-bit Adam/AdamW classes:
- Importing actual Adam/AdamW model and optimizer checkpoints, with and without AMSGrad and with FP32/BF16 default dtype during loading.
- Resuming real model updates and a StepLR schedule, comparing parameters and losses with native PyTorch.
- Restoring actual quantized optimizer checkpoints with scalar or tensor learning rates, preserving the optimizer-state subclasses and matching subsequent updates exactly.

Original source: 30 failures and six passing tensor-LR controls. Patched source: all 36 new cases and 29 existing optimizer/quantization tests pass. Ruff and formatting pass.

Native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/ao/actions/runs/43406217617

This change preserves the loaded moment representation; importing an ordinary Adam checkpoint does not automatically quantize its dense moments.

entries.title: Support strided and broadcast sources when restoring quantized optimizer states
entries.head: 6eda0c4e1c4003d68de96bf79fb3f5ec4383846f
entries.published_body:
## Problem

Quantized optimizer-state `copy_` handlers assume a contiguous, already expanded floating-point source. A transposed or sliced moment tensor can fail at `view`, while row and scalar sources do not implement ordinary `Tensor.copy_` broadcasting. This prevents restoring moments from a native AdamW checkpoint whose parameter and moment tensors use noncontiguous layouts.

## Change

Reshape floating-point inputs when forming quantization blocks and expand them to the destination's logical shape before quantization. Apply the same copy contract to the 4-bit, 8-bit, and FP8 optimizer states. Contiguous same-shape inputs retain the view fast path; inputs that require layout conversion allocate a reshaped copy.

## Validation

Native CPU PyTorch 2.14.0 with normal repository test configuration:

- 27 new cases cover contiguous, transposed, strided-row, strided-column, offset, expanded, row-broadcast, and scalar-broadcast sources, plus native checkpoint restoration for all three AdamW state formats.
- Original source: 21 failures and 6 passes. Patched source: 56 tests pass, including all 27 new cases and 29 existing quantization, slicing, dtype, and optimizer smoke cases.
- Copy tests compare packed codes, scales, and dequantized values to the result of native dense `Tensor.copy_`, and verify that the source data and strides remain unchanged.
- Real native AdamW moments are serialized from transposed parameters, copied into low-bit states, and used for three further compiled optimizer steps. Parameters and moment values match the equivalent contiguous restore exactly.
- Ruff 0.11.6 checks and formatting pass.

Exact production head: `6eda0c4e1c4003d68de96bf79fb3f5ec4383846f`.

entries.title: Stabilize policy entropy values and gradients against logit offsets
entries.head: 9b60b3652af3960de24d7a65d88c32f1aaef2c28
entries.published_body:
## Problem

`compute_entropy` subtracts two large values, `logsumexp(logits)` and the expected logit. A common offset, which does not change the policy, can erase the entropy and introduce incorrect gradients. For example, four equal float32 logits at `1e8` produce entropy zero and a nonzero gradient instead of `log(4)` and zero. This affects the entropy bonus used by the PPO actor. Finite logits near a dtype's extremes can also produce nonfinite results.

## Changes

Compute entropy from `log_softmax` and its probabilities. Replace the log probability of an exactly zero-probability entry with zero before multiplication to preserve the `0 * log(0)` limit in both forward and backward. Keep the existing function signature, output dtype, temperature handling, and NaN-input behavior.

## Validation

Base: `26494490bc237f6c3af62dab6117e6bbb0a78dba`.

- The same 33 new cases on unchanged main: **27 failed, 6 passed**. With the fix: **33 passed**. Including the two existing actor-temperature tests: **35 passed**.
- Uniform distributions use hard-coded `log(vocab_size)` and zero gradients. Nonuniform float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64 distributions use centered double-precision values and an independent closed-form entropy gradient. Both positive and negative common offsets, finite dtype extremes, unchanged inputs and NaN controls are covered.
- A real tiny `GPT2LMHeadModel` through `Actor`, with three temperatures and both offset signs, verifies that two momentum-SGD entropy-bonus steps leave a uniform policy unchanged. No pretrained checkpoint is downloaded.
- Two explicit `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` tests run with the native CPU Inductor backend and compare values and gradients against the reference.
- Full repository run with the same final tests: unchanged source **210 passed, 44 failed**; patched source **237 passed, 17 failed**. The remaining failure set is identical. Sixteen are `test_pretrain_targets_and_gradients_follow_valid_next_tokens` cases: the workspace denies the Unix socket used by the datasets multiprocessing manager. The remaining `test_save_model_lora_tied_embeddings_zero3` failure is the existing `_TinyConfig` fixture lacking `.get`, which installed PEFT expects.
- `compileall`, all repository pre-commit hooks applicable to the changed files, and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_actor_entropy_temperature.py -q
python -m pytest -q
python -m compileall -q openrlhf examples tests
pre-commit run --files openrlhf/models/utils.py tests/test_actor_entropy_temperature.py
```

Linux, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.15.0+cpu. The tests reuse this module's existing import loader, which isolates optional DeepSpeed/flash-attn/PEFT imports and loads the actual Actor and utility code; tensor outputs and the GPT-2 model are not mocked. The explicit compiled cases invoke the real compiler. GPU, multi-rank execution, and a full RL training run were not performed. The full repository suite still has the 17 failures listed above.

Checked upstream history, all-state related PRs/issues and all user-fork heads. #983 introduced the entropy expression; #1319 fixes temperature selection before entropy computation. Neither changes this numerical reduction. The independent selective-log-probability implementation is outside this change.

entries.title: Support independent snapshots of low-bit optimizer states
entries.head: e4da8a230aaf9ca316b67dc1cd1cb5cea2f6893c
entries.published_body:
## Summary

Calling `clone()` or `copy.deepcopy(optimizer.state_dict())` on an initialized 4-bit, 8-bit, or FP8 optimizer currently raises an unimplemented `aten.clone` dispatch error. This prevents keeping an independent in-memory checkpoint while training continues.

Implement clone dispatch for the three quantized optimizer-state tensor subclasses. The clone preserves the logical shape, dtype, signedness, and block layout, and owns copies of the quantized codes, scales, and quantization map. Both preserve and contiguous memory formats are supported.

## Validation

- 60 clone/deepcopy cases cover signed and unsigned 4-bit/8-bit states, FP8 states, FP32/BF16 logical dtypes, vector/matrix shapes, explicit memory formats, metadata equality, storage isolation, and deepcopy's repeated-reference behavior.
- 12 model-training cases cover Adam/AdamW with 4-bit, 8-bit, and FP8 states in FP32/BF16. Each snapshots a trained model and optimizer, advances the original model, verifies the snapshot stayed unchanged, and compares two resumed training steps with an independently serialized checkpoint.
- On the exact upstream base, all 72 new cases fail. With this change, all 72 pass; 29 existing optimizer tests also pass.
- Ruff lint and formatting pass.

Native CPU PyTorch validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/ao/actions/runs/43407399050

This change concerns snapshot correctness. It does not claim a training speedup or GPU validation.

entries.title: Preserve statistic scale in permutation-test comparisons
entries.head: 0851fd270d460d8ce4cf582d19ba8cb1a6a1307a
entries.published_body:
### Description

`permutation_test` uses NumPy's default absolute tolerance when deciding which null statistics tie the observed statistic. Rescaling a statistic can therefore change a result even though it preserves every ordering:

```python
x, y = [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]
stat = lambda a, b: abs(np.mean(a) - np.mean(b))
permutation_test(x, y, func=stat)                      # 0.1
permutation_test(x, y, func=lambda a, b: 1e-12*stat(a,b)) # previously 1.0
```

The paired exact result similarly changes from `0.25` to `1.0`. The default relative tolerance also merges distinct float64 statistics separated by `1e-7` around one.

Use a relative tie tolerance of 100 times the observed floating-point statistic dtype's machine epsilon, with zero absolute tolerance. Integer statistics use exact comparisons instead of floating-point coercion. This follows the roundoff approach described in [SciPy's permutation-test notes](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.permutation_test.html#notes). Sampling, seeds, exact enumeration and the randomized-test correction remain unchanged.

### Validation

Base: `1aee767ef57b84a8191511a08955c583b65de382`.

- Thirteen new native regression/control cases: **8 failed, 5 passed** on unchanged master; **13 passed** with the fix.
- Exact results are checked against independent enumeration using integer sums. Cases cover paired/unpaired tests, scales `1e-12`, `1`, `1e12`, float32/float64 custom statistics, genuine floating-point ties, nearby distinct values, and integer statistics above `2**53`.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest mlxtend/evaluate/tests/test_permutation_precision.py mlxtend/evaluate/tests/test_permutation.py -q`: **23 passed**.
- Changed-file Black, isort, Flake8 and `git diff --check` passed.

Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5. The full repository suite was not run.

### Related issues or pull requests

The existing #1269 fixes integer observation storage in paired permutations. This changes only statistic comparison, so the two fixes are independent; no observation-buffer changes are included here.

- [x] Added regression/control tests under `mlxtend/evaluate/tests`.
- [x] Documented numerical comparison behavior in the public docstring.
- [x] Relevant tests and changed-file style checks pass.

entries.title: Preserve automatic class inference across refits and cloning
entries.head: 41c53b0b097fae747c6686f37797a159e7f91cc6
entries.published_body:
### Description

`SoftmaxRegression` and `MultiLayerPerceptron` overwrite the `n_classes=None` constructor parameter with the first dataset's inferred class count. Later calls to `fit` retain that old output width: adding a class raises `IndexError`, while fitting fewer classes leaves extra outputs. Cloning an already fitted model also carries the accidental fixed class count into the clone.

Keep the constructor parameter unchanged and infer the output width when initializing parameters. One-hot encoding uses the fitted output layer's actual width, so `init_params=False` continues training the existing model and explicit `n_classes` settings retain their behavior. No additional fitted-state field is introduced.

### Validation

Base: `1aee767ef57b84a8191511a08955c583b65de382`.

- Ten new regression/control cases: **6 failed, 4 passed** on unchanged master; **10 passed** after the fix.
- Both estimators are checked for growing and shrinking class vocabularies, cloning after fitting, explicit class counts, and continued training. Refitted/cloned outputs and costs match a fresh estimator with the same seed; continued training matches an uninterrupted run.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_inferred_class_count.py mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_softmax_regression.py mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_multilayerperceptron.py -q`: **37 passed**.
- Changed-file Black, isort, Flake8 and `git diff --check` passed.

entries.title: Fit Adaline reliably with rank-deficient features
entries.head: 827006c66fc727b418f6ecffacba613d637e6c25
entries.published_body:
### Description

Adaline's default analytical fit explicitly inverts `Xb.T @ Xb`. Duplicate or constant features, or more features than observations, make that matrix singular and prevent fitting. Nearly collinear features can also produce inaccurate fitted values because forming the normal equations squares the design matrix's condition number.

Solve the augmented least-squares problem directly with `numpy.linalg.lstsq(..., rcond=None)`. Full-rank inputs retain their ordinary least-squares solution. Rank-deficient inputs receive the minimum-norm solution, including the intercept; this behavior is now documented. The iterative SGD path is unchanged.

### Validation

Base: `1aee767ef57b84a8191511a08955c583b65de382`.

- Six new regression/control cases: **5 failed, 1 passed** before the change; **6 passed** afterward.
- Duplicate, constant, zero-valued and wide feature matrices previously raised `LinAlgError`. On the near-collinear example, the old fitted values differed from the independent reference by up to **1.081**.
- The independent reference uses SciPy's pivoted-QR `gelsy` solver. Tests check coefficients, fitted values, residual orthogonality, predictions and input preservation.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_adaline_least_squares.py mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_adaline.py -q`: **18 passed**.
- Changed-file Black, isort, Flake8 and `git diff --check` passed.

Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0. The full repository suite and downstream model-quality benchmarks were not run.

### Related issues or pull requests

The historical stable-OLS change #575 introduced alternative solvers for `LinearRegression`. This change addresses `Adaline`, whose analytical path still performs the normal-equation inverse.

entries.title: Align prefit voting probabilities with classifier labels
entries.head: cf80c72190f17e49bd230779ee261eb254b9a6c4
entries.published_body:
### Description

entries.title: Resample fit parameters with bootstrap training rows
entries.head: 243f619bf8497cef2932958a133815edee844442
entries.published_body:
### Description

Both `bootstrap_point632_score` and `bias_variance_decomp` resample training rows but pass the original fit parameters to each fitted model. A `sample_weight` vector therefore becomes detached from the observations it describes. Duplicated observations can receive different weights, silently changing the model and the reported estimate.

Resample fit parameters that have one entry per training observation using the same bootstrap indices as X and y. Reuse scikit-learn's existing fit-parameter indexing helper, including support for lists, pandas Series and Pipeline-prefixed parameter names. Scalars, `None` and parameters of other lengths pass through unchanged. Both public docstrings now describe this behavior.

A deterministic weighted-mean regression example in the new tests illustrates the effect:

| Estimate | Original result | Correct weighted bootstrap |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| First OOB replicate MSE | 54.163005 | 45.831706 |
| Bias-variance decomposition expected loss | 17.846246 | 15.136038 |
| Bias-variance decomposition variance | 3.472789 | 1.115966 |

These values are checked against weighted means computed directly from the sampled observation indices, independently of the estimator and mlxtend's implementation.

### Validation

Base: `1aee767ef57b84a8191511a08955c583b65de382`.

- Twenty-two new regression/control cases: **18 failed, 4 passed** on unchanged master; **22 passed** with this fix.
- The cases cover OOB and .632 scoring, the full MSE bias-variance decomposition, NumPy/list/Series weights, non-default pandas indices, Pipeline parameter names, input preservation, estimator cloning, scalar weights, and non-sample fit parameters.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest mlxtend/evaluate/tests/test_bootstrap_fit_params.py mlxtend/evaluate/tests/test_bootstrap_point632.py mlxtend/evaluate/tests/test_bias_variance_decomp.py -q -k 'not keras'`: **38 passed, 2 deselected**.
- Changed-file Black, isort, Flake8 and `git diff --check` passed.

entries.title: Resolve class labels in probability-based counterfactuals

entries.title: Preserve MLP momentum history when continuing training
entries.head: 8840df2926c26d7a2c98e907c03d76a9cb9fe1c7
entries.published_body:
### Description

Continuing a `MultiLayerPerceptron` fit with nonzero momentum raises `UnboundLocalError`: the previous-gradient arrays are local variables initialized only when `init_params=True`.

Store those four history arrays on the fitted model. Each update retains the history for the next fit or a serialized-model round trip; reinitializing the parameters resets it. The existing momentum update equation is unchanged.

Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5. Validation covers a fixed momentum configuration and checkpoints produced by the corrected model. Enabling momentum after a zero-momentum fit and migrating older pickles without this history are outside this change's validation. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: Apply MLP learning-rate decay once per epoch
entries.head: 5d2286368bd22a55dd1632ff70415135dc983a9c
entries.published_body:
### Description

`MultiLayerPerceptron` divides its current learning rate inside every minibatch. With nonzero `decrease_const`, this compounds the decay repeatedly within an epoch and across epochs, instead of using the documented `eta / (1 + epoch * decrease_const)` schedule.

Compute that rate once at the start of each epoch and share it across all minibatches. The existing epoch-cost history supplies the completed-epoch count, so continued fitting retains the schedule and parameter reinitialization restarts it.

### Validation

Base: `1aee767ef57b84a8191511a08955c583b65de382`.

- Nine new regression/control cases: **7 failed, 2 passed** on unchanged master; **9 passed** with the fix.
- Training parameters and costs are compared with explicit constant-rate one-epoch updates for two decay strengths and three minibatch counts. Identical training rows isolate the schedule from shuffled minibatch ordering. Additional cases cover continuation, reinitialization and zero decay.
- The existing deterministic decay fixture's expected training accuracy changes from **0.98 to 1.0** because the corrected rates change its training trajectory; its exact assertion is updated. This is not a general model-quality benchmark.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_mlp_learning_rate_schedule.py mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_multilayerperceptron.py -q`: **23 passed**.
- Changed-file Black, isort, Flake8 and `git diff --check` passed.

Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: Apply the reported L1 penalty during MLP training
entries.head: a951ff1bab7c5aa14f42604c998806bd96dc3c9a
entries.published_body:
### Description

`MultiLayerPerceptron._compute_cost` includes an L1 penalty, but the weight updates omit its derivative. Changing `l1` therefore changes the reported cost without changing the trained weights.

Add the existing penalty's subgradient to both weight matrices. The existing cost convention is `0.5 * l1 * sum(abs(weights))`, so the update uses the corresponding factor of 0.5 and a zero subgradient at zero weights. Biases remain unpenalized. Document this cost convention; the default `l1=0` path is unchanged.

### Validation

Base: `1aee767ef57b84a8191511a08955c583b65de382`.

- Seven regression/control cases: **4 failed, 3 passed** on unchanged master; **7 passed** with the fix.
- Central finite differences of the existing reported cost independently check the observed one-step weight updates for two positive L1 strengths, with and without L2. Controls cover zero L1, zero-valued weights and unchanged biases.
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m pytest mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_mlp_l1_updates.py mlxtend/classifier/tests/test_multilayerperceptron.py -q`: **21 passed**.
- Changed-file Black, isort, Flake8 and `git diff --check` passed.

Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5. Validation checks the training update against the existing objective; it is not a model-quality benchmark. The full repository suite was not run.

entries.title: [Perf] sampling: Keep bounded atomic stop regex windows finite
entries.head: 3e2b9ff667f11c0a4c3eb56fd857389b3d57c102
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

A bounded stop regex such as `(?>STOP)` or `a{2,6}+Z` is currently assigned a window of `2**30` characters because its Python regex token is unrecognized. `Req._stop_match_tail_len` then retains the whole generated history for repeated stop checks, despite the pattern having a fixed maximum length.

Atomic groups and possessive quantifiers restrict backtracking; they do not increase the maximum number of characters a bounded expression can consume.

## Modifications

- Recurse through the body of `ATOMIC_GROUP`.
- Handle `POSSESSIVE_REPEAT` with the existing bounded/unbounded repetition calculation.
- Add four methods to the existing registered sampling-parameter tests. Unbounded bodies and look-around context keep the existing conservative fallback.

This is separate from #49915's regex admission checks, #26892's token-set optimization, and #47280's UTF-8 width handling. Their actual patches retain the unhandled atomic/possessive window behavior.

## Accuracy Tests

The complete native sampling-parameter test module passes: **87 methods and 48 subtests**.

On the original implementation, the new checks report **eight failed finite-window subtests plus one failed normalization method**. The four conservative-fallback subtests already pass. Finite upper bounds are checked against concrete longest strings accepted by Python's real regex engine. Normalization and a native msgspec round trip preserve the maximum bound across multiple stop patterns.

Test target: `test/registered/unit/sampling/test_sampling_params.py`.

The local CPU launcher scopes an empty, unused Triton import at the shared test-utility boundary, as permitted by the unit-test README. SGLang parameter normalization, regex parsing, test classes, and msgspec serialization are native. No GPU kernel, server, or model inference was run. The full `Req` test module could not be collected because torchvision is unavailable in this environment.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

The measured window values are `1073741824 -> 4` for `(?>STOP)` and `1073741825 -> 7` for `a{2,6}+Z`. At the existing tail-length calculation, these finite bounds allow five or eight trailing tokens for a single-token step instead of the full generated sequence, subject to other configured stop conditions.

No end-to-end latency or throughput benchmark was run, and no speedup factor is claimed. This change addresses the overly conservative bound; it does not change the regex matcher or solve the independent UTF-8/token-width limitation tracked in #47280.

## Checklist

- [x] Format and check the two changed files using the pinned applicable hook implementations directly: isort 7.0.0, Ruff 0.15.1, codespell 2.4.1, and pre-commit-hooks 6.0.0. Repository registration, placement, import, and entrypoint checks also pass. The full pre-commit environment installer was not run.

- [x] Documentation assessed: no new public API or sampling option is introduced.
- [x] Accuracy and speed scope, concrete window measurements, and benchmark limitations documented above.

entries.title: [Fix] embedding: Normalize FP16 pooled embeddings in float32
entries.head: 6cfa1c2b244d2a7b9816ade3d58927e5fb9914bd
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

FP16 pooling can return NaNs for zero embeddings because `F.normalize`'s epsilon rounds to zero. A finite embedding whose norm exceeds FP16's range instead normalizes to an all-zero vector, and subnormal embeddings lose normalization accuracy. These results can propagate to cosine retrieval scores, including after dimension truncation.

## Modifications

Promote FP16 pooled embeddings to float32 before computing the norm and division, then cast the normalized result back to its input dtype. Apply the same helper to the dense and ragged-dimension output paths. BF16, float32, float64, and normalization-disabled paths keep their current behavior.

This changes only normalization. It does not change mean-pooling accumulation or address the independent MEAN accumulation issue in #39754. The actual patches for #11256 and #44152 also leave this FP16 normalization path unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

- Hosted Ubuntu 24.04 CPU execution of the exact source commit: **26 test methods and 27 subtests passed**, comprising the 10 new methods and the existing `test_pooler_score_and_pool.py` module.
- Restoring the exact upstream implementation in the same installed native environment reproduces **two failed methods and 12 failed subtests**. Fifteen control subtests already pass on the baseline.
- Tests cover zero, large, and subnormal FP16 vectors; LAST/CLS/MEAN pooling; equal and ragged dimension truncation; noncontiguous tensors; unchanged input tensors; disabled normalization; and other floating dtypes.
- An independent `math.hypot` reference checks normalized values, and a cosine retrieval example checks the observable nearest-direction result.
- The official CPU CI dependency installation was used, including native Triton/package imports. Torch 2.14.1+cu130 was installed, but all test tensors and execution were on CPU and no GPU was available. No production or dependency implementation was stubbed.

Validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43297074612

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No server, model inference, GPU execution, or end-to-end performance benchmark was run. The FP16 path now uses a temporary float32 tensor during normalization; this change targets finite, accurate embeddings rather than a latency improvement. MEAN pooling's own accumulation range is outside this fix.

entries.title: [Fix] ipc: Preserve unsupported values through the MessagePack fallback
entries.head: b157c3866c7c7313c87a6b1cc59052e78b3121e4
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

The object-field IPC fallback currently decides MessagePack fidelity from the Python type alone. Arbitrarily large Python integers then reach an encoder that only supports signed/unsigned 64-bit integers. NumPy record, object, metadata-bearing and zero-itemsize arrays also reach the raw-buffer codec, whose dtype string cannot preserve their full representation. Requests can fail to encode or silently lose dtype information and shared-object identity.

## Modifications

Make fidelity checks depend on integer range and array dtype. Values outside the existing native codec's lossless domain use the existing shared pickle fallback. Ordinary integers, ordinary NumPy arrays, recursive containers, extension IDs and forwarding behavior retain their current format.

This applies to object-typed fields already supported by the fallback. It does not expand the direct typed ndarray codec or add a new serialization protocol.

## Accuracy Tests

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43404011360

- Eight new test methods cover integer limits, nested containers, record fields/titles/offsets, object arrays, dtype metadata, zero-itemsize arrays, ordinary strided/scalar/empty arrays and shared references.
- A real `TokenizedGenerateReqInput` with `MultimodalProcessorOutput`, Torch features and NumPy metadata is wrapped, encoded, forwarded, re-encoded and decoded using the normal IPC implementation.
- New tests plus existing request-IPC controls: **21 methods passed, 23 subtests passed, 2 existing tests skipped**.
- Restoring the original implementation gives **3 failing methods and 18 failing subtests** (pytest reports 21 failures), with 5 completed methods and 5 passing subtests.
- Full repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

Linux CPU execution validates actual serialization and request classes. No GPU inference or server load test is claimed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No speed improvement is claimed. Flat integer sequences now check each value's bounds to avoid selecting an encoder that cannot represent them. Values requiring the fallback incur its existing pickle cost.

- [x] Add registered CPU regression tests.

CPU Torch tensors can carry lazy conjugate or negative bits. entries.title: [Fix] DynamicGradMode: preserve context state across policy changes
entries.head: 968253dd7b1ecdbf43fb4c507d76ba1142a60597
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

`DynamicGradMode` is intended to select no-grad or inference mode at runtime. A decorator created while inference mode is disabled currently has no `mode` attribute, so enabling inference later makes its next call raise `AttributeError`. Changing the policy while a context is active also makes its exit close a different, uninitialized context and can replace the original model exception.

## Modifications

Always retain the requested mode during construction and cloning. At entry, construct the public PyTorch context selected by the current policy; at exit, close that same context. Both decorator spellings and the existing no-grad fallback for `mode=False` retain their behavior. This does not change the global setter's thread-safety contract.

## Accuracy Tests

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43400001300

- **11 test methods and 24 subtests passed** using the checkout's real implementation and PyTorch on Linux CPU.
- Restoring the original source yields **1 failing test method and 11 failing subtests**, with 10 completed methods and 13 passing subtests. Failures include actual attribute errors and the native model path.
- Tests cover construction before policy changes, repeated decorator calls, cloning with explicit false mode, policy changes inside active contexts, nested caller states, and preservation of the original exception.
- A real Linear model alternates both inference policies and then performs three SGD updates. Outputs, gradients, parameters, and caller grad state match a native PyTorch-context reference.
- Repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

No GPU execution or end-to-end server benchmark is claimed.

entries.title: [Fix] image: Honor patch limits for extreme aspect ratios
entries.head: b3d89f7039501223ecca64f402b986041952575c
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

Dynamic image sizing can exceed `max_num_patches` for long, narrow images. Uniform scaling eventually clamps the short side to one downsampling cell, so the remaining long side still exceeds the budget. The multi-image budget loop can then repeat without reducing the total enough.

## Modifications

After uniform scaling, if the patch product still exceeds the per-image maximum, cap the long side using the remaining capacity and align it to the downsampling grid. Ordinary feasible image sizes keep their existing results.

For example, a 16384×16 image with patch size 16, downsampling factor 2 and a 256-patch limit previously produced 4096×32 pixels (512 patches / 128 image tokens). It now produces 2048×32 pixels (256 patches / 64 image tokens).

## Testing

- Seven new native CPU unittest methods passed with **25 subtests**.
- Restoring the upstream implementation produces **1 failing method and 22 failing subtests**, with 6 completed methods and 3 passing subtests.
- Coverage includes landscape/portrait images, downsampling factors 1/2/4, non-grid limits, two-image prompt budgets, ordinary-size controls and empty/unconstrained budgets.
- Real PIL RGB/grayscale resizing followed by Torch patch aggregation and pixel-unshuffle verifies the pixel allocation and downsampled grid fit the requested budget.
- Full repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

Exact-source validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43408230323

This validates image geometry and preprocessing on CPU, without model inference or quality measurements. Existing behavior for infeasible budgets, such as a maximum smaller than one downsampling cell, is outside this change.

entries.title: [Fix] rotary: Apply CPU offsets once in the native fallback
entries.head: 0828b0d8d3d097f50e15e7b27d6cca75bc955bb1
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

The CPU RoPE entry points add offsets before choosing their backend. Their native fallback then receives both the shifted positions and the same offsets, so it adds the offsets a second time. This changes rotation angles and can index beyond the cache even when the requested position is valid.

## Modifications

Apply the eager position shift only inside the AMX branch. The existing native implementation receives the original positions and offsets and performs its own single shift. This fixes the shared delegation error in the base/linear and DeepSeek rotary implementations.

## Accuracy Tests

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43408946377

- Seven new native CPU test methods passed with **18 subtests**.
- Restoring the original implementation produces **2 failing methods and 14 failing subtests** (pytest reports 16 failures), with 5 completed methods and 4 passing subtests.
- Independent cache-row references cover Neox/GPT-J layouts, FP16/BF16/FP32, linear scaling, DeepSeek layouts, scalar cache-boundary offsets, and zero/absent offsets.
- Real CPU scaled-dot-product attention and input gradients match an independently positioned reference.
- Full repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

The tests select the actual native CPU fallback; they do not replace the RoPE operators. AMX and GPU fused kernels are outside the executed scope.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

This is a correctness fix. No throughput or model-quality improvement is claimed.

entries.title: [Fix] preprocessing: Account for retained buffers in cache budgets
entries.head: 57a8862391bf234f58eb1ccd11d3a540c576d921
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

Preprocessing cache admission currently charges a NumPy view's visible elements and a memoryview's element count. A tiny or empty view can therefore retain a much larger CPU allocation while consuming almost none of the cache's byte budget. Multiple views of the same allocation can also be counted inconsistently.

## Modifications

Follow NumPy base chains and memoryview owners to the retained CPU buffer, including NumPy stride-trick wrappers. Count the measurable owner once through the existing identity set. If a custom array owner exposes no measurable backing buffer, decline automatic admission instead of treating its visible slice as the whole retained allocation.

Existing Torch accounting, explicitly supplied byte sizes, and ordinary owning arrays keep their existing paths.

## Accuracy Tests

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43411501586

- Ten new native test methods plus the existing preprocessing-cache module: **36 passed, 1 existing GPU-dependent skip, and 27 passing subtests**.
- Restoring the original implementation produces **4 failing methods and 18 failing subtests** (pytest reports 22 failures), with 6 completed methods.
- Tests cover sliced, reversed, transposed, broadcast and empty NumPy views; stride-trick wrappers; typed, multidimensional and strided memoryviews; external buffers; shared-owner deduplication; and opaque owners.
- Real cache admission, singleflight completion, and weak-reference eviction checks verify that a small view cannot retain an oversized allocation outside the budget.
- Full repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

This corrects retained-buffer byte accounting. GPU execution, total process RSS bounds, and throughput changes are outside the measured scope.

entries.title: [Fix] layernorm: Follow live parameter dtype
entries.head: ea71bf744ee5b7902dbbe24639f008fd9bba68cb
entries.published_body:
## Motivation

`LayerNorm` caches its constructor dtype, but normal module conversion (`.half()`, `.bfloat16()`, `.double()`, `.float()`, `.to()`) and `load_state_dict(assign=True)` can change its parameter dtype. The stale value then casts inputs to an incompatible dtype and can incorrectly enable a fused backend, causing valid converted modules to fail.

## Modifications

Use the current `weight.dtype` for the native input cast and CUDA/HIP eligibility checks. The output still returns to the input dtype. An unconverted float32 norm retains its existing mixed precision behavior.

Add eight test methods covering public module conversions, mixed input dtype, biasless modules, checkpoint assignment, native SGD updates, and backend fallback eligibility.

## Accuracy Tests

Exact-source native validation: https://github.com/Afloat16/sglang/actions/runs/43401517260

- Linux CPU, with normal repository imports and its actual PyTorch LayerNorm implementation.
- New tests plus existing CPU LayerNorm controls: **12 tests passed, 25 subtests passed**.
- Restoring the original source produces **3 failing methods and 13 failing subtests** (pytest reports 16 failures), with 5 completed methods and 4 passing subtests. These are dtype/dispatch failures after valid module conversion.
- Three native training updates match `torch.nn.LayerNorm` forward values, gradients and parameters.
- Repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed.

The tests check CUDA/HIP fallback eligibility on CPU; they do not execute fused GPU kernels or benchmark model generation.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No throughput or model-quality improvement is claimed. This fixes correctness after parameter dtype conversion.

## Checklist

- [x] Format code with repository pre-commit hooks.
- [x] Add registered CPU regression tests.
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style guidance.
- Documentation: no public API change.
- Accuracy: native LayerNorm and training checks described above.
